passages.text: Summary
Background
COVID-19 continues to show long-term impacts on our health. Limited effective immune-mediated antiviral drugs have been launched.
Methods

We conducted a Mendelian randomization (MR) and colocalization analysis using 26,597 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci (sc-eQTL) to proxy effects of expressions of 16,597 genes in 14 peripheral blood immune cells and tested them against four COVID-19 outcomes from COVID-19 Genetic Housing Initiative GWAS meta-analysis Round 7. We also carried out additional validations including colocalization, linkage disequilibrium check and host–pathogen interactome predictions. We integrated MR findings with clinical trial evidence from several drug gene related databases to identify drugs with repurposing potential. Finally, we developed a tier system and identified immune-cell-based prioritized drug targets for COVID-19.
Findings

We identified 132 putative causal genes in 14 immune cells (343 MR associations) for COVID-19, with 58 genes that were not reported previously. 145 (73%) gene-COVID-19 pairs showed effects on COVID-19 in only one immune cell type, which implied widespread immune-cell specific effects. For pathway analyses, we found the putative causal genes were enriched in natural killer (NK) recruiting cells but de-enriched in NK cells. Using a deep learning model, we found 107 (81%) of the putative causal genes (41 novel genes) were predicted to interact with SARS-COV-2 proteins. Integrating the above evidence with drug trial information, we developed a tier system and prioritized 37 drug targets for COVID-19.
Interpretation
Our study showcased the central role of immune-mediated regulatory mechanisms for COVID-19 and prioritized drug targets that might inform interventions for viral infectious diseases.
Funding
This work was supported by grants from the (2022YFC2505203).
Research in context
Evidence before this study

We searched for key terms in PubMed for publications prior to August 1, 2024, using the following terms: (“COVID-19" or “SARS-CoV-2”) AND (“single-cell eQTL” or “protein” or “transcript”) AND (“Genome-wide association study” or “single-cell Mendelian randomization” or “causal genes”). Our search identified multiple studies that have pinpointed genes or proteins associated with COVID-19. However, there is a notable lack of studies that integrate single-cell eQTLs with Mendelian randomization to systematically investigate the potential causal relationships between immune-related genes and COVID-19 in European populations.
Added value of this study

We systematically evaluated the immune-mediated genes and mechanisms for COVID-19 by combining single-cell eQTL MR and colocalization with pathway and protein–protein interaction information. We identified 343 MR associations for 132 genes in 14 immune-cell types related to four types of COVID-19 outcomes, with 58 genes that, to the best of our knowledge, were not reported previously. NCR3, a gene with robust MR evidence on severe COVID-19, interacted with SARS-COV-2 proteins, and its targeted drug is currently under clinical trials for cancer treatment. We further developed a tier system to prioritize COVID-19 drug targets and identified 37 promising drug target genes that showed multiple layers of evidence.
Implications of all the available evidence
Our study identifies immune-mediated causal genes and mechanisms for COVID-19 and provides a tier system to prioritize immune-related drug targets for COVID-19.
Introduction

The coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic has resulted in nearly 7 million deaths during the past four years (https://covid19.who.int/). Although vaccination against COVID-19 reduces the risk of severe COVID-19 disease and death, the continual emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants with increased transmission and immune evasion has led to breakthrough infections in vaccinated individuals.

Until now, over 700 agents with anti-SARS-CoV-2 mechanisms have been investigated in preclinical and/or clinical studies, with more than 20 anti-SARS-CoV-2 drugs proposed to reduce the risk of severe COVID-19. However, the emergence of drug safety issues, drug resistance, and limited treatment effectiveness have made it imperative to search for new anti-coronavirus drug candidates that are highly specific to one cell type and widely applicable to many people.

Given the strong connections between the immune system and COVID-19, previous studies have extensively investigated the use of immunomodulators, such as systemic corticosteroids, anticoagulants, and cytokine antagonists, to mitigate the dysfunctional responses in patients with COVID-19. Immune cells exhibit diverse states during different stages of infection. In the early stage, the virus enters the body through endothelial cells expressing targets like OAS1 and ACE2. This alters the expression of genes like IFNAR2, affecting cell interactions and downstream gene expression. Consequently, a cascade effect occurs, leading to reduced functionality of natural killer (NK) cells and monocytes/macrophages, as well as coagulation disorders. However, the exact cause of immune cell responses, e.g. NK cell dysfunction, on COVID-19 remains unclear. It is urgently needed to uncover the immune-mediated mechanism and additional drug targets for COVID-19.

Recent studies have shown the value of human genetic evidence in increasing the success rate of drug trials. Existing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified a whole set of genomic loci that are associated with COVID-19. However, the causality of these genes is less clear. Some post-GWAS approaches, such as Mendelian randomization (MR), can estimate the putative causal effects of expression levels of genes and proteins on COVID-19, which have prioritized drug targets, such as OAS1, IL6R, in a cost-effective manner. However, most of the existing studies have used expression data measured in bulk tissues, which may mask the cell-type specific effect of genes and proteins on COVID-19. Advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technology have facilitated the examination of gene expression patterns at the individual cell level. Recent genetic studies have mapped genetic variants with single-cell expression data and identified a list of cell-type specific expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL, which is a genetic variant robustly associated with expression levels of a gene in a certain cell type). Single cell eQTL mapping has proven to be a valuable tool in identifying causal genes and understanding their involvement in disease pathogenesis, including immune diseases and COVID-19 in the Japanese population. However, few studies have integrated single-cell eQTLs with MR to systematically investigate the putative causal relationships between immune-related genes and COVID-19 in other ancestries.

In this study, we conducted a single-cell eQTL MR and colocalization analysis to investigate the putative causal effects of gene expressions from 14 immune cell types on risk of COVID-19 severities. Functional enrichment analysis and predictions of host-pathogen protein interactions were further applied to identify immune-mediated causal genes and networks involved in the pathophysiology of COVID-19. Integrating genetic evidence with clinical trial information, we developed a tier system to prioritize immune-mediated drug targets for COVID-19.
Methods
Ethics

This study did not require ethical approval as all analysis was based on publicly available aggregated statistics without access to individual data. The included GWAS studies obtained informed consent from the study participants and were approved by the relevant local ethics committees.
Instrument selection and validation

In this study, the genetic variants associated with plasma eQTLs were used as genetic instruments for the Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. We started the instrument selection process by accessing the cis-eQTL data from OneK1K data. We selected all conditionally independent cis-eQTLs that were associated with eGenes at a p-value <0.005. To ensure accuracy, we removed highly correlated SNPs by performing linkage disequilibrium (LD) clumping with a clumping r2 cutoff of 0.01. The LD reference panel selected was ‘EUR’. We estimated the strength of the genetic predictors of each instrument using F-statistics. If any eQTLs had F-statistics lower than the widely used threshold of 10, we considered them to have limited power (potentially causing weak instrument bias) and removed these from the MR and follow-up analyses. Weak instrument selection and validation are provided in Supplementary Notes.
Outcome selection

Study design of the Mendelian randomization analysis of immune-cell specific gene expressions on COVID-19. The immune cell specific gene expression data were obtained from single-cell sequencing of the OneK1K participants. The COVID-19 genome-wide association studies were derived from the Genetic Housing Initiative GWAS meta-analysis Round 7.

In the two-sample MR study, GWAS summary statistics of outcome were obtained from the COVID-19 Host Genetic Initiative (HGI) (Round 7, https://www.covid19hg.org/results/r7/) and Long Covid GWAS summary statistics. Data were from European ancestry populations. The sample composition of the four COVID-19 (also shown in Fig. 1) phenotypes and four types of Long Covid were listed in Table S2. Ethical approval was not required for this study since the original GWAS previously received appropriate ethics and institutional review board approval. The number of SNPs for each group of COVID-19 and Long Covid are provided in Table S2.
Single-cell eQTL MR analysis

During the discovery MR analysis, we aimed to estimate the potential causal effects of eGenes at the single cell level on COVID-19 in individuals of European ancestry. To ensure that the genetic signals in the cis-acting region were accurately represented and to increase power, we conducted one of two sets of analyses depending on the number of instruments selected from the exposure. For eGenes with only one eQTL, we utilized the Wald ratio analysis to estimate the effects between eGenes and outcome group. For eGenes with two or more eQTLs, we used the conditional independent eQTLs as genetic instruments and applied a generalized inverse variance weighted (gIVW) approach that considered the correlation between nearby eQTLs. The MR estimates were obtained using the TwoSampleMR R package (github.com/MRCIEU/TwoSampleMR) and were subjected to two thresholds to select MR estimates with good genetic evidence. A Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.05 was applied to select the best MR estimates with robust signals. MR analysis was performed according to the STROBE-MR checklist.

For the definition of novelty of our MR findings, we conducted a comprehensive search of COVID-19 related genes in 10 databases as well as twenty-five COVID-19 associated MR research (Table S3, Table S4, Supplementary Materials, ST1).
Directionality test using MR steiger filtering

A drug that alters disease risk should in theory influence both gene expression and protein levels. To determine the direction of effect of our MR findings, we conducted a directionality test using Steiger filtering. This allowed us to test the directionality of the eQTL-disease associations for all candidate instruments. Any eQTLs flagged by the Steiger filtering as explaining more of the variance in the outcome than the exposure was removed from subsequent MR and follow-up analyses (Table S3, Table S5, Table S7).
Genetic colocalization and LD check analyses

To improve the reliability of MR signals, we conducted three sensitivity analyses for candidate MR signals. Firstly, we used Cochran's Q test for gIVW results to estimate the potential heterogeneity of MR estimates across each eQTL. The results showed that all the gIVW results had limited evidence of heterogeneity (Q-value>0.05). Therefore, we could use these eGenes for the follow-up analyses. The heterogeneity results are listed in the Supplementary Materials.

To distinguish putative causative MR signals from gene–disease pairs confounded by LD, the results that passed the MR corrected p-value (Bonferroni corrected threshold, False discovery rate, FDR) filtering (<0.05) were evaluated using genetic colocalization analysis. For more robust colocalization evidence, we applied two sets of colocalization analyses. First, we developed an approximate colocalization analysis called LD check, which estimated the LD r2 between each eQTL against all variants with GWAS (p < 1 × 10−4) in the region associated with the disease outcomes. Evidence for approximate colocalization was based on an R2 of 0.7 and above between the eQTL and any of the outcome variants.

We then performed genetic colocalization analysis using the ‘coloc’ R package, following conventional methods. To ensure the inclusion of all eQTLs near the phenotype, we expanded the eQTL screening range of each phenotype in the exposure to a range of 100 KB upstream and downstream. A colocalization probability (PP.H4/(PP.H3 + PP.H4) ≥70%) in this analysis indicated a likely colocalization of the two genetic association signals within the test region (Table S3). If any one method passed the test, it could be identified as having a co-localization relationship or a causal effect. Causal genes were confirmed as unreported genes via searches conducted in 10 databases.

Additional methodological details as well as the results of colocalization analysis for multiple causal variants, tissue-specific Mendelian randomization, MR sensitivity analyses, differential gene analysis (DEG), entropy analysis and mediation analysis are provided in Supplementary Notes.
Gene ontology and pathway enrichment analysis

Metascape (version 3.5) is a comprehensive bioinformatics tool that integrates over forty databases. It offers several features such as enrichment analysis of biological pathways, structural analysis of protein interaction networks, and gene annotation capabilities. Cytoscape (version 3.1), is an open-source software platform that allows for the visualization of complex networks and integration with any type of attribute data. In this study, we utilized Cytoscape and Metascape online tools (http://metascape.org/) to analyze the functional enrichment of all identified causal genes (min overlap = 3, p -value cutoff = 0.05, and min enrichment = 1.5). We also used Metascape's combined (all) option for Protein–protein interaction (PPI) analysis (min network size = 3) and visualized the Pathway enrichment results together with PPI results using the ggplot2 R package (R package, ggplot2, v3.4)) and Cytoscape software respectively. The MCODE algorithm was applied to the network to identify neighborhoods where proteins were densely connected. GO enrichment analysis was applied to each MCODE network to extract “biological meanings” from the network component, where the three terms with the smallest p-values were retained.
Enrichment of MR results was conducted via function phyper () with all MR results, all significant MR results, significant MR results in each cell type and MR results in each cell type as values.
Host–pathogen interactome predictions

We used a computational method called ‘DeepHPI’ to predict the host–pathogen network with our putative unreported causal genes and SARS-COV-2 proteins. We used convolutional neural network (CNN) models for the host–pathogen interactions (HPI) prediction process. We also used String (https://string-db.org/) to explore potential relationship with our unreported causal genes and previously identified SARS-COV-2 causal genes. These results were then integrated into a single diagram (Figs. S1 and S2, Tables S8 and S9).
Drug targets prioritization

Most drugs target small-molecule proteins. To identify potential drug targets, we used 132 causal genes from four outcome groups. We integrated our MR findings with clinical trial evidence from OpenTargets, DrugBank, and Drug Gene Interaction database (https://www.dgidb.org/) to identify drugs with repurposing opportunities. The selection of prioritized genes was based on drug targets with current clinical indications for inflammation, respiratory disorders, viral infection and top symptoms from COVID-19 as well as long-COVID.
Role of funders
The funders had no involvement in the design, execution, analysis, or interpretation of the study, nor in the writing or decision to submit the manuscript for publication.
Results
Summary of instrument selection for immune-cell specific gene expressions

In this study, we aimed to select valid instruments using a three-step selection process. We extracted 26,597 independent cis-acting eQTLs associated with expression levels of 16,597 genes in 14 different immune cells (single-cell gene expression data measured in 982 participants from the OneK1K cohort), and used them as candidate genetic instruments for this study (Fig. 1). Given the complexity of single-cell sequencing data, the expression level of a gene in a specific immune-cell type was noted as a gene expression profile of that gene in this study (Supplementary Information: definitions).

CD4 NC: CD4 naïve and central memory T cells; CD8 NC: CD8 naïve and central memory T cells; CD4 ET: CD4+ T cells with an effector memory or central memory phenotype; CD8 ET: CD8+ T cells with an effector memory or central memory phenotype; CD4 SOX4: CD4+ T cells expressing SOX4; CD8 S100B: CD8+ T cells with expression of S100B; NK: natural killer cells; NK R: NK recruiting cells; B IN: immature B cells; B Mem: memory B cells; Mono C: classical monocytes; Mono NC: nonclassical monocytes; DC: dendritic cells; Plasma: plasma cells. (b) Bar plot for statistic results of eGenes (a gene with an eQTL) with their independent eQTLs (the central and the right one) in each cell type from numerous tested samples (left one).

For the instrument selection, we removed highly correlated genetic variants by performing linkage disequilibrium (LD) clumping with a LD r2 cutoff of 0.01. The Europeans from the 1000 Genome project were used as the LD reference panel. After clumping, a total 17,959 independent cis–eQTLs for expression levels of 16,597 genes in 14 cell types were selected (Fig. 2a, Table S1). Second, we calculated F-statistics for each eQTL and excluded 20 eQTLs with F-statistics<10 from further analysis, since they may suffer from potential weak instrument bias. Third, we used Steiger filtering to verify the directionality of the instruments. This approach tested whether an eQTL explained more variance for the exposure (gene expression profile of a gene) than the outcome (COVID-19). All of our cis-eQTLs showed right directionality and were kept as valid instruments (Table S1). In summary, 17,939 eQTLs for expression levels of 16,597 genes in 14 immune cells had been selected as valid instruments for the MR analysis.

Our instruments and eGenes (in which eGene means a gene with one or more eQTLs) were consistently enriched in CD4 naïve and central memory T cells before and after instrument selection (CD4 NC; Fig. 2a and b), where CD4 SOX4 and plasma cells showed the smallest number of instruments and eGenes.
Identification of putative causal genes for COVID-19 infection

We then estimated the putative causal effects of gene expression profiles in 14 immune cell types on COVID-19 outcomes using two-sample MR. Four types of COVID-19 outcome data were extracted from the COVID-19 Genetic Housing Initiative GWAS meta-analysis Round 7 (https://www.covid19hg.org/results/r7/), including “very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 vs. population” (noted as “A2”, N case = 13,769, N control = 1,072,442); “Hospitalized COVID-19 vs. population” (“B2”, N case = 32,519, N control = 2,062,805); “COVID-19 vs. population” (“C2”, N case = 122,616, N control = 2,475,240) and “hospitalized COVID-19 vs. not hospitalized COVID-19” (“B1”, N case = 16,512, N control = 71,321) groups (see “Outcome selection” in Fig. 1). For COVID-19 outcomes, only GWAS summary statistics of participants of European ancestry were used. For “hospitalized COVID-19 vs. not hospitalized COVID-19” (B1), GWAS summary statistics of the European only data were not publicly available, we therefore used data from an admixed population instead, the proportion of which were European was 81% in this data (Table S2).

After harmonizing the exposure data (gene expression profiles of tested genes) and outcome data (COVID-19 outcomes), 14,249–14,485 MR estimates of gene expressions on COVID-19 were calculated for the four types of COVID-19 outcomes respectively (Fig. 3a). Following false discovery rate (FDR) correction, a total of 144, 3, 191 and 40 MR associations (which means association of one gene expression profile against one type of COVID-19 outcome with MR and colocalization evidence, see Supplementary Information: definitions) remained for A2 (“very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 vs. population”), B1 (“hospitalized COVID-19 vs. not hospitalized COVID-19”), B2 (“Hospitalized COVID-19 vs. population”) and C2 (“COVID-19 vs. population”) respectively (Fig. 3a). In order to examine heterogeneity in the MR results, we conducted a Cochran's Q test for 16 MR associations estimated by two or more instruments, which found little evidence to support heterogeneity among instruments (Q-value>0.05). To distinguish causality from confounding by linkage disequilibrium (LD), we applied two colocalization approaches, LD check, genetic colocalization, Susie and SharePro colocalization. These analyses showed that 343 of the 378 (91%) MR associations showed colocalization evidence (defined as colocalization probability ≥70% for colocalization or r2 ≥ 0.7 for LD check; Susie and SharePro colocalization probability>0.9; Fig. 3a, Table S3). These 343 MR associations were related to expressions of 132 genes in 14 immune cell types.

We conducted a comprehensive search of COVID-19 related genes in 10 databases as well as twenty-five COVID-19 associated MR research (Table S3, Table S4, Supplementary Materials, ST1). We found that 58 of the 132 identified genes were not reported before for COVID-19 (Fig. 3a, Table S3).

When comparing MR associations between four COVID-19 outcomes, we found 54 genes showed MR and colocalization evidence in two or more COVID-19 outcomes. One gene, NBEAL2, showed evidence in four COVID-19 outcomes, 12 genes showed evidence in three outcomes, where 41 genes showed evidence in two outcomes (Fig. 3b). As an example, the NBEAL2 gene, showed robust MR and colocalization evidence in all four types of COVID-19 outcomes (Fig. 3c–e). These 54 genes showed associations with two or more COVID-19 outcomes were considered as the replicable genes (Supplementary Information: definitions) connected with COVID-19. Mendelian randomization on Long COVID is provided in Supplementary Notes.
Immune-cell type specific effects of gene expressions on COVID-19 outcomes

Immune-cell type specificity of the top Mendelian randomization findings across four types of COVID-19 outcomes. (a) The whole profiles of all the demonstrated eGenes in cell types and groups. Histogram graph in the external ring represents cell-type combined with groups for all identified eGenes. Chord plot in the middle shows the recurring eGenes in groups connected by gradient lines. (b) Sector bubble chart summaries cell-type and group distribution characteristics of high-frequency (at least occurred in two groups) eGenes. Bar plot on the top represents the total number of occurrences of eGenes in each group from all cell types. Bar plot on the right refers to the total number of eGenes in each cell type with groups. (c) Bar plot shows final proportions of all the putative causal eGenes in groups as well as cell types compared with the figure of exposure.

We further estimated the cell-type specificity of the 132 putative causal genes for COVID-19, which included 343 MR associations (200 gene-COVID-19 pairs) in total. Of them, 145 of the 200 (73%) pairs only showed effects on COVID-19 in one specific immune cell type (Fig. 4a). Similarly, 30 (56%) of the 54 replicable genes (with robust MR evidence in two or more COVID-19 outcomes) showed cell-type specific effects in only one immune cell type (Fig. 4b). In contrast, seven genes showed MR associations in five or more immune cell types, for example TOMM7 expressions in 13 immune cell types were associated with COVID-19. This implied a generalized immune-mediated effect of these genes on COVID-19 (Fig. 4b).

The cell-type specific MR analysis provided some evidence to support CD4 NC cell as an enriched cell type for COVID-19. However, we also observed that CD4 NC had the largest number of eGenes (Fig. 2a and b). We then estimated the ratio between number of identified causal genes versus number of eGenes for each of the 14 immune cell types (Fig. 4c). The results showed that the COVID-19-associated genes were enriched in three immune cell types: natural killer (NK) recruiting, plasma and CD4 SOX4 cells, after adjusting the influence of eGenes' number. In contrast, the figure was de-enriched in some other cell types like NK cells. By using another enrichment method via function ‘phyper’, compared with all the significant MR results and significant cell type MR results, as shown in Supplementary Materials ST5, the figure was consistent with that of from Fig. 4c.
Enrichment of the COVID-19 associated genes in immune-viral related mechanisms

Pathway and gene-set enrichment analysis results of the unreported genes associated with COVID-19 risk. (a) Lollipop chart illustrated representative results of functional enrichment analysis via GO and KEGG for all putative causal genes. The details were listed in Table S11. (b) Circle plot (lower right side) shows protein–protein interaction (PPI) network of all putative causal eGenes via Metascape online. Dot size for each eGene represents the degree of interaction with other genes. The Molecular Complex Detection (MCODE) algorithm was applied to identify tightly connected network components when the network contained 3 to 500 proteins. Four MCODE networks for all genes were collected and shown in the lower left and upper right corners, respectively. Pathway and process enrichment analyses are applied independently to each MCODE component, and the three items with the highest p-value values are retained as characterization, as shown in Table S10.

To explore the immune-mediated mechanisms that were enriched by the identified COVID-19 associated genes, we performed a set of functional enrichment analysis including ontology clusters, pathway analysis, and gene cluster analysis. Among the 132 genes associated with COVID-19, 119 genes could be converted into Entrez gene ID and were included in the enrichment analysis. The results showed that the 119 genes were enriched in pathways such as interferon signalling, cytokine signalling in immune system and interferon alpha/beta signaling (Table S10, “MyList_MCODE_ALL” part), consistent with findings reported in a previous study. The enrichment results could be classified into six types of biological pathways: virus response pathways, immune-inflammatory pathways, cellular process pathways, metabolic process pathways, response to stimulus and disease pathways (Fig. 5a, Table S11). We then performed protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis for the identified causal genes. Among the 119 genes included in this analysis, 15 of their encoded proteins showed little evidence of interaction with any other proteins, leaving 104 protein coding genes for the PPI analysis. 34 of the 104 gene-coding proteins (33%) were further clustered into four modules using Metascape (Fig. 5b).

In light of identifying potential immune-related drug targets for COVID-19, we conducted two analyses. First of all, we searched for drugs that target the 132 identified genes in PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) and in existing drug–gene interaction databases, including OpenTargets, DrugBank and Drug-gene interaction database. This search identified 32 candidate drugs that target 24 of the identified genes (Table 1). The main indications of the 32 drugs were chronic cough, various types of pain (neuropathic, musculoskeletal, and inflammatory), tumour and lipid metabolism abnormalities, which were symptoms that occurred in patients with COVID-19 infection and post-COVID sequalae. 10 of the 24 identified genes were unreported genes that were not reported in any previous studies and 90% of them showed an effect on the severe COVID-19 (“very severe and hospitalized COVID-19 cases” in A2 and B2 groups) and eight genes only showed MR associations in one specific cell type.
Evidence triangulation to prioritize drug targets for COVID-19

Evidence synthesis for the unreported genes and drug targets for COVID-19 risk. (a) All the putative causal genes underwent systematic prioritization using four lines of evidence and were classified into three tiers (Table S17). (b) Causal network of genes in Tier 1–2 and known targets via String (score ≥ 0.7) with their respective evidence results.

Combining the above evidence obtained from this study, the following criteria were used to prioritize promising drug target genes for COVID-19 (Supplementary Information: definitions): (i) the gene showed MR and colocalization to support it as a putative causal gene for COVID-19 and was not reported by previous studies (therefore it has to be an unreported gene, and the gene will get an extra score if it is also a replicable gene); (ii) the unreported gene was enriched in related pathways or included in the four clustered modules; (iii) the gene showed predicted interaction with SARS-COV-2 proteins and/or associations with existing host proteins for COVID-19; (iv) the gene is a druggable gene (either as a target for an existing drug or as a druggable target). For the 58 unreported genes with MR and colocalization evidence to support their causality, we scored and ranked them into three tiers based on the above criteria. 18 genes were ranked as Tier 1 drug targets (overall score ≥1). 23 genes, including 19 protein-coding genes and 4 non-coding genes, were ranked as Tier 2 targets (overall score between 0.35 and 1) and the remaining targets were ranked as Tier 3 targets (Table S17). Except 4 non-coding genes, the remaining 37 Tier 1 and Tier 2 genes were treated as promising drug targets genes for COVID-19 (Fig. 6). Of them, NCR3 was ranked as the top candidate gene with highest score of 2.1, which showed good evidence from all tested criteria. Similarly, EHMT2, RHEB and HSPA1B also showed good evidence from multiple criteria (overall score between 1.85 and 1.95). Additional findings of results are provided in Supplementary Notes.
Discussion

In this study, we systematically evaluated the immune-mediated genes and mechanisms for COVID-19 by combining single-cell eQTL MR and colocalization with pathway and protein–protein interaction information. Through MR and colocalization analyses, we identified 343 MR associations for 132 genes in 14 immune-cell types related to four types of COVID-19 outcomes, with 58 genes that we believe have not been reported before. The MR associations were enriched in some specific immune cell types such as NK recruiting, plasma and CD4 SOX4 cells, but de-enriched in other cell types such as NK cells. Of note, 145 gene-COVID-19 pairs (73%) showed causal effects in one specific immune cell type. We also found two pathways, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) signalling and primary ovarian insufficiency, that were enriched by the genes we identified. By using a deep learning model, we observed 107 causal genes (81%) that were predicted to interact with SARS-COV-2 proteins. We further developed a tier system to prioritize COVID-19 drug targets and identified 37 promising drug target genes that showed multiple layers of evidence like functional enrichment, interactions with SARS-COV-2 proteins and druggability. Collectively, our study identifies immune-mediated causal genes and mechanisms for COVID-19 and provides a tier system to prioritize immune-related drug targets for COVID-19.

Our study provided a comprehensive demonstration of cell-type specificity for the prioritized COVID-19 associated genes. The MR results revealed that 73% of the identified gene-COVID-19 pairs only showed effects on one specific immune cell type. For instance, the MR associations of NBEAL2 and ZNF311 were exclusively identified in CD4 NC cells. Recent studies have showed that NBEAL2 acts as a causal gene for gray platelet syndrome and bovine pigmentation disease, and also regulates the expression of CTLA-4 in conventional T cells and thereby influences the number and status of effector T cells. In conjunction with the pathway enrichment findings and the tissue-specific MR results, it is hypothesized that this gene might impact the inflammatory responses of immune cells through the regulation of granulocyte degranulation. Additionally, considering recent discussions on coagulation issues in COVID-19, NBEAL2 could also play a role in platelet function by influencing the differentiation of myeloid cells. In summary, our study illustrated that cell-type specificity is commonplace for causal genes influencing COVID-19 risk.

The cell type enrichment analysis suggested that the identified genes for COVID-19 were de-enriched in NK cells but were enriched in NK R cells. NK cells in patients with severe COVID-19 exhibit significant phenotypic and functional changes, such as a decrease in number and impaired function, which might partly explain the de-enrichment of NK cells we observed. In addition, our study suggested that most of the causal genes identified in NK recruiting cells were associated with hospitalized COVID-19 cases (B2) and severe COVID-19 cases (A2). Although the role of NK cells in COVID-19 has been summarized before, few studies have linked NK recruiting cells with COVID-19. The distinguished enrichment pattern between NK and NK recruiting cells may suggest that the causal genes may specifically activate NK recruiting cells to fight against SARS-COV-2 infected cells by recruiting other immune cells via cytokine productions, rather than other NK cell functions. Additional functional investigations are warranted for specific immune cell types, such as NK recruiting cells.

Our mediation results (see Supplementary Information) detected a few cell-type eGenes (48 MR associations, accounting for 12%) that could be mediated by smoking (5 MR results) or obesity (48 MR results, BMI was utilized as an indicator of obesity) in their impact on the development of COVID-19 (2–13% mediation proportions), which are consistent with conclusions drawn in previous literature identifies smoking as a significant risk factor for the progression and exacerbation of COVID-19.

More and more research has indicated that COVID-19 infection could lead to damage in multiple systems of the human body. It is noted that the genes identified in the present study and their enriched pathways were also involved in various systems. For instance, the BDNF signalling pathway (including FRS3) is known to play an important role in a variety of neurological diseases, and recent studies have also found that serum BDNF levels were decreased in individuals with COVID-19, which suggests a potential mechanism for immune-cell mediated neurological pathways on COVID-19 infection. MSH5, has been linked to male azoospermia and female primary ovarian failure and is proposed to influence the development and function of the reproductive system by participating in DNA mismatch repair during meiosis. Given the observed disruption of the HPG axis in patients with COVID-19 affecting spermatogenesis and epididymis, our identification of those immune-cell derived reproductive-related genes and pathways might offer some insight into this impairment.

Recent studies have prioritized drug targets for complex diseases using human genetics tools. However, there is still a huge gap between causal genes and promising drug targets for COVID-19. Therefore, we developed a tier system to prioritize drug targets from the 132 COVID-19 associated genes, which combined four pieces of evidence from multiple independent data sources. This approach prioritized 37 genes as the most promising drug targets for COVID-19 (Tier 1 and Tier 2 genes). Among them, NCR3, got the highest score, which showed causal effects on three COVID-19 outcomes (very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 vs. population; Hospitalized COVID-19 vs. population; and COVID-19 vs. population). This gene showed effects in two cell types, CD4 SOX9 and Mono NC. Combining this evidence, NCR3 could be considered as a druggable target with cell-specificity upon different types of COVID-19 severity. The drug targeting of NCR3 is under clinical trial investigation for tumour and tumour metastasis. This finding aligned with our pathway enrichment results, which suggested that NCR3 is related to leukocyte activation and proliferation. Furthermore, emerging studies suggest that COVID-19, particularly severe COVID-19, may serve as a biomarker for tumour formation. We hypothesized that this could be a contributing factor to tumourigenesis, as several of our causal genes were known to be associated with tumours, such as FUBP1, YY1AP1, HLA-A, HLA-C, ICAM3, STK19, RHEB and NOTCH4.

Our study has several limitations. Due to the lack of gene expression data before and after cell activation, we are unable to understand the dynamic causal pattern of our identified genes on COVID-19, which may identify additional causal genes and mechanisms for COVID-19. Second, it is worth noting that due to the smaller number of cases in the Long COVID dataset and COVID-19 outcome B1 (hospitalized COVID-19 vs. not hospitalized COVID-19), we had limited statistical power to identify causal genes in these groups compared with other COVID-19 outcomes. Third, the COVID-19 genome-wide association study data is related to prevalent COVID-19 cases. Thus, the new targets identified in this study might be better suited for COVID-19 prevention. However, it is fully possible that a target for disease prevention can also be a target for disease treatment, such as OAS1 for COVID-19. Therefore, the causal genes identified in this study still require further experimental confirmation and population-based verification to determine their specificity for COVID-19 treatment.

In conclusion, we comprehensively examined the immune-mediated genes and mechanisms across 14 immune-cell types for COVID-19. The tier system we developed supports identification of 37 genes as promising drug targets for COVID-19. Future studies are warranted to understand the causal mechanisms, optimal targets, efficacy and safety of these targets and their potential benefits on preventing and treating COVID-19.

passages.text: Background

Conventional epidemiological studies have reported inconsistent results regarding the potential adverse effects of long-term use of antihypertensive drugs on cancer risk. Nevertheless, evidence of their impact on pancreatic cancer risk is limited and deserves further elucidation.
Methods

We selected genetic variants from the genes encoding the target proteins (angiotensin-converting enzyme, beta-1 adrenergic receptor, and solute carrier family 12 member 3) of the examined antihypertensive drugs as instruments based on expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) studies. Genetic summary statistics of blood pressure and pancreatic cancer were obtained from genome-wide association studies (GWASs) in Europeans and East Asians. Inverse-variance weight and MR-Egger methods were employed to estimate the effect of genetic variations in the drug targets on pancreatic cancer risk, and meta-analysis was used to combine the results from 3 independent datasets. Positive control analysis was conducted by using Wald ratio test to justify the genetic instruments of the drug by demonstrating the expected effect on the blood pressure which has an established causal relationship with the drug of interest.
Results

Genetically proxied ACEIs were associated with lower pancreatic risk (OR = 0.506, 95% CI: 0.284–0.901, P = 0.021; OR = 0.265, 95% CI: 0.094–0.751, P = 0.012; OR = 0.236, 95% CI:0.078–0.712, P = 0.010, respectively) in 3 independent datasets and the combined results were validated in a meta-analysis using a random effects model (OR = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.22–0.64, P < 0.01) or fixed effects model (OR = 0.39, 95% CI: 0.25–0.62, P < 0.01). Other drug targets did not show consistent significant associations with pancreatic cancer risk in all 3 independent datasets.
Conclusions

Our study indicated that genetically proxied therapeutic inhibition of ACE was associated with a lower risk of pancreatic cancer, which may have translational potential in clinical practice. However, further long-term randomized controlled trials and observational studies are needed to clarify the effect of ACEIs on the pancreatic cancer risk.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12885-025-13824-7.
Introduction

Pancreatic cancer (PC) is currently the fastest-growing contributor to cancer-related mortality, causing approximately 62,200 diagnoses and 48,800 deaths in the United States each year. PC is considered the most aggressive cancer, and the main curative options for PC currently include surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. Moreover, cancer patients commonly present with comorbidities, and both the comorbidities and the therapeutic agents may affect tumor biology, which poses a great challenge for cancer therapy and further research.

Hypertension, which affects 30% of adults worldwide, is increasingly becoming a serious public health problem. It is also one of the most common comorbidities among cancer patients. However, there is uncertainty about the impact of antihypertensive therapy on cancer. Several observational studies have shown that long-term use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI)-based antihypertensive drugs has potential adverse effects on cancer, whereas other studies have reported the opposite findings. Furthermore, β-blockers and thiazide diuretics are commonly used antihypertensive agents, as well as ACEIs. A meta-analysis showed that β-blockers increased the risk of skin melanoma, while thiazide diuretics and ACEI antihypertensive drugs were not associated with skin cancer risk. Fewer findings from epidemiological studies on the risk of PC are ambiguous and controversial. Conventional epidemiologic studies are subject to a variety of biases, such as confounders and selection biases, which may affect the accuracy and reliability of results. This approach has some limitations in inferring causality.

Mendelian randomization is an extensively utilized causal inference method in which genetic variants naturally occurring in the genes encoding antihypertensive drug targets can serve as proxies to explore the impact of drug therapy on diseases. Because genetic variants (alleles) are randomly assigned during meiosis, participants in an MR study are ‘randomized’ according to the presence of alleles. Therefore, MR employs a ‘randomization’ method to reinforce the inference of exposure-outcome associations by diminishing potential confounding factors and eliminating reverse causality. Alternatively, MR analyses can exploit the impact of long-term modulation of drug targets on cancer risk. Consequently, MR studies of drug targets can be used to simulate the effects of pharmacological modulation of drug targets in clinical trials and have been used in previous studies to predict the clinical benefits and adverse effects of therapeutic interventions. The evolution of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and molecular mechanism characterization have contributed to a favorable foundation for the implementation of MR studies. At present, no study has comprehensively explored the causal relationship between antihypertensive drugs and PC through MR analysis. The use of MR to investigate drug impact will help clinical doctors make better prescription decisions for patients with comorbidities. Here, we aimed to conduct an MR analysis to investigate the causal association between antihypertensive drugs (ACEIs, β-blockers and thiazide diuretics) and pancreatic cancer based on the genome-wide association study (GWAS) data.
Materials and methods
Study design and data sources

The outline of the study design is shown in Fig. 1. In this particular study, we first selected the target genes of three antihypertensive drugs as previously reported: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, the target of ACE inhibitors), beta-1 adrenergic receptor (ADRB1, the target of beta blockers) and solute carrier family 12 member 3 (SLC12A3, the target of thiazide diuretics). Second, eligible single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from the genes responsible for encoding the target proteins of these antihypertensive drugs were chosen as instrumental variables based on the eQTL dataset. The validity of our MR study relies on the following four assumptions: (I) SNPs are associated with drug target genes; (II) SNPs are not associated with potential confounders; and (III) SNPs can only affect outcomes via drug target genes; and (IV) SNPs are in the range of cis-action of drug target genes (kb = 100). Third, we conducted MR analyses to assess whether there was a causal effect between drug target genes (the exposure) and PC (the primary outcome) in separate datasets and combined the results on 3 different GWAS datasets for PC using fixed and random effects meta-analysis. Finally, we conducted MR for the genetically instrumented antihypertensive drugs and associated them with systolic and diastolic blood pressure (positive control outcomes) to evaluate the validity of the selected genetic instruments.

Overview of the study design. Abbreviations: SNPs, single nucleotide polymorphisms; MR, mendelian randomization; ACE, angiotensin-converting enzyme; ADRB1, beta-1 adrenergic receptor; SLC12A3, solute carrier family 12 member 3

All publicly available exposure and outcome summary data in this study were obtained from the IEU OpenGWAS project (https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/, accessed on December 29, 2023). The patients with PC included in this study are diagnosed by International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes. Specifically, the sample sizes of PC datasets were 476,245(1196 patients, ebi-a-GCST90018893, European ancestry), 196,187 (442 patients, bbj-a-140, East Asian ancestry), and 159,700 (499 patients, ebi-a-GCST90018673, East Asian ancestry). The details on these datasets are listed in Table 1. For more information on the statistical analysis, imputation, and quality control measures, please refer to the original publications. The original GWASs were approved by the relevant institutional review boards and all the participants provided informed consent, therefore our study did not require approval from the ethics committee.

Instrumental variable selection

In the present study, we identified eligible independent significant SNPs (linkage disequilibrium (LD) clumping threshold of r2 = 0.3 with a physical distance threshold of 100 kb; minor allele frequency > 0.01, to ensure the independence of SNP avoiding LD; genome-wide P value < 5 × 10− 8) as instrumental variables from the eQTLs of drug target genes (Assumption I). F-statistic was also used to evaluate the strength of the selected SNPs and SNPs with F-statistic values less than 10 were excluded to reduce weak instrumental bias. Afterwards, with the use of the PhenoScanner database (http://www.phenoscanner.medschl.cam.ac.uk/), SNPs that were associated with confounders or outcomes were removed (Assumptions II and III). Considering that cis-eQTLs were more proximal to the drug target genes in the study, we selected cis-eQTLs within ± 100 kb from each gene’s genome position (Assumption IV). The relevant SNPs were extracted from the GWAS summary data for the outcome variables (pancreatic cancer, systolic blood pressure, and diastolic blood pressure). When harmonizing the exposure and outcome data, palindromic SNPs with intermediate allele frequencies were also removed. Basic information on the selected instrumental variables used to assess the associations of drug targets with PC and systolic and diastolic blood pressure are listed in Tables S1 and S2. The detailed selection process is presented in Table S3.
MR analyses and meta-analysis

We conducted MR analyses using the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method and MR-Egger method to verify the causal relationship between antihypertensive drug targets and the outcome variable (pancreatic cancer). If a single instrumental variable was obtained, the causal effect was estimated by the ratio of genetic associations with PC and drug target genes (Wald ratio test). Random effects IVW was the primary method used when the instrumental variables consisted of multiple SNPs (≥ 4), as it offered more accurate estimates and confidence intervals than did the fixed effects IVW method. The MR-Egger method was used as a supplement to the IVW approach, and it provided a consistent estimate of the causal effect under a weaker assumption—the Instrument Strength Independent of Direct Effect (InSIDE) assumption. The intercept derived from MR-Egger regression was used to detect potential horizontal pleiotropy, and a P value less than 0.05 indicated that horizontal pleiotropy was present. If horizontal pleiotropy was detected, the MR‐Egger results were applied in our analysis. SNP heterogeneity was evaluated using I2 (< 25%: low heterogeneity, 25–50%: moderate, 50–75%: high and > 75%: very high) and Cochran’s Q methods (P < 0.05 as the significance level). We also conducted a sensitivity analysis using leave-one-out analysis. By removing each SNP in turn, the leave-one-out analysis could assess the possibility that a single SNP drives the observed associations. All the analyses above were completed using the TwoSample MR package in R software (version 4.1.0). All tests were at the alpha = 0.05 significance level.

Fixed effects and random effects meta-analyses were performed to assess the pooled causal effects of drug target genes on PC using IVW estimates from the 3 outcome datasets (bbj-a-140, ebi-a-GCST90018673 and ebi-a-GCST90018893). Cochrane Q tests, and I-squared and τ2 statistics were used to test for and quantify between-study heterogeneity. The analyses were conducted using “meta” package in R software (version 4.1.0).
Positive control analysis

The purpose of the positive control analysis is to validate the effectiveness of the selected instrumental variables and statistical methods by examining the causal relationship between drug target genes and known clinical outcomes. In this study, we selected the antihypertensive drug target gene ACE as the target and used blood pressure (including both systolic and diastolic blood pressure) as the positive control outcome, as changes in blood pressure are the expected therapeutic effect of antihypertensive drugs. We used eQTLs of the ACE gene as instrumental variables and employed the Wald ratio method to assess the causal relationship between ACE inhibitors and blood pressure. This approach was used to confirm whether ACE inhibitors reduce blood pressure as expected, thereby demonstrating that the selected instrumental variables and statistical methods effectively reflect the biological effects of targeting ACE in antihypertensive drug therapy.
Results
Instrumental variable selection

By using the method mentioned above, we identified 6 SNPs as proxies for ACE, 45 SNPs as proxies for ADRB1, and 13 SNPs as proxies for SLC12A3 respectively to assess the causal relationship between drug targets and the risk of PC (Table S1). The power calculation is presented in Table S4. Specifically, the mean F statistics of the instruments were 135.74 for ADRB1, 48.08 for SLC12A3, and 51.98 for ACE, indicating that weak instrument bias was unlikely to contribute to the analyses. Furthermore, we identified 1 SNP as genetic instrument in ACE to validate the association between ACE and blood pressure from GWAS data (Table S2). The F statistic of the SNPs was also greater than 10. The detailed characteristics of the included SNPs are presented in Table S5.
Causal association of antihypertensive drugs with PC based on eQTLs data of drug target genes

The causal effect estimates of the MR analyses for the association of drug targets of antihypertensive drugs (ACE, ADRB1, and SLC12A3) with PC are depicted in Fig. 2. Based on GWAS summary datasets, our results demonstrated that inhibition of the genetic proxy ACE was associated with a lower risk of PC (OR = 0.506, 95% CI: 0.284–0.901, P = 0.021, for ebi-a-GCST90018893; OR = 0.265, 95% CI: 0.094–0.751, P = 0.012, for ebi-a-GCST90018673; OR = 0.236, 95% CI:0.078–0.712, P = 0.010, for bbj-a-140). Although inhibition of the genetic proxy ADRB1 was linked to an increased risk of PC by using IVW method (OR = 1.509, 95% CI:1.110–2.049, P = 0.009), the results were inconsistent when MR-Egger was used (OR = 2.052, 95% CI:0.992–4.246, P = 0.079). Notably, no significant association was detected between the genetic proxy SLC12A3 and the risk of PC (P > 0.05). There was no evidence of heterogeneity in the causal association of ACEIs with PC (I²=5%, Cochran’s Q = 1.0577, P = 0.3037) (Table 2).

Causal association analysis of aceis with systolic and diastolic blood pressure (positive control)

To validate the instruments used in our study to proxy ACEI, we pooled summary genetic association data from published GWASs of systolic blood pressure (SBP) (ebi-a-GCST90029011) and DBP (ieu-b-39) using the Wald ratio test (Table 3, Supplemental Fig. 1). ACEIs was associated with lower SBP (OR = 0.919, 95% CI: 0.865–0.976, P = 0.0062). This mean that the genetically proxied serum ACE level per 1-SD decrease may be associated with a 0.919 mmHg decrease in SBP. Similarly, SNPs for ACE was associated with lower diastolic blood pressure (DBP) (OR = 0.373, 95% CI: 0.222–0.627, P = 0.0002), indicating that 1-SD decrease in the serum ACE level was associated with a 0.373 mmHg decrease in DBP. In summary, positive control analyses confirmed that the selected genetic instruments for ACEI were effective.

Discussion

This is the first MR study to evaluate the potential impact of antihypertensive drugs on PC. We employed genetic variants mimicking antihypertensive drug targets to investigate their respective effects on PC risk. The results showed that genetically proxied ACEIs were associated with lower PC risk. In contrast, such an association was not observed with other antihypertensive drugs. To ensure a strong association between the instrumental variables and the exposure, we applied a stringent threshold for SNPs selection, which consequently resulted in a limited number of SNPs included in the analysis. However, we implemented a positive control analysis, which served to validate the credibility and robustness of the selected instruments. These findings were validated by multiple MR approaches and different independent datasets, which exhibited reliability and consistency. The heterogeneity statistics showed no significant across the datasets. This suggests that the effect sizes observed in the different studies are consistent and that the datasets are sufficiently homogeneous for the purposes of our analysis. The absence of significant heterogeneity strengthens the validity of our findings, as it indicates that the observed associations are unlikely to be influenced by substantial differences in study design or population characteristics across the included datasets.

Regarding the carcinogenic potential of antihypertensive drugs, prior studies have yielded somewhat controversial results. An early observational study reported that long-term use of ACEIs may protect against cancer. Two subsequent meta-analyses based on randomized trials revealed no consistent evidence that antihypertensive medication use had any effect on cancer risk, although an increased risk of cancer resulting from the combination of ACEIs and ARBs or calcium channel blockers cannot be ruled out. However, one recent study suggested that cessation of antihypertensive medications was associated with PC diagnosis in the next 2 years. All of the above results imply that the connection between antihypertensive drugs exposure and the risk of cancer is so inconsistent. The interpretation of these findings is complicated by the variable duration of drug use, and the heterogeneous effects of prescriptions.

A previous MR analysis have investigated the association between antihypertensive drugs and risk of 4 common cancers (breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancer), which suggested that genetically proxied long-term ACE inhibition was associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer in the European population.

However, the prior MR analysis has not reported results separately for PC. Our study is the first to indicate the potential protective role of AECIs on PC at a causal level. To date, the evidence indicating the association between ACEIs and the risk of PC is limited. One conventional observational study have demonstrated no association between the use of ACEI and PC risk in patients with chronic pancreatitis, and another study showed that ACEI medication was not associated with a decreased risk of PC compared to other antihypertensive drugs. The discrepancy between these two findings and our conclusion can be explained by the heterogeneous study population and comparator groups. Notably, a multicenter retrospective study revealed that ACEIs might slow the progression of branch-duct intrapapillary mucinous neoplasms (BD-IPMNs), which are considered as precursor lesions of PC. These real-world data present modest evidence of the preventative effect of ACEIs on PC.

In terms of beta blockers, several observational studies and experimental studies have confirmed the latent therapeutic effect of these agents on PC. However, evidence exploring the causal association between beta blockers and PC risk is rather limited. Our results on beta blockers showed no association with PC risk, which contradicts the findings of a nested case‒control study showing the preventive effect of beta-blockers on PC. This may be attributed to the inflated effect of observational studies caused by immortal time bias. To our knowledge, there is no prior research on the impact of thiazide diuretics on PC risk. Our study also did not reveal a causal effect of thiazide diuretics on PC risk. However, some studies have suggested that thiazide diuretics can lead to hyperglycemia and diabetes. Therefore, further clinical studies with long-term follow up are needed. In summary, when treating high-risk PC patients (e.g., chronic pancreatitis patients and diabetic patients) with antihypertensive drugs, ACE inhibitors may be a potential option to consider.

The underlying mechanisms responsible for the association between genetically proxied ACE inhibition and PC risk remain unknown. Actually, the MR analysis primarily examines the causal relationship between genetically proxied ACE inhibition and PC risk, without elucidating the specific molecular pathways involved. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms may be postulated in light of the current evidence. Two meta-analyses showed that ACEI treatment more effectively improved insulin sensitivity. These ameliorative effects may be partially mediated by the bradykinin system. This might decrease the risk of the initiation and development of PC driven by hyperinsulinemia. Second, ACEIs appear to act as modulators for receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) axis. Several studies have revealed that ACEIs can increase the level of soluble RAGE (sRAGE), which serves as an anti-inflammatory factor to neutralize advanced glycation end products(AGEs) and block the inflammatory response mediated by RAGE activation. Furthermore, AGEs can form endogenously through normal physiological metabolism or exogenously from environmental exposure (e.g., common foods and tobacco smoke). Consequently, ACEIs likely abolish chronic inflammation triggered by the RAGE axis, which has been demonstrated to be associated with pancreatic carcinogenesis in observational and experimental studies. Moreover, Fendrich et al. demonstrated that angiotensin II type 1 receptor (AT1) was not detected in normal pancreatic tissue except in blood vessels, but its expression became stronger in pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) and PC. Using a genetically engineered mouse model of PC, they provided the first evidence that an ACEI (enalapril) might be a promising chemopreventive agent by delaying the progression of PanINs and partially inhibiting the formation of murine PC. The possible mechanisms may be related to the downregulation of VEGF and NF-kB, but regretfully, no further mechanism has been elucidated. Additionally, there are no current studies investigating which biological processes and pathways the corresponding SNPs may be involved in, thereby potentially reducing the risk of pancreatic cancer. Further basic research is needed to explore these mechanisms.

Leveraging large-scale genetic data, our study has several strengths. First, we employed an MR design to make causal inferences, eliminating confounding bias and reverse causality. This includes confounding the environmental and lifestyle variables of users, which cannot be completely adjusted for an observational study. Second, we specifically selected SNPs from the range of cis-actions of drug target genes (kb = 100) as instruments that may be linked to gene function or expression. Moreover, we only kept only genetic variants with an F statistic > 10 to reduce weak instrumental bias. Finally, we conducted a positive control analysis that predicted the impact of antihypertensive drugs on the anticipated indications and additional defined outcomes to demonstrate the validity of the chosen genetic instruments. In conclusion, this study supports the idea that targeting ACE can reduce the risk of PC. However, randomized trials need to be conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the prevention of PC.

There are several limitations to this study. The properties of MR analysis limit its ability to investigate the long-term and on-target (i.e., target-mediated) effects of therapeutic drugs. Therefore, the effects that we have estimated may not fully reflect the association between ACEI medication and PC. Moreover, the possibility that ACEIs alter PC risk via other gene targets (off-target effects) cannot be excluded. Second, there was a considerable overlap between the two-sample GWAS data from the UK Biobank, and potential ‘healthy volunteer’ bias persisted. Third, our results were inferred by using data from the entire study population and we did not perform further stratification by age and sex or additional subgroup analysis. Fourth, horizontal pleiotropy could not be completely excluded despite various sensitivity analyses being conducted to assess the assumptions of the MR study. Fifth, the study lacks clinical real-world data validation and therefore serves merely as a hypothesis-generating basis for subsequent studies, which may involve clinical trials or observational cohort studies to validate these associations. Consequently, confirmatory evidence from long-term follow-up of clinical trials is warranted.
Conclusion

The present study indicated a protective effect of genetically proxied ACEIs on PC risk in both European and East Asian populations. This study supports the repurposing of antihypertensive medication in the field of comorbidity treatment and PC chemoprevention. Further studies should be conducted to confirm the effects and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved.

passages.text: Background

Although several preclinical and epidemiological studies have shown that blood lipids and lipid-lowering drugs can reduce the risk of breast cancer, this finding remains controversial. This study aimed to explore the causal relationship between dyslipidemia,lipid-lowering drugs, and breast cancer. We also aimed to evaluate the potential impact of lipid-lowering drug targets on breast cancer.
Method

Data of 431 lipid- and lipid-related phenotypes were obtained from genome-wide association study (GWAS), and mendelian randomization (MR) analyses were performed using two independent breast cancer datasets as endpoints. Genetic variants associated with genes encoding lipid-lowering drug targets were extracted from the Global Lipid Genetics Consortium. Expression quantitative trait loci data in relevant tissues were used to further validate lipid-lowering drug targets that reached significance and combined with bioinformatics approaches for molecular expression and prognostic exploration. Further mediation analyses were performed to explore potential mediators.
Result

In two independent datasets, phosphatidylcholine (18:1_0:0 levels) was associated with breast cancer risk (discovery: odds ratio (OR) = 1.255 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.120–1.406]; p = 8.936 × 10–5, replication: OR = 1.016 [95% CI, 1.003–1.030]; p = 0.017), HMG- CoA reductase (HMGCR) inhibition was genetically modeled and associated with a reduced risk of breast cancer (discovery: OR = 0.833 [95% CI 0.752–0.923], p = 5.12 × 10–4; replication: OR = 0.975 [95% CI 0.960–0.990], p = 1.65 × 10–3). There was a significant MR correlation between HMGCR expression in whole blood and breast cancer (OR = 1.11 [95% 1.01–1.22] p = 0.04). Bioinformatics analysis revealed that HMGCR expression higher in breast cancer tissues than in normal tissues, along with poor overall survival and relapse-free survival, and was associated with multiple immune cell infiltration. Finally, the mediation analysis showed that HMGCR inhibitors affected breast cancer through different immune cell phenotypes and C-reactive protein levels.
Conclusion

In this study, we found for the first time that phosphatidylcholine (18:1_0:0) levels are associated with breast cancer risk. We found that HMGCR inhibitors are associated with a reduced risk of breast cancer, and part of their action may be through pathways other than lipid-lowering, including modulation of immune function and reduction of inflammation represented by C-reactive protein levels.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s12672-025-02041-0.
Introduction

Breast cancer (BC) is one of the most common malignancies worldwide, and the most common malignancy in women. In 2020, over 2.3 million women were diagnosed with BC globally, with 685,000 deaths. Circulating lipids play an important role in endocrine tumors by enhancing cell proliferation and migration. However, owing to the influence of confounding factors in clinical studies, current evidence of the relationship between circulating lipids and BC risk is conflicting. Lipid-lowering drugs are commonly used to prevent cardiovascular diseases and may improve cardiovascular outcomes. Drug pleiotropy has led to the use of lipid-lowering drugs for a variety of diseases, and their relationship with oncological diseases has been extensively studied. Preclinical data have shown that lipid-lowering drugs attenuate the inflammatory response, inhibit the proliferation of cancer cells, and inhibit the progression and micrometastasis of BC. Lipid-lowering drugs also reduce BC recurrence and have a protective effect on prognosis. However, there is limited evidence from previous observational clinical studies showing that lipid-lowering drugs are associated with the risk of BC development.

Lipid-lowering drugs are widely used to prevent hyperlipidemia, atherosclerosis, and cardiovascular diseases. During BC treatment, patients are prone to dyslipidemia, especially during endocrine therapy. For example, tamoxifen, letrozole, and other drugs may affect the blood lipid levels of patients with BC to varying degrees and increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases and metabolic syndrome. Therefore, the relationship between lipid-lowering drugs and BC needs to be clarified. Clarifying the relationship between lipid-lowering drugs and BC is not only of scientific research significance but also of practical significance for the prevention and prognosis of BC. In a multicenter cohort study involving 7528 white women in the United States, participants who used lipid-lowering drugs had a significantly lower risk of BC than those who did not.These findings reveal the potential application of lipid-lowering drugs in the prevention of BC. However, long-term use of lipid-lowering drugs was not associated with BC risk in an analysis of the Cancer Prevention Study II Nutrition Cohort based on a 10-year follow-up period. This inconsistency in the results of these studies may be because of the complex polygenic and multifactorial nature of BC, which cannot be completely overcome by observational and traditional analyses.

There are limitations to clinical studies that lead to biased results, such as confounding factor interference and reverse causality interference, ethical issues in the design of experiments with limited observation times, and potential adverse effects that may result from prolonged administration of the drug to the subjects. Owing to the increasing popularity of genome-wide association studies (GWAS), mendelian randomization (MR), an epidemiological method that avoids confounding and reverse causation through the use of genetic variation in a population, may be an effective way to overcome the above problems.This is similar to a randomized controlled trial in which participants are randomly assigned to either the experimental or control group. Simultaneously, MR is not subject to reverse causation because the genetic variation remains constant throughout life. It can also predict drug effects based on mutations in risk factors or drug target genes as tools. This provides preliminary evidence of causality to inform subsequent intervention studies, drug monitoring, and public health approaches. MR studies have been widely used in rheumatic, neurological, and oncological diseases.

The widespread use of lipid-lowering drugs in the treatment of cardiovascular diseases has raised concerns regarding their potential association with the risk of BC. The urgency and importance of studying the relationship between circulating lipids, lipid-lowering drugs, and BC risk are self-evident.In this study, health management for the patient, doctor decision-making, and public health policy are of great significance, and we analyzed the influence of the characteristics of BC and discussed the lipid-lowering drug targets for BC subtypes and their potential impact.
Materials and methods
Study design

We first assessed the causal association of 431 lipid and lipid-related phenotypes with BC using two-sample MR analysis. We then performed MR analyses of 9 commonly used lipid-lowering drug targets with BC and summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) analyses of important lipid-lowering drug targets to validate the results, followed by the application of multiple bioinformatics methods to analyze lipid-lowering drug targets and mediation analyses to explore potential mediators.

Outline of the study design. LDL-C low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, TG triglyceride, HMGCR HMG-CoA reductase, NPC1L1 Niemann-Pick C1-like protein 1, PCSK9 proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9, ABCG5 ATP-Binding Cassette Subfamily G Member 5, ABCG8 ATP-Binding Cassette Subfamily G Member 8; APOB Apolipoprotein B-100, LDLR LDL Receptor, ANGPTL3 angiopoietin-like 3; APOC3 Apolipoprotein C-III, LPL lipoprotein lipase

There are three basic assumptions behind the MR approach: (1) genetic variation and exposure are closely related ("correlation"); (2) genetic variation is independent of confounders affecting the relationship between exposure and outcome ("independence"); and (3) genetic variation only influences outcome through exposure of interest of exposure ("exclusion restriction") affecting outcome. This study followed the enhanced reporting of observational studies in the Mendelian epidemiology guidelines for randomized reporting (Table S1). Figure 1 presents an outline of the study flow. Data sources were based on publicly available summary-level data from the GWAS study and expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) study, which were desensitized before uploading and did not involve personal privacy or identifiable information. This study did not involve confidential information and data and informed consent authorization of the institution; thus, no approval from the ethical review board was required. The details of these datasets are presented in Table S2.
GWAS data sources of exposure

A total of 431 lipid and lipid-related phenotypes were used as exposures (Table S3-S7), of which 179 lipids were obtained from a study published in 2023 that provided pooled GWAS data for each metabolite, with sample sizes ranging from 5172 to 7174. Furthermore, 249 lipids and lipid-related profiles were obtained from a study published in 2022. In this study, sample sizes ranged from 110,051 to 115,082 for the different metabolites. Finally, GWAS summary statistics for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), total cholesterol (TC), and triglycerides (TG) were obtained from a GWAS meta-analysis conducted by the Global Lipids Genetics Consortium, a program with sample sizes ranging from 173,082 to 187,365.
GWAS data sources for outcomes

Summary statistics for outcomes were obtained from two separate GWAS datasets from the Breast Cancer Association Consortium (BCAC) and UK Biobank (UKB). The primary outcome was BC, and the secondary outcomes were the subtypes of BC, including (estrogen receptor (ER)-positive and ER-negative). The BCAC is an international collaborative project initiated in 2005 to study genetic susceptibility to BC and includes 122,977 female cases and 105,974 female controls of European origin. In the BCAC, BC cases were mainly from hospitals and cancer registries. To replicate the primary outcome analyses, we obtained another BC GWAS dataset from the UK Biobank, which included 13,879 cases and 198,523 controls, all of whom were of the European origin38. Previous studies have described the study designs, participants, and quality control (QC) methods in detail.
Data filtration and genetic instrument selection

In our analysis of lipids and BC risk, we set an inclusion threshold for single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) (p < 5 × 10–8), in addition to an r2 threshold of 0.001 to prevent linkage disequilibrium (LD) and a distance of 10,000 Kb for SNPs. The strength of each genetic variant was assessed using F-statistical analysis (calculated as F = β^2 / SE^2, where β is the allelic effect value and SE is the standard error) to test the hypothesis of correlation. Typically, an F-statistic > 10 indicates the absence of weak instrumental bias.
