passages.text: Common lipid-lowering drugs and novel therapies include statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, bile acid sequestrants, mipomersen, fibrates, angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3) inhibitors, and antisense oligonucleotides targeting apolipoprotein C-III (APOC3) mRNA (Table 1). The DrugBank database (https://go.drugbank. com/) and related studies were used to identify the genes encoding the pharmacological targets of these drugs. Based on their primary pharmacological effects, these target genes were further categorized into low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-C lowering target genes (LDL receptor (LDLR), HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR), Niemann-Pick C1-like protein 1 (NPC1L1), PCSK9, apolipoprotein B-100 (APOB), ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters G5 (ABCG5) and G8 (ABCG8)), and TG-lowering target genes (lipoprotein lipase (LPL), ANGPTL3, and APOC3) (Table 1).

For the selection methodology of genetic variation tools, we referred to previous similar studies. In a GWAS meta-analysis by the Global Lipids Genetics Consortium, SNPs identified within the corresponding genes (± 100 kb of the gene location) and strongly associated with LDL-C or TG levels in a genome-wide sense (p < 5 × 10–8), clustered further to an LD threshold of r2 < 0.30 and a physical distance threshold of 100 kb, were selected as proxies for lipid-lowering drug targets. Owing to the proximity of the ABCG5 and ABCG8 genes (ABCG5: chr2:44,039,611-44,065,978 [ensembl]; ABCG8: chr2:44,066,110-44,105,605 [ensembl]), variants near these genes were combined in our analysis. Nine drug targets were identified: i.e. HMGCR, NPC1L1, PCSK9, APOB, ABCG5/ABCG8, LDLR, ANGPTL3, APOC3, and LPL (Table S8).

For drug targets important for BC risk in the MR analysis, we used eQTLs available for drug target genes as proxies for exposure to each lipid-lowering drug target. eQTLs were obtained at the summary level from the eQTLGen consortium (https://www.eqtlgen.org/) or the GTEx consortium V8 (https://gtexportal.org/), the details of which are provided in Table S2. We identified common (minor allele frequency [MAF] < 1%) SNPs of eQTLs significantly associated with HMGCR expression in blood as well as NPC1L1 expression in adipose tissue (p < 5.0 × 10–8), and only cis-eQTLs were included in the present study to generate the genetic instrumentation, which were defined as encoding eQTL within 1 Mb on either side of the gene.
Survival analysis

The Kaplan–Meier plotter database (http://kmplot.com) is a survival analysis tool that integrates data from public databases, including GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus), EGA (European Genome-phenome Archive), TCGA (The Cancer Genome Atlas), and other public databases for breast cancer (BC) patients. This tool can be used to assess disease progression. The 'mRNA gene chip' module was employed to investigate the prognostic value of HMGCR in BC.
TME and immune cell infiltration

We calculated the tumor microenvironment (TME) scores for the BC samples using the ‘estimate’ package. We then compared these differences based on HMGCR expression levels. Using the single sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) algorithm available in the R package—GSVA, we evaluated 24 immune cells in the BC tissue samples and assessed the correlation between HMGCR expression and them using the spearman analysis using the ‘ggplot2’ package. We used the ‘ggplot2’ and ‘pheatmap’ packages to visualize the correlations.
Statistical analysis

In analyses where only a single SNP was available for the construction of instrumental variables, the Wald ratio method was used to derive MR estimates. If multiple SNPs were available to construct instrumental variables, the inverse variance weighting (IVW) method was used as the primary analysis method, because it provided the most accurate and robust estimates.
To validate the selection of genetic variants as drug targets, positive control analyses were performed using coronary artery disease (CAD) as the endpoint.

We also performed a series of sensitivity analyses owing to their resilience to violations of certain assumptions underlying the MR study. Heterogeneity and multivalence among the SNPs were assessed using Cochran's Q test and the MR-Egger intercept test. For MR sensitivity analyses, multiple validity residuals and outliers (MR-PRESSO) were used to reduce the bias caused by correlation level pleiotropy. A significance level of p < 0.005 (0.05/9) using Bonferroni correction was used to adjust for multiple testing of the nine drug targets. For the other analyses, the observed 2-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses described above were performed using 'TwoSampleMR, 'MRPRESSO' in R (version 4.3.0).

As lipid-lowering drugs have anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, and these two properties are closely related to the development of BC, we used a "two-step MR" approach to conduct mediation analysis to explore whether there is a mediating effect (exposure-mediator-outcome pathway) between lipid-lowering drug targets and BC. We used the "coefficient product" method to evaluate the indirect effect of each potential mediator, the effect of lipid-lowering drug targets on BC risk, and the proportion of mediators.
Results
Lipid traits and BC risk

In the discovery dataset, we identified two lipid traits that were causally associated with BC (p < 1.31 × 10–4) and an increase in the level of the phosphatidylcholine (18:1_0:0) was associated with BC risk (odds ratio (OR) = 1.255 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.120–1.406]; p = 8.936E−05), a finding that was similarly confirmed by the replication cohort (OR = 1.016 [95% CI, 1.003–1.030]; p = 0.017). An increase in associated HDL_C levels was associated with an elevated BC risk (OR = 1.170 [95% CI 1.082–1.264]; p = 7.877E−05). In the replication dataset, this finding was not significant (OR = 1.000 [95% CI, 0.991–1.008]; p = 0.949). The comprehensive MR analysis results for lipid traits are presented in the supplementary tables (S9-S10), while the results of the heterogeneity and pleiotropy tests are detailed in the supplementary tables (S11-S12).
Lipid-lowering drug targets and BC risk

Association between genetically proxied drug targets and the risk of breast cancer. Forest plot of the association between a 1-mmol/L (LDL-C, 38.7 mg/dL; TG, 88.9 mg/dL) change in the lipid levels of nine lipid-lowering drug targets with breast cancer risk in the discovery dataset (A), and breast cancer risk in the replication dataset (B). Data are represented as ORs with 95% confidence intervals (error bars). An OR of < 1.00 suggests a decreased risk of disease associated with lipid-lowering drug treatment. Associations are significant after correcting for multiple testing (9 genes, p < 0.05/9). LDL-C low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, TG triglycerides, OR odds ratio, HMGCR HMG-CoA reductase, NPC1L1 Niemann-Pick C1-like protein 1, PCSK9 proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9, APOB Apolipoprotein B-100, ABCG5 ATP-Binding Cassette Subfamily G Member 5, ABCG8 ATP Binding Cassette Subfamily G Member 8; LDLR LDL Receptor, ANGPTL3 angiopoietin-like 3, APOC3 Apolipoprotein C-III; LPL, lipoprotein lipase

In the discovery dataset, HMGCR target inhibition was significantly associated with a lower risk of BC (OR = 0.83 [95% CI 0.752–0.923], p = 5.12 × 10–4) (Fig. 2A). In the replication dataset, we validated this finding (OR = 0.97 [95% CI 0.960–0.990] p = 1.65 × 10–3) (Fig. 2B). In the discovery dataset, NPC1L1 target inhibition was significantly associated with a reduced risk of BC (OR = 0.72 [95% CI 0.575–0.903], p = 4.55 × 10–3), but analyses obtained from the dis replication dataset showed the opposite trend (OR = 1.05 [95% CI 1.024–1.078], p = 1.63 × 10–3) (Fig. 2A, B). PCSK9 target inhibition was significantly associated with a reduced risk of BC in the discovery dataset (OR = 0.90 [95% CI 0.842–0.969], p = 4.55 × 10–3), but this observation was not validated in the replication dataset (OR = 0.99 [95% CI 0.986–1.002], p = 0.20) (Fig. 2A, B). Results for the other five lipid-lowering drug targets (APOB, ABCG5/ABCG8, LPL, ANGPTL3, and APOC3) failed to be corrected by p-value (Fig. 2A, B). Cochran's Q test with the MR-Egger intercept test did not reveal evidence of heterogeneity or multiplicity, which strengthened the causal inference of exposure and outcomes (Tables S13 and S14). Further analyses showed that HMGCR target inhibition was primarily associated with a reduced risk of ER-positive BC (OR: 0.84 [95% CI 0.743–0.949], p = 0.005), and the results of the analyses in the ER-negative BC dataset were not significant (p = 0.07) (Table S15). The positive control studies have demonstrated a clear association between the exposure levels of each drug and coronary heart disease, further validating the effectiveness of the selected genetic instruments (Table S16).
Gene expression and BC risk

The results of the target analyses were validated using the SMR approach. Results revealed that a 1-SD increase in blood tissue HMGCR expression was associated with a higher risk of BC (OR = 1.11 [CI 95% 1.01–1.22] p = 0.04). Furthermore, given the inconsistent findings on the relationship between enhanced genetic variation in NPC1L1 and BC risk, we further explored this relationship using NPC1L1 expression in adipose tissue; however, the analysis was not significant (OR = 1.04 [CI 95% 1.00–1.08] p = 0.07) (Table S17). The analysis of PCSK9 in blood tissue and breast cancer did not yield statistically significant results (OR = 1.00 [CI 95% 0.93–1.08] p = 0.92).

First, we obtained the expression profiles of HMGCR in 33 human tumors from the TIMER2.0 database (http://timer.comp-genomics.org/timer/) and found that HMGCR was aberrantly expressed in many types of human tumors, including BC, indicating that HMGCR is a tumor-associated gene (Fig. 3A). We compared the expression profile of HMGCR in BC tissues with that in normal tissues and found that HMGCR expression was significantly increased in BC. The immunohistochemistry data presented in Fig. 3E are derived from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA). The results demonstrate an increase in HMGCR expression compared to the control group. However, as no statistical analyses were conducted, it was not possible to ascertain whether this increase reached a statistically significant level (Fig. 3B). We then performed survival analyses based on survival time and HMGCR expression profiles in the Kaplan–Meier Plotter database (http://kmplot.com/analysis/), which showed that a high HMGCR expression group was associated with a poorer prognosis for patients (Fig. 3C, D). Overall, HMGCR expression was elevated in BC tissues, indicating a poor prognosis.

The results showed a negative correlation between HMGCR and immune status in the IS and ESTIMATE scores (Fig. 3E). subsequently We investigated the relationship between immune cell infiltration and HMGCR expression profiles and found that HMGCR expression was associated with various immune cell infiltrations (Fig. 4A, B). Mediation analysis

Considering that differential expression of HMGCR targets was significantly associated with multiple immune cell infiltrations, it is reasonable to speculate that inhibitors of HMGCR targets may lead to a reduced risk of BC by altering immune function. Further analyses were performed to explore potential mediators between inhibitors of HMGCR targets and BC causality. We performed mediation analyses of 731 immune cell phenotypes using GWAS data as mediators. The GWAS Catalog (GCST90001391–GCST90002121) summarizes the GWAS statistics for each immune characteristic. It contains comprehensive data collected from 3757 Europeans and consists of 731 immune phenotypes.

Our analysis showed that HMGCR-targeting inhibitors were positively associated with 61 immune cell phenotypes (OR > 1, p < 0.05) and the remaining significant 52 traits were negatively associated with HMGCR-targeting inhibitors (OR < 1, p < 0.05) (Table S18). Subsequently, in our MR analysis of immune cell phenotypes and BC, we found that 18 phenotypes were positively associated with the risk of BC (OR > 1, p < 0.05), and 22 immune cell phenotypes were associated with a reduced risk of BC (OR < 1, p < 0.05) (Fig. 5A, B) (Table S19). In subsequent calculations, the HMGCR target inhibitors were shown to be effective in modulating three immune cell phenotypes (including " IgD + CD38 + B cell Absolute Count " (mediation proportion: 7.72%), "Transitional B cell Absolute Count" (mediation proportion: 12.3%), "HLA DR on CD33- HLA DR + " (mediation proportion: 9.99%)) to reduce the risk of BC.

GWAS data for 91 circulating inflammatory proteins were summarized from a meta-analysis including 14,824 participants of the European descent from 11 independent cohorts (accession numbers GCST90274758 to GCST90274848). Furthermore, we added C-reactive protein (CRP), a commonly used inflammatory marker, as it was not included in this study. The results showed that HMGCR inhibitors had a positive causal relationship with eight inflammatory factors (OR > 1, p < 0.05) and a negative causal relationship with 12 inflammatory factor phenotypes (OR < 1, p < 0.05) (Table S20). Further analysis suggested that five inflammatory factor phenotypes were positively causally associated with BC and eight inflammatory factor phenotypes were negatively causally associated with BC (Fig. 5C, D) (Table S21). We found that only CRP level (mediation ratio: 7.42%) had a significant mediating effect.
Discussion

In this study, we first performed a MR analysis of 431 lipid and lipid-related phenotypes in relation to BC and found that phosphatidylcholine (18:1_0:0) levels were positively correlated with the risk of BC. Subsequently, In the drug-target analysis, HMGCR was identified as a drug target that significantly reduces the risk of BC. This finding was validated using different methods for constructing genetic instruments and two independent BC datasets. Our study provides strong evidence that HMGCR is a promising drug target for reducing the risk of BC, particularly ER-positive BC.

By integrating multiple bioinformatics methods, we performed further exploratory analyses to identify the biological functions and potential regulatory mechanisms of HMGCR in BC.We found that the expression level of HMGCR was upregulated in BC, high expression of HMGCR was correlated with poorer overall survival(OS) and relapse-free survival(RFS) in BC, and the expression level of HMGCR was correlated with a variety of immune-infiltrating cells. Based on this finding, we conducted a mediation analysis and found that HMGCR inhibitors reduced the risk of BC by affecting a variety of immune cell phenotypes and regulating CRP levels.

The effects of elevated LDL-C, TG, and TC levels on the risk of total and ER-positive BCs were markedly heterogeneous according to the study design, menopausal status, and subject body mass index. Regarding the inherent bias of residual confounding and reverse causation in observational studies, MR is an increasingly used methodology that uses genetic variants as instrumental variables to draw definitive conclusions regarding the causality of the association between exposure and disease. MR takes advantage of the random assignment of genetic alleles affecting exposure, which can avoid reverse causality bias and minimize confounding by other determinants in a manner similar to that of randomized controlled trials. In this study, we minimized the bias caused by observational study confounders. The results of previous MR studies have been controversial and we adopted a more rigorous analytical strategy using two independent GWAS datasets for validation. Based on the available evidence, we found that LDL-C, TG, and TC may not be considered causative risk factors for BC, implying that LDL-C, TG, and TC levels do not independently affect BC, which is consistent with the results of previous MR and observational studies. Meanwhile, we found for the first time that phosphatidylcholine (18:1_0:0) levels were associated with BC risk using GWAS data from 428 liposomes.

Compared with a previous MR study reported by SUN, we used two independent sets of GWAS results data and further validated them using SMR analysis to extend the analysis to nine common lipid-lowering drug targets. The results of this study support the idea that HMGCR inhibitors can reduce the risk of BC, and HMGCR inhibitors may be recommended to reduce the incidence of BC, especially ER-positive BC, in women with hyperlipidemia. This is consistent with the results of a multicenter prospective cohort study and preclinical evidence that statins can reduce breast cancer cell growth and induce apoptosis in various experimental models. In addition, several epidemiological studies have confirmed the correlation between the use of statins and the reduction in the risk of disease recurrence after adjuvant therapy, and the use of cholesterol-lowering drugs at the same time of adjuvant endocrine therapy in patients with hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer may have a certain role in the prevention of breast cancer recurrence. In our study, lipid-lowering agents were associated with a reduced risk of BC in ER + , a finding that provides an initial qualification of the population for whom lipid-lowering agents would benefit. Consistent is previous studies reporting that statins may be particularly associated with ER + BC. Cholesterol is the building block of hormones (such as estrogen and progesterone) and the recently discovered selective endogenous estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), 27-hydroxycholesterol, which is associated with ER-dependent tumor proliferation and immune escape. Therefore, inhibition of cholesterol synthesis may lead to decreased cell proliferation in hormone receptor-positive breast tumors.

Statins are HMGCR inhibitors, a class of drugs containing a naphthyl ring backbone structure that regulate plasma lipoprotein concentrations by inhibiting cholesterol synthesis. Because the hydrophilic moiety of statins resembles the HMG portion of the substrate, statins can be used as competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA. Statins play a role in diseases such as diabetes mellitus, neurological disorders, and neoplasms. Such drugs have the potential to alter the patterns of cholesterol synthesis and isoprenylation by controlling the mevalonate pathway, thereby affecting the functions of proteins and oncoproteins that regulate proliferation, migration, invasion, cell cycle, cell fate, and apoptosis. Furthermore, HMGCR inhibitors have been demonstrated to possess notable anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, which ultimately result in anti-tumour effects. Specifically, such inhibitors are capable of engaging the immune system, restoring the capacity to monitor tumour cells and enhancing the immunogenicity of tumour cells, thereby enhancing the anti-tumour response of the immune system. Our preliminary studies indicate a potential correlation between HMGCR expression and the presence of immune cells in the breast cancer tumour microenvironment. This finding is of particular interest as the level of cholesterol synthesis and metabolism exerts a profound effect on the function of immune cells, including their ability to migrate to the tumour site, their recognition of cancer cells, and the signalling pathways within the immune cells. These changes may upset the balance between immunosuppression and anti-tumour immune responses, which in turn has important implications for breast cancer (BC) risk.

Moreover, previous studies have identified the cholesterol metabolite 27-hydroxycholesterol (27HC) as a principal mediator of cholesterol's influence on the growth and progression of breast tumours. 27HC contributes to tumour progression by acting as a ligand for the liver X receptor in myeloid immune cells, thereby establishing an immunosuppressive programme and modifying the tumour microenvironment through exosome-dependent and non-exosome-independent mechanisms. Choe et al. demonstrated that atorvastatin, an HMGCR inhibitor, effectively enhanced the anti-tumour immune response and inhibited the immune escape of T cells by decreasing PD-L1 expression and reducing the secretion of extracellular vesicles (EVs). The mediator MR analysis in this study suggests that HMGCR inhibitors may reduce the incidence of BC by modulating three immune phenotypes: IgD + CD38 + B cell absolute count, transitional B cell absolute count, and HLA DR in CD33- HLA DR + myeloid cells. We did not identify their mechanism of action in BC; however, in some cases, they may play a role in immune function modulation.

Chronic inflammation promotes cancer development. Mechanisms by which inflammation promotes tumorigenesis include the induction of growth factors that produce proliferation, pro-angiogenic growth factors, and the promotion of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Specifically, chronic inflammation may increase the risk of BC through activation of redox-sensitive transcription factors, augmentation of local estrogen production, and induction of angiogenesis. Statins exert anti-inflammatory effects. The main mechanisms include inhibition of neutrophil migration, oxidative stress, suppression of the intrinsic immune response, and increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin (IL)-10, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), and transforming growth factor β1 (TGF-β1). Our study confirmed that HMGCR can affect multiple inflammatory factor phenotypes and that multiple inflammatory phenotypes are associated with the risk of BC, with CRP as a significant mediator.

Our study also has some limitations. MR estimates represent long-term modulation of disease risk by drug targets, which may suggest that they are not capable of reflecting the relationship between lipid-lowering drugs and BC risk over time; therefore, the results observed in clinical studies may differ from the results of the present study. Horizontal pleiotropy could not be completely ruled out in the present study despite the fact that various sensitivity analyses were performed to test the hypotheses of the MR analysis. Finally, because all data in our study were obtained from individuals of the European ancestry, this somewhat circumvents the heterogeneity that exists between different ethnic groups; however, the results of this study may not be applicable to other ethnic groups.

In conclusion, this study is the first to demonstrate that phosphatidylcholine (18:1_0:0) levels are associated with the risk of BC, suggesting that HMGCR inhibitors are associated with a reduced risk of BC, and part of the mechanism may be through pathways other than lipid-lowering efficacy, such as modulating immune function and inflammatory factors. This study provides evidence for further exploration of the relationship between HMGCR inhibitors and BC.

PMC11927037.title: Identifying potential drug targets for sepsis-related adult respiratory distress syndrome through comprehensive genetic analysis and druggability assessment

passages.text: Identifying potential drug targets for sepsis-related adult respiratory distress syndrome through comprehensive genetic analysis and druggability assessment

infons.alt-title: Weng et al. Drug targets for sepsis-related ARDS
infons.license: This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

passages.text: Background

Sepsis-related adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a life-threatening condition characterised by a high mortality rate. This underscores the pressing requirement to identify and develop potential therapeutic targets for the severe condition. This study investigated the genetic predisposition to sepsis-related ARDS in this study.
Methods

We utilised summary-based Mendelian randomisation (SMR), two-sample MR (TSMR), mediating MR, and multivariate MR (MVMR) analysis to explore the genetic susceptibility of sepsis-related ARDS by integrating over 10 000 cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTLs) and over 100 000 participants. Subsequently, we performed drug target analysis to identify potentially druggable cis-eQTL genes.
Results

The SMR analysis identified 677 cis-eQTL genes associated with sepsis. Further TSMR validation filtered 72 cis-eQTL genes causally associated with sepsis. Sepsis was causally associated with ARDS (beta = 1.80, standard error (SE) = 0.36, P < 0.001). After conducting the mediating MR and MVMR analysis, 50 cis-eQTL genes were reported to be causally associated with sepsis-related ARDS. Subsequent drug target analysis confirmed the role of four targets (PSMA4, PDK2, RPS18, and NDUFV3) as druggable genes for sepsis-related ARDS.
Conclusions

Through an extensive analysis, we identified potential drug targets for sepsis-related ARDS. Additional research is imperative to substantiate our discoveries and to pave the way for the development of novel pharmaceuticals aimed at these specific targets.

Sepsis, a critical condition arising from an exaggerated immune reaction to infection, manifests as a systemic inflammatory response. This response, if not swiftly and effectively addressed, can escalate to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, posing a significant threat to life. The lungs frequently bear the brunt of sepsis, often being the initial organ compromised by this condition. Typically, this manifests as adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), underscoring the need for vigilant monitoring and immediate therapeutic intervention. Despite the progress made in supportive care approaches, the mortality rate associated with ARDS remains distressingly high. This highlights an urgent need to identify and develop novel therapeutic targets for individuals who are at an elevated risk of developing this critical condition.

Recently, emerging studies concentrated on the biomarkers of both sepsis and ARDS. Those studies, which encompassed a limited scope by focusing on a few thousand protein biomarkers or participants, failed to address the interplay between these two entities. This oversight urges a comprehensive understanding of sepsis-related ARDS and the development of targeted therapies. Hence, a drug-target Mendelian randomisation (MR) analysis is aptly suited for exploring the relationship in such scenarios. In the MR analysis, the genetic variants are utilised as instrumental variables to establish causality between drug targets and disease outcomes, offering a robust approach to identifying potential therapeutic interventions. Based on the literature review, we found two articles focusing on the genetic predisposition to sepsis-related ARDS through MR analysis. Nevertheless, they did not conduct a genome-wide MR analysis and they genotyped on a relatively small sample size. To advance this research, we investigated the genetic predisposition to sepsis-related ARDS at a genome-wide scale. In this study, we delved into the genetic susceptibility of sepsis-related ARDS by integrating over 10 000 cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTLs) and over 100 000 participants.
METHODS

This study utilised the genome-wide association study (GWAS) data from the IEU OpenGWAS database (https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk) and the eQTLGen Consortium (https://www.eqtlgen.org/). We applied the summary-based MR (SMR), two-sample MR (TSMR), mediating MR, and multivariate MR (MVMR) analysis to investigate the sepsis-mediated causal role of cis-eQTL genes in ARDS. Further drug target analysis was conducted to find potentially druggable cis-eQTL genes (Figure 1).

The study flowchart indicated the application of SMR, TSMR, mediating MR, and MVMR analysis to investigate the sepsis-mediated causal role of cis-eQTL genes in ARDS. ARDS – adult respiratory distress syndrome, cis-eQTL – cis-expression quantitative trait locus, HEIDI – heterogeneity in dependent instruments, IVW – inverse variance weighted, MVMR – multivariate Mendelian randomisation, SMR – summary-based Mendelian randomisation, SNP – single nucleotide polymorphism, TSMR – two-sample Mendelian randomisation.
Exposure, mediator, and outcome phenotypes

The 16 989 cis-eQTL genes served as the exposure traits, which derived from the eQTLGen Consortium. The eQTLGen consortium was a collaborative endeavour on a grand scale, with the primary objective of meticulously charting the influence of genetic variations on gene expression. This consortium amassed and scrutinised both genetic and transcriptomic data from a vast array of individuals, numbering in the tens of thousands. The overarching aim was to pinpoint the genetic variants that modulate gene expression and to harness this knowledge to deepen our comprehension of the genetic underpinnings of complex diseases (Table S1 in the Online Supplementary Document).

The sepsis data were included as the mediator trait in this study. We extracted the GWAS data of sepsis from the UK Biobank. A total of 10 154 cases and 454 764 controls with over 12 million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were included. The data could be accessed through https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk (Table S1 in the Online Supplementary Document).

The ARDS data were incorporated to serve as the outcome trait. The GWAS data came from the FinnGen study. The research encompassed 216 528 subjects and incorporated 16 380 461 SNPs, which was collected and curated by the IEU OpenGWAS database and could be accessed through https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk (Table S1 in the Online Supplementary Document).
SMR analysis

We performed the SMR analysis to investigate the causal role of 16 989 cis-eQTL genes in sepsis. Genes with a P-value of <0.05 for the SMR test and >0.05 for the heterogeneity in dependent instruments (HEIDI) test were considered to have a causal association with the sepsis phenotype.
TSMR validation

For those cis-eQTL genes that passed the SMR analysis, the TSMR analysis was used to reconfirm and validate their causal role. We also performed a TSMR analysis between those cis-eQTL genes and ARDS traits and between sepsis and ARDS traits. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were clumped with the following parameters: P-value = 0.00000005, kilobase (kb) = 10 000, coefficient of correlation (r2) = 0.001. The TSMR effect based on the inverse variance weighted (IVW) with multiplicative random effects was considered the primary outcome. A Bonferroni-corrected P-value was used to infer a causal association.
Sensitivity analysis

For the TSMR validation, sensitivity analysis was performed. The TSMR effect based on another four methods was calculated: IVW, MR-Egger, MR-Egger (bootstrap), and weighted median. Heterogeneity and pleiotropy analysis were conducted. The MR-Egger (bootstrap) method was recommended if a significant pleiotropy existed. The IVW with multiplicative random effects method was recommended if a significant heterogeneity existed.
MVMR analysis

To investigate the direct effect of those cis-eQTL genes that passed the SMR analysis and TSMR validation on ARDS, an MVMR analysis was conducted. Similarly, a Bonferroni-corrected P-value was used to infer a causal association.
Mediating MR analysis

The mediating MR analysis was performed to explore the relationship among those cis-eQTL genes that passed the SMR analysis and TSMR validation, sepsis, and ARDS traits. The total effect was defined as the TSMR effect of those cis-eQTL genes on ARDS. The direct effect was defined as the MVMR effect of those cis-eQTL genes on ARDS. The mediating effect was defined as the product of the TSMR effect of those cis-eQTL genes on sepsis and the TSMR effect of sepsis on ARDS. In the clinical setting, the ARDS disease often arises as a consequence of sepsis. Therefore, our study concentrated on those cis-eQTL genes that were implicated in the pathogenesis of ARDS via a sepsis-mediated mechanism. In other words, a cis-eQTL gene that demonstrated a significant mediating effect on ARDS, while exhibiting no substantial total or direct effects, held greater significance in the context of this study. Thus, we focused on the cis-eQTL genes that only yielded significant mediating effects.
Drug target analysis

For those cis-eQTL genes with only significant mediating effects on ARDS, a comprehensive database search was applied to identify druggable targets. Generally, three databases were reviewed: DrugBank, ChEMBL, and DGIdb. We presented targets with available drugs across all three databases. A drug target was deemed adequately validated if corresponding drugs were identified across all three databases.
Statistical analysis

The principal analysis was conducted using R version 4.4.0 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria), GraphPad Prism version 9 (San Diego, California, USA), and the Hiplot Pro platform (https://hiplot.com.cn/). The TwoSampleMR, Rmediation, and Cmplot (https://github.com/YinLiLin/CMplot) were the main packages. The data were presented as beta effect size with corresponding confidence interval (CI).
RESULTS
The general design was presented in Figure 1.
The SMR analysis identified 677 cis-eQTL genes associated with sepsis

After the SMR test, a total of 900 cis-eQTL genes were considered causally associated with sepsis, with an SMR-test P < 0.05 (Figure 2, Panel A). The 900 genes were forwarded to the HEIDI test, 796 of which yielded a HEIDI-test P-value >0.05 (Figure 2, Panel B). We further excluded 119 cis-eQTL genes without a gene symbol name (Table S2 in the Online Supplementary Document). Finally, 677 genes were included for further TSMR validation (Figure 1).

The SMR and TSMR validation of cis-eQTL genes from the eQTLGen Consortium. Panel A. The scatter plot of all cis-eQTL genes. The pink points indicated genes with a P-value <0.05. Panel B. The scatter plot of cis-eQTL genes that passed the SMR test in Panel A. The pink points indicated genes with a HEIDI-test P-value >0.05. Panel C. The TSMR validation of cis-eQTL genes that passed both the SMR and HEIDI tests in Panels A–B. Chr – chromosome, HEIDI – heterogeneity in dependent instruments, SMR – summary-based Mendelian randomisation.
Subsequent TSMR validation filtered 72 cis-eQTL genes causally associated with sepsis

Those 677 cis-eQTL genes were forwarded to further TSMR validation and a Bonferroni-corrected P-value (0.05 / 677) was used to deduce a causal association (Figure 1). We identified a total of 72 genes that exhibited a consistent causal association with sepsis (Figure 2, Panel C). The TSMR results, heterogeneity test, and pleiotropy test are presented in Table S3 in the Online Supplementary Document.
The mediating MR analysis narrowed down to 50 cis-eQTL genes with sepsis-mediated effect on ARDS

The causal effect of sepsis on ARDS was calculated. The random-effect IVW method indicated a positive causal effect of sepsis on ARDS (beta = 1.80, standard error (SE) = 0.36, P < 0.001) (Figure 3; Table S4 in the Online Supplementary Document).

The MR analysis indicated a positive causal effect of sepsis on ARDS. ARDS – adult respiratory distress syndrome, CI – confidence interval, IVW – inverse variance weighted, MR – Mendelian randomisation.

The total MR effect of the 72 cis-eQTL genes mentioned above on ARDS was investigated. Based on a Bonferroni-corrected P-value (0.05 / 72), a total of 8 cis-eQTL genes were thought significantly associated with the ARDS phenotype (Figure S1 and Table S5 in the Online Supplementary Document).

Furthermore, the direct effect of the 72 cis-eQTL genes on ARDS was calculated, which was derived from the MVMR analysis (the effect of both cis-eQTL genes and sepsis on ARDS). Based on a Bonferroni-corrected P-value (0.05 / 72), a total of 2 cis-eQTL genes were thought significantly associated with the ARDS phenotype (Table S6 in the Online Supplementary Document).

Focusing on the cis-eQTL genes that only yielded significant mediating effects, 50 cis-eQTL genes were filtered as a result of their significant association with sepsis (Figure S2 in the Online Supplementary Document). The mediating effects of these 50 genes on ARDS are described in Table 1.

passages.text: ARDS – adult respiratory distress syndrome
*The sepsis-mediated effect of gene targets on ARDS.
DISCUSSION

In this study, we found 50 cis-eQTL genes with causal impacts on sepsis-mediated ARDS. The number was narrowed down to 4 cis-eQTL genes after drug target analysis across the DrugBan, ChEMBL, and DGIdb databases (PSMA4, PDK2, RPS18, and NDUFV3). In our recent investigation, the PSMA4 gene emerged as a promising candidate for a drug target in ARDS. Several inhibitors have been developed on the target (IXAZOMIB, BORTEZOMIB, CARFILZOMIB, OPROZOMIB, MARIZOMIB, COTININE, and IXAZOMIB CITRATE). Conversely, to date, no agonists have been formulated to specifically target the PDK2, RPS18, and NDUFV3 genes. The databases only provided antagonists on these targets. From this point of view, we should be cautious about utilising those drugs among patients with sepsis or sepsis-mediated ARDS.

Sepsis often triggers the malfunction of crucial organs, with a notable increase in vulnerability particularly in the lungs. ARDS, a severe pathological respiratory condition, is commonly viewed as a prevalent clinical complication during sepsis. Despite considerable research endeavors to elucidate the pathogenesis of sepsis-related ARDS and to discover new therapeutic targets and approaches, the rates of morbidity and mortality associated with this condition have persistently remained high. This underscores the need for ongoing research to uncover effective treatment strategies and preventative measures for sepsis-mediated ARDS. Thus, we conducted such a study to explore the potential drug target for sepsis-related ARDS. As the ARDS disease usually follows sepsis in the clinical scenario, we paid attention to the genetic susceptibility of sepsis-mediated ARDS. That was to say, genes that yielded a significant total effect or direct effect on ARDS were not within the scope of our study. Based on such criteria, we identified 50 cis-eQTL genes with causal impacts on sepsis-mediated ARDS. Additional research is imperative to substantiate our discoveries and to pave the way for the development of novel pharmaceuticals aimed at these specific genes.

In our study, we identified the significant role of PSMA4 in the development of sepsis-related ARDS. Furthermore, we have discovered existing inhibitors that target PSMA4, which could potentially be leveraged for therapeutic purposes. PSMA4, as a vital component of the proteasome complex that consists of the 19S regulatory particle and the 20S core particle, is essential for the process of protein degradation. This function is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis by ensuring that damaged or unneeded proteins are effectively broken down and recycled. Indeed, the PSMA4 gene has been reported to impact a series of inflammatory disorders, including nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and ankylosing spondylitis arthritis. Moreover, it was recognised that the proteasome inhibitor (BORTEZOMIB) (Table 2), which targeted components like PSMA4, had the potential to modulate excessive inflammation and regulate the expression of cytokines that were triggered by a variety of stimuli. This regulatory effect could be beneficial in managing inflammatory responses that are often dysregulated in conditions such as sepsis and ARDS, where an overactive immune response can lead to tissue damage and organ dysfunction. Additionally, we also provided several other proteasome inhibitors targeting PSMA4 (Table 2). These novel insights could serve as a valuable guide for future research endeavors focusing on sepsis and ARDS. We must also be cautious about the potential challenges in the clinical application of these drugs. For example, the common side effects of IXAZOMIB include thrombocytopenia and diarrhea, which should be avoided in certain patient populations.

We assumed that another three cis-eQTL genes (PDK2, RPS18, and NDUFV3), which were negatively associated with sepsis-induced ARDS, could be targeted with potential drugs in ARDS treatment. However, only inhibitors were found across the three databases. The application of these inhibitors in patients suffering from sepsis and ARDS should be approached with caution, as there might be a potential risk of worsening the conditions. The literature review yielded conflicting results on the role of PDK2, RPS18, and NDUFV3 genes in inflammatory diseases. We anticipate conducting further research to explore the role of these targets in sepsis-related ARDS and to develop agonists that can modulate their activity.

Our results provided potential drug targets for sepsis-related ARDS through a comprehensive analysis, including SMR, TSMR, mediating MR, and MVMR methods with a Bonferroni-corrected P-value. Additionally, the filtered cis-eQTL genes were examined across the three mainstream databases, and we finally discovered PSMA4 as a promising druggable target for sepsis-related ARDS treatment. We have successfully navigated around the constraints typically encountered in conventional new drug development processes and our results would provide significant understanding to guide future pharmaceutical development initiatives targeting genes found in our study.

Several limitations should be admitted. We only extracted the summary statistics of GWAS data, which prevented us from validating the primary sources of data and developing a multigene predictor set. Our study exclusively included participants of European ancestry, which restricted the generalisability of our findings to other ethnic groups. The lack of cellular and animal studies impeded the validation of our research findings. Individual samples in the real-world clinical setting should also be collected to test our hypothesis. Despite these challenges, we conducted a series of sensitivity analysis including the heterogeneity and pleiotropy tests to ensure the robustness of the research results.
CONCLUSIONS

We discovered potential drug targets for sepsis-related ARDS through a comprehensive analysis, among which four druggable targets (PSMA4, PDK2, RPS18, and NDUFV3) should be dialectically treated. Preclinical studies and randomised control trials would be needed to assess their effectiveness and safety. Also, the development of agonists for underexplored targets (like PDK2, RPS18, and NDUFV3) will be impactful.

passages.text: Background

Malignant mesothelioma is a highly aggressive cancer with a poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a pivotal role in driving tumor progression, with immune cells influencing disease outcomes. However, the molecular mechanisms underpinning mesothelioma’s progression remain insufficiently understood. HLA-C, a class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecule, has been implicated in immune modulation and cancer progression, but its specific role in mesothelioma has yet to be thoroughly investigated.
Methods

This study employed a comprehensive multi-omics approach, integrating single-cell RNA sequencing, expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) analysis, and Mendelian randomization (MR), to elucidate the role of HLA-C in mesothelioma progression. We first analyzed HLA-C expression within the TME, with particular focus on immune cells, especially macrophages. Survival analysis was conducted using data from the TCGA mesothelioma cohort to assess the clinical relevance of HLA-C expression. We utilized mediated MR analysis to investigate the impact of DNA methylation on HLA-C expression, identifying key mediators such as inflammatory cytokines, immune cell populations, blood cell types, and metabolites that could potentially influence patient prognosis.
Results

HLA-C was predominantly expressed in macrophages, T cells, and NK cells within the TME, and higher expression levels were associated with improved patient survival. MR analysis revealed that DNA methylation regulates HLA-C expression, which in turn impacts mesothelioma outcomes. Mediated MR analysis, encompassing 91 inflammatory cytokines, 731 immune cell populations, 91 blood cell types, and 1400 metabolites, highlighted several critical mediators of HLA-C’s effect on prognosis, including IL-10, CD33 expression on CD33dim HLA DR- myeloid cells, the reticulocyte perturbation response, and the ADP-to-citrate ratio. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed significant enrichment of immune-related and inflammatory pathways in patients with high HLA-C expression.
Conclusion

HLA-C, regulated by DNA methylation, plays a central role in mesothelioma prognosis by modulating immune responses, inflammatory cytokines, blood cell populations, and metabolic processes within the TME. Our findings suggest that HLA-C could serve as both a prognostic biomarker and a potential therapeutic target for mesothelioma, offering new insights into the molecular mechanisms driving this aggressive cancer.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00262-025-04012-4.
Introduction

Mesothelioma is a highly aggressive malignancy primarily linked to asbestos exposure, representing a significant global health challenge, particularly in industrialized regions with high occupational asbestos use. This cancer primarily originates in serosal tissues, including the pleura, peritoneum, and pericardium, and exhibits considerable geographical variability in its incidence. Characterized by cellular atypia, infiltrative growth, and frequent metastasis, mesothelioma presents a poor prognosis due to its aggressive nature. Despite advancements in diagnostic techniques such as histopathological evaluation and immunohistochemistry (e.g., markers like Wilm's tumor 1 [WT1], mesothelin, and calretinin, the molecular mechanisms underlying mesothelioma progression remain incompletely understood.

Emerging evidence suggests that mesothelioma progression is influenced by a complex interplay between genetic alterations, immune responses, inflammation, and metabolism. These factors collectively shape the tumor microenvironment (TME), which plays a critical role in disease progression and response to therapy. Among the key modulators of immune responses, HLA-C, a major component of the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I family, has drawn attention for its potential role in various cancers. Known for its interaction with natural killer (NK) cells and T cells, HLA-C is crucial in regulating immune surveillance. However, its exact role in mesothelioma progression and its impact on the broader immune and inflammatory landscape remain largely unexplored.

This study aims to bridge this gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of HLA-C’s role in mesothelioma. Using a multi-omics approach, we investigated how HLA-C expression influences a wide array of tumor microenvironment (TME)-related factors, including immune cells, inflammatory cytokines, blood cell populations, and metabolites. By employing Mendelian randomization (MR) and mediation MR analysis, we explored how DNA methylation regulates HLA-C expression and its downstream effects on immune responses, inflammation, metabolism, and blood cells within the TME. These analyses offer a deep understanding of how HLA-C functions as a key modulator in mesothelioma progression.

Our findings reveal that HLA-C expression is strongly associated with immune-related pathways, including cytokine signaling and antigen processing. Additionally, we identify DNA methylation as a crucial regulator of HLA-C expression, influencing mesothelioma prognosis. Notably, our analysis highlights key mediators of HLA-C’s prognostic effect, such as IL-10, CD33 on CD33dim HLA DR- myeloid cells, and metabolic factors like the ADP-to-citrate ratio, which modulate immune responses and inflammatory pathways within the TME. This suggests that HLA-C not only serves as a potential prognostic biomarker but also as a therapeutic target, with the identification of blood cell populations and metabolites offering new avenues for clinical intervention.

By examining these multifaceted interactions, our study contributes new insights into mesothelioma biology and provides evidence that HLA-C is a pivotal player in the immune regulation and metabolic reprogramming of the TME. The findings suggest that targeting HLA-C, alongside its identified mediators, could provide novel strategies for therapeutic intervention in mesothelioma, especially in combination with immune modulation and metabolic reprogramming.
Methods
Source of druggable gene data

The druggable genes analyzed in this study were primarily sourced from the comprehensive dataset compiled by Juan P. Casas et al., which identifies 4,479 druggable protein-coding genes. To integrate gene expression data with genetic variants, expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data for these genes were obtained from the eQTLGen Consortium (https://www.eqtlgen.org/).
Mesothelioma outcome data

Mesothelioma outcome data were derived from the Finnish R12 version of the mesothelioma dataset, which includes detailed clinical and genomic information for 442 mesothelioma patients and 378,749 control subjects of European ancestry. This dataset was used to explore the associations between genetic variations and mesothelioma prognosis. The inclusion of both patient and control cohorts provides a robust foundation for analyzing genetic factors that influence disease outcomes.
single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis

scRNA-seq data for mesothelioma were obtained from the GSE190597 dataset, which includes tumor tissue samples from mesothelioma patients. Data analysis was conducted using R (version 4.4) and the Seurat package for data preprocessing and visualization. Raw count matrices were processed with quality control measures to ensure data integrity, removing cells with fewer than 200 detected genes or those with mitochondrial gene content exceeding 5%. Additionally, genes expressed in fewer than three cells were excluded. Dimensionality reduction was performed using t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) to visualize cellular heterogeneity and identify distinct cell clusters. Cell-type annotation was done using the Celldex package, which assigns cell identities based on gene expression profiles using pre-built reference datasets. Differential gene expression analysis was performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function to compare gene expression profiles between identified cell clusters. A p value threshold of < 0.05 and a log2 fold change cutoff of > 0.5 or < -0.5 were used to identify significant differentially expressed genes associated with mesothelioma.
Two-sample MR analysis

Two-sample MR was utilized to investigate causal relationships between genetic variants and disease outcomes, using data from large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS). The Wald ratio method was employed for single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) exposures, and the inverse variance weighted (IVW) method was applied for multiple SNPs, assuming no pleiotropy. Horizontal pleiotropy was assessed using MR-Egger regression, while heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q statistic. The robustness of the results was tested with a leave-one-out analysis, and causal direction was assessed with the Steiger test. Sensitivity analyses were conducted using the weighted median method to address potential instrument validity issues. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05.
Stratification of mesothelioma samples based on HLA-C expression

In the mesothelioma cohort from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), samples were stratified according to HLA-C expression levels, as determined by data distribution. The top 25% of samples with the highest HLA-C expression were classified as the “high expression” group, while the remaining 75% were classified as the “low expression” group. This stratification was chosen to reflect a natural cutoff in HLA-C expression, ensuring meaningful comparisons.

To extend this analysis, we also stratified mesothelioma datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), namely GSE112154 and GSE29354. For these two datasets, samples were equally divided into two groups based on HLA-C expression levels: the top 50% of samples with the highest HLA-C expression were classified as the “high expression” group, while the bottom 50% were classified as the “low expression” group. This 50% threshold was selected to create a balanced comparison between the high and low HLA-C expression groups within each dataset, allowing for consistent analysis across datasets and further validation of the findings observed in the TCGA cohort.
Survival analysis

Survival analysis was performed using the survival package in R. The proportional hazards assumption was tested, and Cox regression models were employed to assess the prognostic value of HLA-C expression. Survival curves were generated and visualized using the survminer and ggplot2 packages to evaluate the relationship between HLA-C expression and patient survival.
Differential gene expression analysis

Differential gene expression between high and low HLA-C expression groups was conducted using the DESeq2 and edgeR packages in R. Differentially expressed genes were identified based on an adjusted p-value (padj) < 0.05, controlling for false discovery rates and ensuring statistical rigor.
GSEA

GSEA was performed using the clusterProfiler package in R. Genes were ranked by their signal-to-noise ratio, and predefined gene sets were tested for enrichment. Gene sets containing 5–5,000 genes were considered, and statistical significance was defined by a p-value < 0.05 and a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.1, highlighting biologically relevant pathways linked to HLA-C expression and mesothelioma prognosis.
Analysis of DNA methylation quantitative trait loci (mQTL) and mediation MR

MR using mQTL was employed to explore the causal relationships between DNA methylation and various phenotypes. mQTL data were sourced from GoDMC database. The mQTL data were curated to select SNPs consistently associated with DNA methylation changes at specific loci. A two-step mediation MR analysis was performed: in the first step, HLA-C methylation traits associated with mesothelioma were identified using two-sample MR, and total effect values (βall) were computed. In the second step, these methylation traits were used to assess their effects on HLA-C expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) traits (β₁), followed by two-sample MR to evaluate the causal effect of HLA-C eQTL traits on mesothelioma (β₂). The mediation effect (β₁ × β₂) and its proportion in the causal pathway were calculated, with statistical significance defined as p < 0.05.
Data sources for 91 circulating inflammatory cytokines, 731 immune Cells, 91 blood cells, and 1,400 plasma metabolites, and mediation MR analysis

GWAS data for 91 circulating inflammatory cytokines were obtained from the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI) GWAS Catalog. These data were derived from a study using Olink Target 96 Inflammation Panels to quantify 91 plasma proteins in 14,824 European participants across 11 cohorts. Data on 731 immune cell types were sourced from a study by Rahul C. Deo et al. which analyzed blood cell responses in a cohort of over 2,600 individuals. Additionally, data on 91 blood cell types were sourced from the same study. Plasma metabolite data, including 1,400 metabolites, were obtained from a landmark study published in Nature Genetics and included 1,091 metabolites and 309 metabolite ratios from 8,299 individuals in the CLSA cohort. Mediation MR analysis was performed to explore the effects of inflammatory markers, immune cell traits, blood cell characteristics, and plasma metabolites on the relationship between HLA-C eQTL traits and mesothelioma. The analysis followed the two-step procedure described above, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.
Immune infiltration analysis using the xCell algorithm

Immune cell infiltration was assessed using the xCell algorithm, which utilizes predefined immune cell markers to estimate the relative abundance of various immune cell types within tissue samples. The xCell R package provides a comprehensive set of 64 immune cell markers, which were used to define gene sets for each immune cell type. For each sample, the algorithm calculates enrichment scores for these immune cell gene sets, inferring the immune cell composition based on gene expression data. This analysis provides quantitative insights into the immune microenvironment of each sample, allowing for the investigation of immune infiltration patterns across different conditions.
Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.4.
Results
Identification of HLA-C as a prognostic marker in mesothelioma

Identification of HLA-C as a prognostic marker in mesothelioma. (A) Venn diagram illustrating overlap between macrophage marker genes and genes associated with mesothelioma prognosis, derived from MR analysis of druggable genome eQTL data. (B) MR analysis exploring the relationship between HLA-C and mesothelioma prognosis. (C) Survival analysis of HLA-C expression in the TCGA mesothelioma cohort. (D) Expression of HLA-C across various immune cell types in mesothelioma

Considering the critical role of tumor-associated macrophages in modulating immune responses and tumor progression in mesothelioma, we focused on analyzing macrophage-associated genes identified in the GSE190597 scRNA-seq dataset. A total of 3,233 marker genes were linked to mesothelioma-associated macrophages. We then performed MR using eQTL data from over 4,700 druggable genes, identifying 267 genes significantly associated with prognosis. Of these, 67 genes overlapped with macrophage-associated markers and were selected for further analysis (Fig. 1A).

Survival analysis using the TCGA mesothelioma cohort revealed that seven genes—CYP27A1, NFKBIA, GNS, LGALS1, LIMK1, AKR1B1, and HLA-C—were consistent with MR findings (Suppl. Table 1). Due to the limited research on HLA-C in cancer prognosis, we examined its potential role in mesothelioma. MR analysis using the IVW method showed an odds ratio (OR) for HLA-C of less than 1, consistent with results from the weighted median and mode methods, confirming our findings (Fig. 1B).

In the TCGA mesothelioma cohort, high HLA-C expression was significantly associated with improved prognosis relative to low expression (Fig. 1C), indicating its potential as a favorable prognostic marker. Figure 1D illustrates that HLA-C is primarily expressed in mesothelioma-associated macrophages, with significant expression observed in T cells and NK cells. These findings provide insight into the mechanisms by which HLA-C may influence prognosis.
DNA methylation regulates HLA-C expression and influences mesothelioma prognosis

Methylation sites regulating HLA-C expression and their impact on mesothelioma prognosis. (A) Forest plot showing the causal relationship between methylation sites and mesothelioma risk. (B) Forest plot illustrating the causal relationship between methylation sites and HLA-C expression. (C– L) Mediation MR analysis depicting the influence of methylation sites on mesothelioma prognosis mediated through HLA-C expression

Through methylation data analysis, we identified 46 methylation sites linked to the HLA-C gene (Suppl. Table 2). To explore their potential causal relationship with mesothelioma prognosis, we performed MR analysis. This analysis identified 14 methylation sites significantly correlated with prognosis outcomes. Specifically, 12 sites (cg01006124, cg02827714, cg03216697, cg09970392, cg14931776, cg16097079, cg17096289, cg17974398, cg18020334, cg18747378, cg18785300, and cg24877963) exhibited OR greater than 1, suggesting that hypermethylation at these loci is associated with a worse prognosis. Conversely, cg05619024 and cg13872627 exhibited ORs less than 1, indicating that hypomethylation at these loci is linked to better outcomes (Fig. 2A).

To investigate the regulatory role of these methylation sites in HLA-C expression, we performed an MR analysis (Fig. 2B). The results demonstrated a significant association between hypermethylation at loci such as cg01006124, cg02827714, cg03216697, cg09970392, cg10409680, cg14931776, cg14972843, cg15634083, cg17096289, cg17974398, cg18020334, cg18747378, and cg18785300 and reduced HLA-C expression. These findings suggest that DNA methylation at these loci plays a crucial role in regulating HLA-C expression in mesothelioma.

Additionally, we conducted mediation MR analysis to assess how these methylation sites influence mesothelioma prognosis through HLA-C regulation. The results revealed that 10 methylation sites significantly mediated the effect of prognosis via HLA-C expression. Notably, cg01006124 accounted for 95.78% of the effect, followed by cg03216697 (94.99%), cg18747378 (87.77%), cg09970392 (87.15%), cg02827714 (84.31%), cg17974398 (64.74%), cg14931776 (57.04%), cg16097079 (50.64%), cg18785300 (47.03%), and cg17096289 (46.14%) (Fig. 2 C–L). These results provide evidence that DNA methylation-mediated regulation of HLA-C expression plays a significant role in mesothelioma prognosis, with specific methylation sites influencing patient outcomes.
HLA-C influences mesothelioma prognosis via IL-10

Association of HLA-C with inflammatory cytokines and mesothelioma prognosis. (A) Forest plot of the causal relationship between inflammatory factors and mesothelioma prognosis. (B) Forest plot showing the causal link between HLA-C expression and levels of CD6 and IL-10. Mediation MR analysis of the effect of HLA-C on mesothelioma prognosis mediated through IL-10 (C) and CD6 (D) levels

Considering the known relationship between HLA-C and the immune system, we examined whether HLA-C modulates mesothelioma progression through inflammatory factors. Initially, we evaluated the correlation between 91 inflammatory cytokines and mesothelioma prognosis. Among these markers, OR for Axin-1 and Interleukin-10 (IL-10) were less than 1, indicating that higher levels of these factors correlate with more favorable prognosis. Conversely, ORs for the CD6 isoform and Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF-21) were greater than 1, suggesting that elevated levels of these markers correlate with worse outcomes (Fig. 3A).

We then investigated the relationship between HLA-C and these inflammatory markers using MR analysis. Figure 3B demonstrates that HLA-C is correlated with increased CD6 expression (OR < 1) and decreased IL-10 levels (OR > 1). Further mediation MR analysis revealed that IL-10 mediates 23.56% of the effect of HLA-C on mesothelioma prognosis (Fig. 3C), whereas CD6 accounted for only 6.22% (Fig. 3D). These results indicate the significant role of IL-10 in mediating the effect of HLA-C on mesothelioma outcomes.
HLA-C modulates mesothelioma prognosis via myeloid cells (CD33 on CD33dim HLA DR-)

Immune cells mediating the effect of HLA-C on mesothelioma prognosis. (A) Forest plot of the causal relationship between immune cell types and mesothelioma prognosis. (B) Forest plot depicting the causal relationship between HLA-C and the abundance of specific immune cell types. (C–F) Mediation MR analysis identifying immune cell types that significantly mediate the effect of HLA-C on mesothelioma prognosis

To investigate the mediation of HLA-C's effect on mesothelioma by immune cells, we assessed 731 immune cell populations. First, we analyzed the impact of these immune cells on mesothelioma prognosis using MR analysis. The results revealed that B cells (including Memory B cells, IgD + CD24 + lymphocytes, IgD- CD38- activated B cells, CD19 on CD20- CD38- cells, and CD24 on IgD + CD38- cells), conventional dendritic cells (cDCs), regulatory T cells (Tregs), and T cell maturation stages (HVEM on TD CD4 +) exhibited ORs less than 1, correlating with a more favorable prognosis in mesothelioma (Fig. 4A).

In contrast, MR results for other immune cells, including B cells (such as IgD + CD38bright B cells, CD19 on CD20-, and CD24 on IgD- CD38dim cells), cDCs (like CD86 + plasmacytoid DCs and CD62L on C62L + myeloid DCs), Tregs (e.g., CD25hi T cells, CD45RA + CD28- CD8bright T cells, and CD39 + monocytes), T cell maturation stages (such as Naive CD4 + T cells and CD3 + Naive CD4 + T cells), myeloid cells (including Mo MDSCs, CD33 on CD33dim HLA DR- cells, Gr MDSCs, and CD33 + on basophils), and TBNK cells (e.g., CD4/CD8bright T cells and HLA DR + CD8bright T cells) showed ORs greater than 1, suggesting that these immune cells may act as risk factors in mesothelioma (Fig. 4A).

Among these immune populations, HLA-C was found to negatively regulate CD25hi T cells in the Treg panel but positively regulate CD62L- monocytes in the cDC panel, as well as CD33 on Mo MDSCs, CD33 on CD33dim HLA DR- cells, CD33 on basophils, and CD33 on immature MDSCs in the myeloid cell panel (Fig. 4B). To determine whether HLA-C mediates mesothelioma prognosis through these immune cells, we performed mediation MR. The results indicated that only CD33 on CD33dim HLA DR- cells exhibited a mediation proportion greater than 10% (Fig. 4C), whereas the mediation proportions of the other four immune cell populations were below 10% (Fig. 4D–F). These findings highlight the specific role of CD33 on CD33dim HLA DR- cells in mediating the influence of HLA-C on mesothelioma prognosis.
HLA-C modulates mesothelioma prognosis via reticulocyte perturbation response

Reticulocyte perturbation response mediating the effect of HLA-C on mesothelioma prognosis. (A) Forest plot showing the causal relationship between blood cell responses to perturbations and mesothelioma prognosis. (B) Forest plot illustrating the causal relationship between HLA-C expression and reticulocyte perturbation response. (C) Mediation MR analysis of the effect of reticulocyte perturbation response on mesothelioma outcomes mediated by HLA-C

To further explore the role of HLA-C in mesothelioma prognosis, we assessed the mediation effects of 91 blood cell types. The reticulocyte perturbation response, characterized by the side scatter median of reticulocyte 1 following ciprofloxacin perturbation, was associated with a protective effect (Fig. 5A). In contrast, red blood cell (RBC) responses, measured by the forward scatter standard deviation after KCl perturbation, and an unidentified cell population, determined by the side scatter coefficient of variation following TMAO perturbation, were correlated with higher mesothelioma risk (Fig. 5A). Among these cell types, HLA-C positively regulates the reticulocyte perturbation response (Fig. 5B). Mendelian MR analysis revealed a mediation proportion of 16.14% (Fig. 5C), indicating that HLA-C may influence mesothelioma prognosis via this perturbation response.
HLA-C modulates mesothelioma prognosis via ADP-to-citrate ratio

Metabolites mediating the effect of HLA-C on mesothelioma prognosis. (A) Forest plot showing the causal relationship between metabolites and mesothelioma prognosis. (B) Forest plot illustrating the causal relationship between HLA-C expression and metabolites. (C–G) Mediation MR analysis identifying metabolites that mediate the effect of HLA-C on mesothelioma prognosis

To examine the role of metabolic factors in HLA-C-mediated mesothelioma prognosis, we analyzed 1,400 metabolites from patient samples. Initial screening identified 55 metabolites significantly associated with prognosis (Suppl. Table 2), with 13 of these metabolites being regulated by HLA-C. Protective metabolites included 1-oleoyl-2-linoleoyl-GPE (18:1/18:2), 3-hydroxybutyroylglycine, and the ADP-to-citrate ratio, while metabolites like X-24456 (an unannotated plasma metabolite) and 1-(1-enyl-palmitoyl)-GPC (p-16:0) were linked to increased risk of poor outcomes (Fig. 6A). Notably, HLA-C was found to positively regulate sphingomyelins (e.g., d17:1/16:0, d18:1/15:0) and Oleoyl-linoleoyl-glycerol (18:1/18:2), but negatively regulate several other metabolites, including the ADP-to-citrate ratio (Fig. 6B).

Among the 13 metabolites, only the ADP-to-citrate ratio showed a significant mediation effect on mesothelioma prognosis, with a mediation proportion of 12.01% (Fig. 6C). Other metabolites exhibited lower mediation effects, such as the inosine to EDTA ratio at 9.64% (Fig. 6D–G). The ADP-to-citrate ratio serves as a key intermediary in the relationship between HLA-C and mesothelioma prognosis, reflecting its potential role in regulating metabolic reprogramming in tumor cells. These findings emphasize the importance of metabolic changes, specifically ADP-to-citrate ratio, in mesothelioma progression and suggest that HLA-C might regulate tumor metabolism to influence patient outcomes.
HLA-C potentially modulates mesothelioma outcomes via immune-related pathways

Pathway enrichment analysis of HLA-C in mesothelioma. Volcano plots and GSEA results of differentially expressed genes between high vs. low HLA-C expression groups in the TCGA (A, B), GSE112154 (E, F), and GSE29354 (I, J) mesothelioma cohorts. xCELL analysis showing immune cell type abundance and ImmuneScore in the high and low HLA-C expression groups in the TCGA (C, D), GSE112154 (G, H), and GSE29354 (K, L) mesothelioma cohorts

Our study suggests that HLA-C expression influences mesothelioma outcomes through immune-related pathways. To explore this, we first performed differential expression analysis using TCGA mesothelioma data, comparing high HLA-C expression with low expression groups with low expression groups. GSEA revealed significant enrichment in immune-related pathways, including interferon signaling, IL-12 signaling, antigen presentation, and cytokine signaling (Fig. 7A). These results suggest that elevated HLA-C expression enhances anti-tumor immunity through the interferon α/β pathway, promotes IL-12-induced immune activation, and improves antigen presentation, which may contribute to reduced immune escape and improved patient survival (Fig. 7B).

Further analysis using xCELL revealed that high HLA-C expression was associated with increased infiltration of immune cell types, including activated dendritic cells (aDCs), basophils, CD4 + effector memory T cells (Tem), CD8 + T cells, and Tγδ cells, when compared to low HLA-C expression (Fig. 7C). Additionally, the ImmuneScore was higher in the high HLA-C expression group (Fig. 7D), indicating HLA-C’s role in modulating the tumor immune microenvironment.

To validate these findings, we analyzed two independent mesothelioma cohorts: GSE112154 (Fig. 7E) and GSE29354 (Fig. 7I). In both datasets, high HLA-C expression was associated with the activation of key immune-related pathways. In GSE112154, significant enrichments included interferon signaling, cytokine signaling, the innate immune system, and viral infection pathways (Fig. 7F). In GSE29354, enriched pathways included interferon α/β signaling, natural killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and antigen processing (Fig. 7J).

xCELL immune infiltration analysis further confirmed that high HLA-C expression was linked to higher immune cell abundances in both cohorts. In GSE112154, this included increased numbers of aDCs, CD4 + memory T cells, CD8 + central memory T cells, and Th2 cells, along with a higher ImmuneScore (Fig. 7G and H). In GSE29354, elevated levels of aDCs, basophils, macrophages (both M1 and M2), and other immune cells were observed in the high HLA-C expression group, accompanied by a higher ImmuneScore (Fig. 7K and L).

These results from the TCGA, GSE112154, and GSE29354 datasets demonstrate that HLA-C significantly influences the immune landscape in mesothelioma. The enhanced immune activation associated with high HLA-C expression suggests its potential as a therapeutic target for immunotherapy, aimed at improving anti-tumor responses.
Discussion

This study investigates the role of HLA-C expression in mesothelioma, a malignancy characterized by poor prognosis and high resistance to therapy. Our findings provide new insights into the complex mechanisms regulating HLA-C expression and underscore its potential as both a prognostic marker and a therapeutic target in mesothelioma. By leveraging multiple omics approaches, we show that HLA-C expression is predominantly observed in mesothelioma-associated macrophages, T cells, and NK cells, with higher expression correlating with improved survival outcomes. These observations suggest that HLA-C plays a crucial role in modulating immune responses within the TME, enhancing tumor recognition and promoting anti-tumor immunity.

A key contribution of this study is the identification of DNA methylation as a key regulator of HLA-C expression in mesothelioma. Our MR analysis highlights the involvement of epigenetic modifications in controlling HLA-C expression, linking DNA methylation to mesothelioma prognosis. These insights suggest that HLA-C expression, influenced by epigenetic factors, shapes the immune landscape of mesothelioma and potentially alters the immune system's ability to detect and eliminate tumor cells. This observation opens up exciting prospects for therapeutic strategies aimed at reversing epigenetic silencing and restoring HLA-C expression, thereby enhancing anti-tumor immunity.

We also identified several novel mediators that contribute to the prognostic effect of HLA-C. Among these, IL-10, CD33 on CD33dim HLA DR- myeloid cells, reticulocyte perturbation response, and the ADP-to-citrate ratio stand out as potential therapeutic targets. IL-10, in particular, emerges as a key modulator of immune responses within the TME. Recent studies have demonstrated that IL-10 can activate tumor-resident CD8 + T cells, reversing T cell exhaustion and enhancing anti-tumor immunity. Targeting IL-10 in mesothelioma could optimize its immunomodulatory effects, especially in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors or virotherapies, which may further strengthen the immune response against the tumor. A more mechanistic understanding of how HLA-C influences IL-10 signaling in the TME could provide insights into designing novel therapeutic strategies aimed at enhancing anti-tumor immunity.

The term “reticulocyte perturbation response” refers to a disruption in erythropoiesis, particularly the maturation process of reticulocytes. This altered response may indicate metabolic or stress signaling changes within the TME, affecting immune cell recruitment and retention. Specifically, in mesothelioma, these perturbations could influence the production and function of immune cells, such as macrophages and myeloid cells, which play essential roles in anti-tumor immunity. Further research into the dynamics of reticulocyte maturation and its relationship with immune cell populations in mesothelioma is needed to understand its full impact on tumor progression.

The ADP-to-citrate ratio, a metabolic indicator of cellular energy status, is another important mediator identified in our study. In mesothelioma, alterations in cellular respiration and the TCA cycle could significantly impact immune cell function. A high ADP-to-citrate ratio reflects increased metabolic activity within immune cells, facilitating a stronger immune response. Given that metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer, including mesothelioma, the ADP-to-citrate ratio could serve as a valuable biomarker for tumor progression and immune cell activation. The interaction between HLA-C expression and immune cell metabolism warrants further investigation to understand how metabolic alterations in the TME influence the overall immune response.

Furthermore, our GSEA of differentially expressed genes from the TCGA, GSE112154, and GSE29354 mesothelioma cohort corroborates the role of HLA-C in regulating immune-related pathways, including interferon signaling, antigen processing, and cytokine signaling. These pathways are essential for orchestrating the immune system’s recognition and elimination of tumor cells. Additionally, our findings from xCELL immune analysis show that patients with low HLA-C expression have significantly fewer immune cell types in their TME as well as a markedly reduced ImmuneScore. These results highlight the pivotal role of HLA-C in shaping the immune cell landscape of mesothelioma, reinforcing its potential as a therapeutic target for modulating the TME and enhancing immune cell infiltration.

While this study highlights the critical role of HLA-C in regulating immune responses, inflammatory cytokines, and metabolic pathways in mesothelioma, several key mechanisms remain to be explored. The potential link between HLA-C expression and immune cell metabolism, particularly its modulation of the ADP-to-citrate ratio, is an intriguing avenue for further investigation. Although we propose that HLA-C influences immune cell metabolism through cytokines like IL-10, direct evidence supporting this hypothesis is still lacking. Future studies should focus on dissecting the mechanisms by which HLA-C modulates immune cell activation and metabolic reprogramming within the TME.

Although the involvement of HLA-C in cancer prognosis has been established in other cancers, such as colorectal and breast cancers, this study represents the first mechanistic investigation of HLA-C in mesothelioma. Our study emphasizes the importance of epigenetic regulation in controlling HLA-C expression and its downstream effects on immune modulation and tumor metabolism. However, functional validation of the key mediators identified, such as IL-10, CD33dim HLA DR- myeloid cells, and metabolic indicators like the ADP-to-citrate ratio, is required through in vitro and in vivo studies. Prospective clinical trials are needed to evaluate the potential clinical utility of HLA-C as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target for mesothelioma.
Conclusion

This study offers novel insights into the role of HLA-C expression in mesothelioma, an aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options. We demonstrate that HLA-C—regulated by DNA methylation—significantly influences immune responses, inflammatory pathways, and metabolic processes within the TME. Our findings suggest that HLA-C not only serves as a potential prognostic biomarker but also represents a promising therapeutic target, particularly through the modulation of immune-related pathways and epigenetic reprogramming.

The identification of key mediators, such as IL-10, CD33 on CD33dim HLA DR- myeloid cells, reticulocyte perturbation response, and metabolic factors like the ADP-to-citrate ratio, introduces new avenues for therapeutic strategies. By targeting these factors, it may be possible to modulate the immune landscape of mesothelioma, enhance anti-tumor immunity, and improve patient outcomes. Further investigation into the functional roles of these mediators and the development of strategies to restore HLA-C expression holds promise for improving the prognosis and treatment of mesothelioma.
