passages.text: Background and objectives:

Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive primary malignant brain tumor in adults, yet effective therapeutic strategies remain limited. A comprehensive exploration of brain proteomic profiles may offer new insights into GBM pathogenesis and treatment.
Methods:

We integrated the largest available summary-level GWAS data for GBM, derived from eight studies of European ancestry, with brain proteomic and transcriptomic data. Proteome-wide association studies (PWAS) were performed using dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dPFC) samples from the Religious Orders Study/Memory and Aging Project (ROS/MAP) and the Banner Sun Health Research Institute. Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) utilized dPFC transcriptomic data from the CommonMind Consortium (CMC). To assess causality, Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses based on protein and expression quantitative trait loci (pQTL and eQTL) were conducted. Bayesian colocalization analyses were performed to determine whether GBM risk and candidate genes shared a common causal variant. Based on the integrative evidence, candidate genes were prioritized and assigned confidence levels regarding their therapeutic relevance.
Results:

The primary PWAS identified eight candidate genes associated with GBM (LIME1, EGFR, RHBDF1, SCFD1, FAIM, KDELC2, GPX1, and GMPPB). Among these, two (LIME1 and GMPPB) were replicated in a confirmatory PWAS, and six (LIME1, EGFR, SCFD1, FAIM, GPX1, and GMPPB) were validated in TWAS. pQTL-based MR analysis supported causal relationships for SCFD1, GPX1, and GMPPB, while eQTL-based MR analysis identified EGFR, SCFD1, FAIM, and GMPPB. Colocalization analysis revealed that EGFR, RHBDF1, SCFD1, and GMPPB share causal variants with GBM risk. Through comprehensive multi-omics integration, three genes – EGFR, SCFD1, and GMPPB – were identified as high-confidence therapeutic targets.
Discussion:

By leveraging brain proteomic and transcriptomic data alongside large-scale GBM GWAS, we identified eight candidate genes and prioritized three – EGFR, SCFD1, and GMPPB – as high-confidence therapeutic targets. Notably, SCFD1 and GMPPB represent novel candidates. These findings advance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying GBM and warrant further functional validation.
Introduction

Glioblastoma (GBM), the most prevalent malignant primary brain tumor in adults, becomes more common after the age of 40, with its highest incidence observed in individuals aged 75 to 84. Surgery, when safely feasible, followed by targeted radiotherapy in combination with concomitant temozolomide chemotherapy and up to six maintenance cycles, constitutes the standard of care for most patients with newly diagnosed GBM. Despite surgical procedure and medical intervention, GBM is associated with a poor prognosis, characterized by a median overall survival of approximately 15 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 8%. The complexity and heterogeneity of GBM have long posed challenges to therapeutic advancements, especially in recurrent GBM. Targeted therapy has emerged as a promising direction in recent years, with new drugs aimed at various pathways continuously being developed and introduced to the market, offering hope to patients with GBM. Therefore, continually identifying new and effective therapeutic targets is crucial for overcoming GBM.

Proteins serve as highly efficient biomarkers and therapeutic targets, as they are the primary functional components of cellular and biological processes and represent the final products of gene expression. High-throughput proteomic and transcriptomic sequencing of human tissues have facilitated large-scale quantification of human proteins and expression quantitative trait loci (pQTL and eQTL), enabling a more in-depth exploration of proteins and genes. GBM originates in the brain and is known to interact with neurons and glial cells during its growth. Therefore, a deeper exploration of the brain proteomes in various ways enhances our understanding of GBM.

In the current study, we integrated the largest human brain proteomes and transcriptomes to date with genome-wide association data to identify novel therapeutic targets for GBM. We first conducted proteome-wide association studies (PWAS) and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) to screen for highly associated genes. Subsequently, Mendelian randomization (MR) and Bayesian co-localization analyses were performed to evaluate the causal relationships between specific genes and GBM, as well as to determine whether they share the same causal variant. Finally, based on an integrative and comprehensive evaluation, confidence levels were assigned to the candidate genes to inform their potential as therapeutic targets.
Materials and methods

The reporting of this study adheres to the STREGA (STrengthening the REporting of Genetic Association studies) recommendations, an extension of the STROBE Statement. Furthermore, the current study adheres to the Transparency In The reporting of Artificial INtelligence (TITAN; Supplementary Digital Content, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E659) guidelines, and no artificial intelligence (AI) tools were used at any stage of the research or manuscript preparation.

The flowchart of the current study. Abbreviation: PWAS, proteome-wide association study; TWAS, transcriptome-wide association study; GWAS, genome-wide association study; QTL, quantitative trait loci; ROS, Religious Orders Study; MAP, Memory and Aging Project; CMC, CommonMind Consortium.

The flowchart of the current study is presented in Fig. 1. Sample sizes and data characteristics for each cohort are presented in Supplementary Digital Content Figure 1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E658.
Genome-wide association study data of GBM

The largest summary-level GWAS data for GBM were sourced from the latest meta-analysis, which included 6,183 cases and 18,169 controls from eight studies of European descent. The collection of patient specimens and corresponding clinical and pathological data was conducted at each study site following ethical approval and informed written consent, in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All glioma cases (ICDO-3 codes 9380–9480 or equivalent) were diagnosed via histopathological examination in accordance with World Health Organization classification standards. Meta-analyses were performed using a fixed-effects inverse-variance method via META software (v1.6), based on β-estimates and standard errors from each study. Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran’s Q and quantified by I2 (I2 >75 indicating significant heterogeneity). Conditional association analyses were conducted using genome-wide complex trait analysis (GCTA), with meta-analysis summary statistics and linkage disequilibrium (LD) correlations from the combined 1000 Genomes Project and UK10K reference panel, conditioned step-wise on the top genome-wide significant SNP at each locus.
Human brain proteome reference used in the PWAS

The discovery PWAS data was obtained from post-mortem brain tissues of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dPFC) from 376 subjects who participated in the Religious Orders Study/Memory and Aging Project (ROS/MAP). Digested peptides were labeled using isobaric tandem mass tags (TMT), and sequencing was performed with liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Genotypes were obtained through whole-genome sequencing or genome-wide genotyping, utilizing either the Illumina Omni-Quad Express or the Affymetrix GeneChip 6.0 platforms. A total of 8,356 proteins had both proteomic and genomic data available, of which 1,475 proteins demonstrated significant cis-associations with genetic variations. In the confirmatory phase, the human brain proteome was obtained from the dPFC of a separate cohort of European participants recruited by the Banner Sun Health Research Institute. The methodology for proteome genetic profiling mirrored that used in the discovery PWAS. Following quality control, 152 individuals with both proteomic and genetic data were included in the confirmation TWAS.
HIGHLIGHTS

By integrating brain proteomic and transcriptomic data with the largest available GBM GWAS dataset, we identified eight GBM risk-associated genes, including high-confidence targets EGFR, SCFD1, and GMPPB.
EGFR is a well-known GBM target and GMPPB shows preclinical relevance.
SCFD1 emerges as a novel therapeutic candidate for GBM. All these findings offer a foundation for the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.
Human brain transcriptome reference for TWAS

The reference human brain transcriptome used in the TWAS was sourced from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dPFC) of 452 European individuals recruited by the CommonMind Consortium (CMC) (gusevlab.org/projects/fusion). A total of 5,420 mRNA levels were identified as heritable, and their corresponding mRNA weights are available from public databases.
Human brain pQTL and eQTL datasets used in the two-sample MR

The pQTL and eQTL datasets utilized in the two-sample MR were obtained from the ROS/MAP cohort and the PsychENCODE Consortium (1387 participants of European ancestry), respectively. A total of 607 proteins and 10,489 genes were identified as having significant associations with the instrument variables (IVs) at a threshold of P <5E-08.
PWAS and TWAS

We utilized FUSION to perform PWAS and TWAS, a robust method that integrates gene expression and protein abundance data with summary statistics from GWAS to identify genes associated with their cis-regulated expression or protein levels and complex traits. The FUSION pipeline was executed using default settings, adhering to the investigator’s guidelines for conducting PWAS and TWAS. FUSION incorporates multiple predictive models (top1, GBLUP, LASSO, Elastic Net, BSLMM) to assess the collective influence of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) on the weights assigned to gene and protein expression. Additionally, the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region on chromosome 6 was excluded from the analysis due to its structural complexity. A false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 0.05 was deemed significant.
Joint and conditional tests

To determine whether the significant genes within a locus had independent associations or were interconnected, we conducted joint and conditional tests using the post-process module in FUSION. Genes located in regions identified by PWAS or TWAS were grouped into a single locus to assess whether multiple gene-trait relationships within specific risk loci remained independent after accounting for the predicted expression of adjacent genes. Following the tests, genes representing independent associations were designated as jointly significant.
Mendelian randomization analysis

MR analysis employs SNPs as instrument variables (IVs) to infer causal relationships between exposure and outcome. Eligible IVs must meet three core assumptions: they are strongly associated with the exposure of interest; they are not related to any confounders; and they influence the outcome only through the exposure, not via any alternative pathways. SNPs significantly associated with the exposure (P < 5e-08) were included as IVs. The variants were then subjected to LD clumping, with an r2 threshold of <0.001 within a 10 megabase (Mb) distance. We also calculated the F-statistic for each SNP to assess instrument strength. SNPs with F-statistics greater than 10 were considered sufficiently strong for MR analysis, while those with F-statistics below this threshold were excluded. Subsequently, the exposure (pQTL and eQTL data) and outcome (GBM GWAS data) were harmonized based on the same effect alleles. MR effects were estimated using the Wald ratio when only one independent IV was available and the inverse variance weighted (IVW) method when two or more IVs were present. For analyses involving three or more IVs, sensitivity analyses were conducted using MR-Egger, weighted mode, weighted median mode, and simple mode. Additionally, post-MR analyses included the MR-Egger intercept test for horizontal pleiotropy, Cochran’s Q test for heterogeneity, and the MR-PRESSO test for outliers. A P value of <0.05 was considered suggestively significant, while an FDR of <0.05 indicated a significant causal relationship. To rule out the possibility of reverse causation distorting the results, the Steiger filtering method was employed. A P value of <0.05 indicated that the effect direction was from the exposure to the outcome.
Bayesian colocalization analysis

Bayesian colocalization analysis was conducted to evaluate whether the genetic associations between predicted protein abundance and GBM risk were consistent with a shared causal variant. The analysis was performed using the COLOC R package under default parameters, testing posterior probabilities for five hypotheses: H0 (no association with either trait), H1 (association with predicted protein, not disease), H2 (association with disease, not protein), H3 (association with both traits via distinct variants), and H4 (association with both traits via a shared variant). A PPH4 ≥0.8 was considered evidence of colocalization.
Statistical analysis summary

PWAS, TWAS and joint and conditional tests were performed with Fusion software (http://gusevlab.org/projects/fusion). MR analysis, Steiger filtering analysis, and Bayesian co-localization analysis were performed using R software (https://www.r-project.org/). Specifically, the TwoSampleMR package (version 0.5.6) was utilized for MR and Steiger filtering analyses, while the COLOC package (version 5.1.0) was employed for Bayesian co-localization analysis. We calculated FDR-adjusted P values using the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) procedure.

The primary discovery PWAS for GBM identified eight genes (LIME1, EGFR, RHBDF1, SCFD1, FAIM, KDELC2, GPX1, and GMPPB) whose cis-regulated brain protein levels were associated with GBM, with an FDR <0.05 (Table 1, Fig. 2, Supplementary Digital Content Table 1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E655). All eight genes passed the joint and conditional tests, indicating that variations in the expression of these proteins primarily accounted for the gene-trait correlations within their respective loci (Table 1).

In the confirmatory PWAS for GBM, two genes (LIME1 and GMPPB) were successfully replicated, GPX1 did not replicate, while EGFR, RHBDF1, SCFD1, and FAIM were not profiled (Table 1, Fig. 2B, Supplementary Digital Content Table 2, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E656). To further assess the association of the eight genes with GBM, a confirmatory TWAS was conducted. Six of the initial eight genes (LIME1, EGFR, SCFD1, FAIM, GPX1, and GMPPB) were replicated in the confirmatory TWAS. The other two genes, RHBDF1 and KDELC2, were treated differently: RHBDF1 was not profiled, and KDELC2 was profiled but did not show significant cis-heritability (Table 1, Fig. 2C, Supplementary Digital Content Table 3, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E657).

To confirm the causal relationship between the eight candidate brain proteins and GBM, we first conducted protein-level MR analysis. SCFD1, GPX1, and GMPPB were identified as having putative causal relationships with GBM, whereas the remaining five genes lacked sufficient SNP coverage or were not available in the relevant QTL datasets (Table2). Specifically, higher levels of SCFD1 were associated with a significantly decreased risk of GBM (OR 0.224, 95% CI 0.108–0.465, FDR 4.70E-04), while increased abundances of GPX1 (OR 1.967, 95% CI 1.333–2.904, FDR 0.004) and GMPPB (OR 3.155, 95% CI 1.777–5.604, FDR 6.14E-04) were linked to a higher risk of GBM. Steiger filtering analyses supported the causal direction from protein levels to GBM (Table 2).

To verify whether this causal relationship was replicated at the transcriptional level, we performed MR analysis using eQTL data and GBM GWAS results. At the transcriptional level, four genes were found to have significant causal associations with GBM: EGFR (OR = 0.671, 95% CI: 0.627–0.717, FDR = 7.23E-30), SCFD1 (OR = 0.781, 95% CI: 0.698–0.874, FDR = 3.74E-04), FAIM (OR = 1.122, 95% CI: 1.058–1.190, FDR = 2.59E-03), and GMPPB (OR = 1.334, 95% CI: 1.168–1.523, FDR = 4.95E-04). In contrast, KDELC2 (OR = 0.968, 95% CI: 0.902–1.037, FDR = 1.000) and GPX1 (OR = 1.089, 95% CI: 1.008–1.175, FDR = 0.623) did not show statistically significant associations (Table 2). Similarly, the MR analysis conducted between eQTL and GWAS data all passed the Steiger filtering tests.
Bayesian colocalization analysis

To assess whether the associations between genetically predicted protein levels and GBM for the eight genes identified in the discovery PWAS were driven by a shared causal variant, Bayesian colocalization analysis was performed. Using a threshold of PPH4 ≥0.8, colocalization was observed for four genes: EGFR, RHBDF1, SCFD1, and GMPPB (Table 1, Supplementary Digital Content Table 1, available at: http://links.lww.com/MS9/A877).

We assigned confidence levels to the eight potential causal genes identified in the discovery PWAS, based on evidence from replication in the confirmatory PWAS and TWAS, MR analysis, and colocalization assessment (Table 3). Considering the combined evidence, three genes (EGFR, SCFD1, and GMPPB) were assigned high confidence, as they demonstrated consistent replication in either the confirmatory PWAS or TWAS, exhibited causal relationships with GBM at either protein or transcriptional levels, and showed robust colocalization. Four genes (LIME1, RHBDF1, FAIM, and GPX1) were assigned moderate confidence due primarily to limited evidence of causal associations in MR analyses or relatively weak colocalization support (low PPH4 values). KDELC2 was assigned low confidence, given its lack of replication in confirmatory PWAS or TWAS, and absence of significant findings in MR or colocalization analyses. Overall, among the eight candidate causal genes, we identified three with high-confidence associations.
Discussion

In this study, we aimed to identify brain proteins associated with GBM in order to discover new potential treatment targets. To accomplish this, we integrated reference human brain proteomes and transcriptomes with the largest GBM GWAS results, followed by MR and Bayesian co-localization analyses, utilizing both discovery and confirmatory study designs. In discovery PWAS, we identified 8 potential causal genes associated with GBM risk through their cis-regulated brain proteins. Among the eight genes, two were replicated in the confirmatory PWAS, one did not replicate, and five were not profiled in the confirmatory brain proteome. Consequently, an additional layer of validation based on TWAS was performed, revealing that 6/8 genes had cis-regulated brain mRNA levels associated with GBM. MR analyses at both the protein and transcriptional levels, along with Bayesian co-localization, further supported the causal associations between candidate genes and GBM risk. Based on a comprehensive evaluation, three genes – EGFR, SCFD1, and GMPPB – were assigned high confidence as potential therapeutic targets.

Among the high-confidence genes, GMPPB and EGFR have been previously investigated in the context of GBM. In contrast, SCFD1 has not been investigated in the context of GBM or other types of gliomas. GMPPB, or guanosine diphosphate mannose pyrophosphorylase B, catalyzes the synthesis of guanosine diphosphate mannose, a crucial precursor for the glycosylation of lipids and proteins. GMPPB has primarily been studied in congenital myasthenic syndromes, a heterogeneous group of rare inherited neuromuscular junction disorders resulting from defects in proteins that are crucial for neuromuscular transmission. Recent studies have also established an association between GMPPB and various mental disorders, including depression, suicide attempts, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. To date, only one study has focused on the relationship between GMPPB and glioblastoma (GBM). Huang et al demonstrated that silencing GMPPB inhibits the proliferation, migration, and invasion of GBM cells both in vitro and in vivo, while overexpression of GMPPB produces the opposite effects. Furthermore, they indicated that GMPPB influences GBM through the Hippo/MMP3 pathways. The results were partly consistent with the current study, as we found that increased abundances of GMPPB were associated with a higher risk of GBM at both the protein level (OR 3.155, 95% CI 1.777–5.604) and the transcriptional level (OR 1.334, 95% CI 1.168–1.523). In addition, GMPPB has been identified as a prognostic marker in ovarian cancers.

EGFR, also known as HER1 or ERBB1, is a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase belonging to the ERBB family. EGFR amplification and/or mutation is observed in approximately 57% of primary GBM and serves as both a diagnostic biomarker and a therapeutic target. Among EGFR alterations, the EGFRvIII mutant – characterized by an in-frame deletion of exons 2–7 – is the most frequent and is believed to emerge after amplification of wild-type EGFR, representing a late event in tumor evolution. Current therapeutic strategies targeting EGFR and EGFRvIII include, but are not limited to: tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as dacomitinib and rociletinib; monoclonal antibodies like nimotuzumab and mAb806; peptide vaccines such as rindopepimut; chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells targeting EGFRvIII (currently in clinical trials); and RNA-based approaches, including antisense oligonucleotides, RNA interference, ribozymes, and miRNA-based adjuvant therapies. However, despite extensive efforts, EGFR/EGFRvIII-targeted therapies have not demonstrated consistent clinical benefit. Therapeutic resistance is attributed to factors such as poor blood–brain barrier permeability, intratumoral heterogeneity, activation of compensatory signaling pathways, and the emergence of secondary mutations.

Notably, our study found that genetically predicted higher EGFR expression was associated with a reduced risk of GBM, a finding that may appear counterintuitive given EGFR’s well-established oncogenic role in glioblastoma. This apparent paradox can be explained by distinguishing between baseline physiological expression – as captured by eQTL-based MR – and non-physiological alterations such as gene amplification and activating mutations (e.g., EGFRvIII), which drive constitutive receptor activation and tumorigenesis. Our MR results reflect the effect of inherited variants regulating EGFR expression in normal brain tissue, rather than somatic changes occurring in the tumor microenvironment. Therefore, this inverse association may suggest that endogenous EGFR expression levels are not oncogenic per se, and that the pathogenicity of EGFR in GBM likely depends on its aberrant structural alterations and context-specific overactivation. This mechanistic distinction is critical for interpreting genetically informed associations within cancer research.

SCFD1, or Sec1 Family Domain Containing 1, is located on chromosome 14 and plays a role in anterograde transport from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus. Previous studies have reported that SCFD1 regulates the process of autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Researchers have also indicated that SCFD1 is a risk gene for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). SCFD1 in blood and brain eQTL has shown a prognostic effect on ALS, with increased SCFD1 expression potentially reducing survival in ALS patients. The current study demonstrated that SCFD1 exerts a protective effect on the brain against the risk of GBM at both the protein and transcriptional levels. Given the importance of autophagy and vesicular trafficking in glioma cell survival, metabolism, and immune evasion, dysregulation of SCFD1 could influence GBM progression through multiple mechanisms. For instance, altered SCFD1 function may impair lysosomal degradation of signaling proteins or affect secretion of immunosuppressive factors, ultimately shaping the tumor microenvironment. These potential roles warrant further experimental investigation.

Among the therapeutic targets with low to moderate confidence levels, KDELC2 and GPX1 have been investigated in GBM basic research. KDELC2, a factor associated with Notch signaling, plays a critical role in the maturation of Notch receptors (Notch1–4) and the activation of downstream signaling cascades. Tsai et al demonstrated that KDELC2 overexpression contributes to GBM tumorigenesis and promotes aggressive phenotypes by enhancing Notch signaling pathways. In subsequent studies, KDELC2 was also shown to facilitate glioblastoma angiogenesis by increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, inducing endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and modulating the tumor microenvironment (TME). Glutathione peroxidase 1 (GPX1), another potential target, has been identified as a key enzyme in the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide under hypoxic tumor conditions in GBM. Evidence suggests that GPX1 may play an important role in GBM progression and could serve as a promising candidate for therapeutic intervention.

Despite the benefits of integrating multi-omics data and various methodologies to gain comprehensive insights into the complex biological systems of GBM in the human brain, the current study has several limitations. First, the brain proteomic and transcriptomic data were derived from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex region, with a relatively small sample size and a limited number of detectable proteins, which may affect the robustness and generalizability of the findings. Second, GBM exhibits substantial heterogeneity across subtypes and molecular features, such as IDH1-mutant versus IDH1-wildtype tumors. While we consider our multi-omics results to be broadly independent of these markers, stratified analyses would provide stronger validation. Third, as the study population was exclusively of European ancestry, the applicability of the findings to other ethnic groups remains uncertain. Fourth, the study did not include experimental validation using immunohistochemistry or other wet-lab techniques, which limits the biological interpretation of the computational results. Future work will focus on functional validation to substantiate these bioinformatics-driven findings. Fifth, the absence of detailed clinical information such as gender and age prevented us from performing stratified analyses across these key variables, which may have further refined the interpretability and translational value of our findings. Sixth, while the use of DLPFC-derived QTL datasets offers considerable statistical power and is supported by evidence of cross-regional QTL sharing, the reliance on a single brain region may not fully capture the spatially heterogeneous regulatory landscape relevant to GBM pathogenesis. Seventh, the sample size of the proteomic confirmatory cohort was relatively limited, which may reduce the statistical power to validate associations identified in the discovery phase. While this constraint reflects the current scarcity of brain tissues with matched proteomic and genomic data, it nonetheless warrants cautious interpretation of replication results.
Conclusion

In conclusion, by integrating brain proteomic and transcriptomic data with the largest available GBM GWAS dataset, we conducted a comprehensive multi-omics analysis – including PWAS, TWAS, pQTL/eQTL-based MR, and colocalization approaches – and identified eight potential therapeutic candidate genes for glioblastoma. Based on the strength of evidence across these analyses, we assigned confidence levels to each candidate. Three genes – EGFR, SCFD1, and GMPPB – were classified as high-confidence therapeutic targets. Among them, EGFR is a well-established target in GBM treatment, with ongoing efforts to develop more effective targeted therapies. GMPPB has been explored in preclinical GBM studies, while SCFD1 has not yet been investigated in the context of GBM. Thus, our study highlights two previously unrecognized high-confidence targets for GBM therapy. Overall, these findings provide new insights into brain-specific molecular mechanisms underlying glioblastoma and lay the groundwork for future research into novel therapeutic strategies.

passages.text: Background

Ovarian cancer remains one of the most lethal gynecological malignancies with limited understanding of its genetic architecture and causal mechanisms. While genome-wide association studies have identified numerous susceptibility loci, the causal relationships between gene expression and ovarian cancer risk remain poorly understood.
Methods

We conducted a comprehensive genetic analysis integrating two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) using expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data from the GTEx project and ovarian cancer GWAS data from the Ovarian Cancer Association Consortium (OCAC). Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) analysis was performed to assess causal relationships between gene expression and ovarian cancer risk. Additionally, we analyzed survival outcomes in 3595 ovarian cancer patients from the SEER database to examine the clinical implications of radiation timing and constructed a prognostic nomogram incorporating genetic and clinical factors.
Results

MR analysis identified three genes with significant causal associations with ovarian cancer risk. GSTZ1 variant rs11621440 demonstrated a protective effect (OR = 0.999, 95% CI 0.999–1.000, FDR = 0.001), while PNP variant rs8015430 (OR = 1.006, 95% CI 1.002–1.010, FDR = 0.002) and KIAA1715 variant rs864697 (OR = 0.999, 95% CI 0.999–1.000, FDR = 0.002) showed increased risk associations. TWAS analysis revealed multiple genes with transcriptome-wide significant associations, including SIGLEC family genes (SIGLEC14, SIGLEC12, SIGLEC5) associated with increased risk through decreased expression, and metabolic genes (OCTN2, MSR1) associated with risk through increased expression. Survival analysis demonstrated that radiation timing significantly impacts prognosis, with postoperative radiation showing superior outcomes compared to preoperative radiation (HR = 1.49, 95% CI 1.23–1.82, p = 5.8 × 10−5).
Conclusions
This study provides robust genetic evidence for causal relationships between specific gene expression patterns and ovarian cancer risk.
Introduction

Ovarian malignancy constitutes the fifth most significant contributor to cancer mortality among women globally, accounting for approximately 295,000 newly diagnosed cases and 185,000 fatalities each year. Notwithstanding progress in operative procedures and chemotherapy protocols, the aggregate 5-year survival percentage continues to be discouragingly poor at roughly 47%, predominantly due to delayed diagnostic detection and insufficient comprehension of the molecular processes that drive tumor formation and advancement.

The genomic framework of ovarian cancer exhibits complexity and involves multiple factors, encompassing both inherited susceptibility and spontaneous mutations. Although high-penetrance genes including BRCA1 and BRCA2 contribute to roughly 10–15% of ovarian cancer instances, most cases develop from the combined impact of numerous low-penetrance genetic variations. Genome-wide association investigations (GWAS) have effectively discovered more than 40 susceptibility regions linked to ovarian cancer predisposition, however the biological implications of these variants and their targeted genes continue to be predominantly uncharacterized.

Contemporary methodological developments in genetic epidemiology, especially Mendelian randomization (MR) and transcriptome-wide association investigations (TWAS), have transformed our capacity to determine causal connections between gene expression patterns and disease manifestations. MR employs genetic variants as instrumental variables to reduce confounding factors and reverse causation, delivering solid evidence for causal determination. TWAS combines GWAS summary data with gene expression prediction frameworks to recognize genes whose expression patterns correlate with disease susceptibility, providing understanding into the biological mechanisms underlying genetic correlations.

The glutathione S-transferase zeta 1 (GSTZ1) gene, which codes for an essential enzyme in the tyrosine breakdown pathway and glutathione conjugation processes, has appeared as a potentially protective element in multiple cancers. GSTZ1 operates in cellular detoxification mechanisms and may affect cancer predisposition through its function in processing carcinogenic substances and preserving cellular redox balance. Nevertheless, its particular involvement in ovarian cancer development has not been extensively examined.

Likewise, the sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectin (SIGLEC) gene group constitutes a collection of cell surface receptors mainly found on immune cells, particularly those from myeloid origins. These molecules serve essential functions in immune detection and control, potentially affecting tumor immune monitoring and evasion strategies. The relationship between SIGLEC gene expression and ovarian cancer susceptibility may offer understanding into the immunological components of ovarian cancer initiation and advancement.

This investigation seeks to fill these knowledge voids by performing a thorough analysis that combines MR and TWAS methodologies to recognize causal genes linked with ovarian cancer susceptibility, evaluating the clinical consequences of treatment scheduling, and creating an integrated predictive model. More precisely, we aim to: (1) recognize genes with causal connections to ovarian cancer susceptibility using MR analysis; (2) perform genome-wide TWAS to discover additional susceptibility genes; (3) assess the influence of radiation scheduling on ovarian cancer survival results; and (4) create and validate a predictive nomogram that integrates genetic and clinical elements for individualized risk evaluation.
Methods
Mendelian randomization analysis methods

This study employed a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) design, utilizing genetic variants as instrumental variables to infer causal relationships between gene expression and ovarian cancer risk. Exposure data were derived from expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data from large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS), while outcome data were obtained from ovarian cancer GWAS meta-analysis databases. The eQTL data primarily originated from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project and the Blood eQTL Browser, containing gene expression regulatory information across multiple tissue types. Ovarian cancer GWAS data were sourced from the Ovarian Cancer Association Consortium (OCAC), encompassing genetic variant information from over 25,000 ovarian cancer patients and 40,000 control individuals.
Instrumental variable selection and quality control

Instrumental variable selection adhered to the three core assumptions of Mendelian randomization: (1) Relevance assumption: genetic variants are strongly associated with gene expression; (2) Independence assumption: genetic variants are independent of confounding factors; (3) Exclusion restriction assumption: genetic variants affect ovarian cancer risk solely through gene expression. Specific selection criteria included: single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with gene expression association P-values < 5 × 10−8, linkage disequilibrium r² < 0.001, and minor allele frequency > 0.01. For each target gene, the cis-acting SNP most strongly associated with its expression level was selected as the instrumental variable. SNPs significantly associated with known confounding factors (such as body mass index, smoking, reproductive factors) were excluded through PhenoScanner database queries.
Heterogeneity and Pleiotropy testing

Cochran’s Q statistic was used to test heterogeneity among instrumental variables, with P < 0.05 indicating significant heterogeneity. Horizontal pleiotropy was assessed through the intercept term of MR-Egger regression, with significant deviation from zero indicating pleiotropy bias. The I² statistic was calculated to quantify the degree of heterogeneity, with I² > 50% indicating moderate to high heterogeneity. To further validate the directionality of causal relationships, reverse Mendelian randomization analysis was performed, using ovarian cancer risk as exposure and gene expression as outcome. The Steiger filtering method was employed to verify the correctness of causal direction.
Transcriptome-wide association study analysis

Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) were conducted to identify genes associated with ovarian cancer at the transcriptomic level. TWAS integrated GWAS summary statistics with gene expression prediction models to assess associations between gene expression and ovarian cancer risk. FUSION software was used for TWAS analysis, employing tissue-specific gene expression prediction weights from the GTEx project. Analyses included ovarian tissue and other relevant tissue types (such as fallopian tubes, endometrium). Multiple comparison correction was performed using Bonferroni correction, with corrected P < 0.05 considered transcriptome-wide significant. Manhattan plots were generated to display genome-wide TWAS results, while volcano plots showed the relationship between gene effect sizes and statistical significance.
Model validation and quality assessment

Leave-one-out cross-validation was used to assess the robustness of Mendelian randomization analyses, sequentially removing each instrumental variable and re-performing the analysis. QQ plots were generated to evaluate whether P-value distributions conformed to expected theoretical distributions, validating the reliability of analytical results. False discovery rate (FDR) control methods were employed for multiple comparison correction, with FDR < 0.05 results considered statistically significant. Forest plots displayed the association strength and direction between genetic variants and ovarian cancer risk, including odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals. All analyses were conducted using R software, primarily utilizing specialized packages including TwoSampleMR, SMR, and FUSION.
Statistical analysis methods

Summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) methods were employed to assess causal relationships between gene expression and ovarian cancer risk. SMR analysis integrated eQTL and GWAS summary statistics, calculating causal effect estimates through the Wald ratio method. The primary analysis utilized the inverse variance weighted (IVW) method, which assumes all instrumental variables are valid. To assess result robustness, sensitivity analyses were further conducted using MR-Egger regression, weighted median method, and MR-PRESSO approaches. MR-Egger regression can detect and correct for horizontal pleiotropy bias, the weighted median method provides unbiased estimates when 50% of instrumental variables are valid, and MR-PRESSO can identify and remove outlying instrumental variables.
SEER database analysis methods

This study conducted a retrospective cohort analysis based on the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database from the National Cancer Institute. The SEER database covers approximately 35% of the US population and provides high-quality data on cancer incidence, treatment patterns, and survival outcomes. The study included patients diagnosed with ovarian cancer from 1975 to the most recent data year, with case identification based on International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) codes. Inclusion criteria comprised: (1) histologically confirmed primary ovarian cancer; (2) female patients aged ≥ 18 years; (3) complete demographic, clinicopathological, and treatment information; (4) complete survival follow-up data. Exclusion criteria included: (1) non-epithelial ovarian tumors; (2) patients with multiple primary tumors; (3) cases with missing key variables.Based on multivariate Cox regression analysis results, a nomogram model was constructed to predict 12-month, 36-month, and 60-month survival probabilities for ovarian cancer patients. The nomogram integrated key prognostic variables including age, tumor stage, distant metastasis status, marital status, and radiation timing. Each predictor was assigned corresponding scores based on its regression coefficient in the Cox model, with total scores corresponding to predicted survival probabilities. Bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations) was employed for internal validation to assess model stability and predictive accuracy. Calibration plots evaluated the concordance between model-predicted probabilities and actual observed probabilities, while decision curve analysis (DCA) assessed the clinical utility of the model.
Statistical considerations and ethical statement

All statistical analyses employed two-sided tests, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant. For multiple comparisons, Bonferroni correction or FDR control methods were applied. Missing data were handled using complete case analysis or multiple imputation methods, with specific strategies determined based on missing patterns and proportions. The SEER database and GWAS summary data used in this study are de-identified public data resources, requiring no institutional review board approval. All analyses adhered to the requirements of STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) and STROBE-MR (Strengthening the Reporting of Mendelian Randomization studies) guidelines.
Results
Mendelian randomization analysis results for ovarian cancer-associated genes

This Mendelian randomization analysis demonstrates the associations between three genetic variants and ovarian cancer risk. The GSTZ1 gene variant rs11621440 shows a significant protective effect with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.999 (95% CI 0.999–1.000) and a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.001, suggesting that this variant may reduce ovarian cancer risk. Conversely, the PNP gene variant rs8015430 exhibits an opposite effect with an OR of 1.006 (95% CI 1.002–1.010) and FDR of 0.002, indicating that this variant may increase ovarian cancer risk. The KIAA1715 gene variant rs864697 similarly shows a trend toward increased risk with an OR of 0.999 (95% CI 0.999–1.000) and FDR of 0.002. All three genetic variants have FDR values less than 0.05, indicating statistical significance of these associations. The forest plot visually presents the effect sizes and confidence intervals for each variant, providing important epidemiological evidence for genetic susceptibility research in ovarian cancer (Fig. 1).

Forest plot of Mendelian randomization analysis for ovarian cancer-associated genetic variants. The figure shows the odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and false discovery rates (FDR) for specific SNP variants in three genes (GSTZ1, PNP, KIAA1715). The vertical dashed line represents the null effect line at OR = 1, square sizes reflect study precision, and horizontal lines indicate 95% confidence intervals
Volcano plot results of Mendelian randomization analysis for ovarian cancer

This volcano plot illustrates the relationship between effect sizes and statistical significance of genes in the Mendelian randomization analysis for ovarian cancer. The x-axis represents the beta coefficients from SMR (Summary-data-based Mendelian Randomization), reflecting the direction and magnitude of causal effects of gene expression on ovarian cancer risk. The y-axis shows − log10(P-value), with higher values indicating greater statistical significance. Circle sizes represent the magnitude of neglogP values, while the color gradient from blue to red reflects the degree of statistical significance. The results show that genes such as SIGLEC14, SIGLEC12, and SIGLEC5 are located in the upper left quadrant, indicating that decreased expression of these genes is significantly associated with increased ovarian cancer risk. GSTZ1 gene is positioned in the upper center, demonstrating strong statistical significance. Genes on the right side, such as OCTN2 and MSR1, suggest that increased gene expression may be associated with ovarian cancer risk. This analysis provides important genetic evidence for identifying potential causal genes and therapeutic targets for ovarian cancer (Fig. 2).

Volcano plot of SMR analysis for ovarian cancer. The x-axis shows SMR beta coefficients, and the y-axis represents − log10 (P-value). Circle sizes indicate neglogP values, and color gradients reflect statistical significance levels. Genes on the left are associated with increased ovarian cancer risk through decreased expression, while genes on the right are associated with risk through increased expression
Manhattan plot analysis results for ovarian cancer transcriptome-wide association study

This Manhattan plot displays the genome-wide analysis results from a transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) for ovarian cancer. The x-axis arranges all genes by chromosomal position, while the y-axis represents the negative logarithm of statistical significance (− log10 P-value), with higher values indicating stronger associations between genes and ovarian cancer. Different colored dots represent genes on different chromosomes, forming the characteristic Manhattan skyline pattern. The results reveal multiple genes reaching significant statistical thresholds, with the most significant signal peaks exceeding a − log10 P-value of 50, indicating strong causal associations between these gene expression levels and ovarian cancer risk. Numerous moderate-strength association signals are distributed across the genome with − log10 P-values ranging from 10 to 40, suggesting that ovarian cancer is a complex disease involving multiple genes acting in concert. This TWAS analysis provides crucial transcriptomic evidence for identifying key regulatory genes and potential therapeutic targets for ovarian cancer, contributing to a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying ovarian cancer pathogenesis (Fig. 3).

Manhattan plot for ovarian cancer transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS). The x-axis shows chromosomal positions of genes, and the y-axis represents statistical significance (− log10 P-value). Different colors represent different chromosomes, and the height of dots reflects the strength of association between gene expression and ovarian cancer
QQ plot analysis of model cross-validation P-values in Mendelian randomization

This quantile–quantile plot (QQ plot) evaluates the distribution characteristics of model cross-validation P-values in Mendelian randomization analysis. The x-axis represents theoretical quantiles, while the y-axis shows sample quantiles, with the red line indicating the expected theoretical distribution. The orange solid line displays the observed P-value distribution, and the orange dashed line represents the confidence interval. The results demonstrate that observed values closely align with theoretical expectations across most intervals, indicating good model calibration. However, there is slight deviation at the right end (high quantile region), where the orange line is slightly above the red theoretical line, potentially suggesting the presence of a few statistically significant signals or minor model bias. Overall, the QQ plot shows good model fit, with most P-values conforming to the expected uniform distribution, validating the reliability of the Mendelian randomization analysis results and the reasonableness of statistical assumptions. This provides important methodological quality assurance for subsequent causal inference (Fig. 4).

QQ plot of model cross-validation P-values in Mendelian randomization. The x-axis shows theoretical quantiles, and the y-axis represents sample quantiles. The red line indicates the theoretical expected distribution, the orange solid line shows the observed distribution, and the dashed line represents the confidence interval
Survival analysis of ovarian cancer based on radiation timing

Analysis of survival outcomes reveals marked disparities between ovarian cancer patients based on radiation therapy timing relative to surgical intervention. Throughout the 212-month observation period, patients undergoing postoperative radiation therapy (blue line) consistently exhibited superior survival probabilities when compared to their counterparts receiving preoperative radiation (brown line). Statistical analysis confirmed the significance of this difference (p = 5.8e−5), with preoperative radiation patients facing a 49% elevated mortality risk (HR = 1.49, 95% CI 1.23–1.82). Early divergence of the survival curves occurred within the initial follow-up phase, persisting throughout the study duration. While both treatment groups ultimately converged to approximately 30% survival probability at study conclusion, the postoperative radiation cohort maintained superior survival rates during the majority of the observation timeline. Patient distribution showed considerable imbalance, with 3453 individuals in the postoperative group versus 142 in the preoperative group, with progressive attrition due to mortality events and study censoring (Fig. 5).

Survival analysis of ovarian cancer based on radiation timing. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis demonstrates superior outcomes for ovarian cancer patients receiving radiation therapy following surgical intervention compared to preoperative radiation recipients (p = 5.8e−5). Preoperative radiation was associated with 49% increased mortality risk (HR = 1.49). Despite convergence to approximately 30% survival at follow-up completion, postoperative radiation recipients demonstrated sustained survival advantages throughout the observation period. These results corroborate multivariate Cox regression findings, emphasizing radiation timing as a pivotal therapeutic consideration
Nomogram for predicting survival in ovarian cancer patients based on clinical and treatment factors

Five key prognostic variables form the foundation of this predictive model: patient age, disease staging, metastatic status (M), marital circumstances, and radiation therapy timing relative to surgery. Point allocation for each variable correlates with prognostic severity, where elevated scores typically signify diminished survival prospects. Advanced age (≥ 65 years) generates higher point values compared to younger patients (< 65 years), demonstrating age-associated mortality risk escalation. Progressive disease stages accumulate increasing point values, with Stage IV disease commanding maximum point contribution. Distant metastatic disease (M1) substantially elevates point totals relative to M0 status. Marital status demonstrates protective associations, with married patients receiving reduced point allocations compared to divorced, separated, or widowed individuals, reinforcing marriage-related survival benefits identified in Cox regression modeling. Treatment sequencing significantly influences scoring, with preoperative radiation generating markedly higher point values than postoperative approaches. Clinical application involves identifying patient-specific characteristics across each variable, calculating cumulative point totals, and translating these scores into survival probability estimates at 12, 36, and 60-month intervals. Inverse relationships exist between total point accumulation and projected survival probabilities (Fig. 6).

Nomogram for predicting survival in ovarian cancer patients based on clinical and treatment factors. Comprehensive prognostic evaluation reveals survival outcomes determined through complex interplay among diverse clinical and biological parameters. Critical prognostic dimensions encompass patient age, tumor staging, molecular characterization, and therapeutic intervention strategies. Age-associated physiological deterioration demonstrates positive correlation with tumor grade progression, substantially influencing overall survival trajectories. Radiation and chemotherapy interventions, serving as primary therapeutic modalities, display considerable inter-patient response variability, reflecting tumor microenvironment heterogeneity and resistance mechanism diversity
Discussion

The extensive genetic investigation we conducted has uncovered meaningful discoveries regarding the causal connections between gene expression patterns and ovarian cancer susceptibility, delivering strong evidence for the participation of particular genetic networks in ovarian tumor development. The discovery of GSTZ1, PNP, and KIAA1715 as genes demonstrating causal relationships marks a notable progress in comprehending the molecular processes that drive ovarian cancer predisposition.

The most striking result from our MR analysis involves the protective influence of the GSTZ1 variant rs11621440 against ovarian cancer susceptibility (OR = 0.999, FDR = 0.001). GSTZ1 codes for glutathione S-transferase zeta 1, an essential enzyme within phase II detoxification mechanisms that metabolizes diverse xenobiotics and internal compounds. This enzyme serves a bifunctional role in cellular processes, operating within both the tyrosine breakdown pathway and glutathione conjugation reactions that promote the clearance of potentially cancer-causing substances.

The protective influence of GSTZ1 in ovarian malignancy corresponds with its recognized function in cellular detoxification and oxidative balance maintenance. Increased GSTZ1 expression or enzymatic activity may enhance cellular abilities to neutralize reactive oxygen species and process carcinogenic molecules, thus decreasing the probability of DNA damage and cancerous transformation. This discovery holds particular importance considering that ovarian cancer formation has been associated with oxidative stress and contact with environmental cancer-causing agents.

Earlier research has shown that genetic variations in glutathione S-transferase genes can markedly affect cancer predisposition across different tumor categories. Our findings broaden this knowledge to ovarian cancer and indicate that GSTZ1 might function as a biomarker for risk classification and potentially as a treatment target. The recognition of GSTZ1 as a protective element creates new opportunities for cancer prevention approaches and emphasizes the significance of metabolic networks in ovarian cancer development.

The recognition of purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) and KIAA1715 as risk-linked genes offers further understanding into the metabolic foundations of ovarian cancer. PNP serves an essential function in purine processing, facilitating the phosphorolysis of nucleosides to produce ribose-1-phosphate and purine bases. Disruption of purine metabolism has been connected to multiple cancers, since modified nucleotide concentrations can influence DNA synthesis, repair processes, and cellular growth.

The correlation between reduced SIGLEC expression and elevated ovarian cancer risk indicates a possible function for these molecules in tumor immune monitoring. SIGLEC proteins are mainly found on immune cells, especially macrophages, dendritic cells, and other myeloid cell types that form significant elements of the tumor environment. Diminished expression of these immune detection molecules may compromise immune cell capabilities to identify and destroy malignant cells, enabling tumor evasion and advancement.

Our survival examination showing the improved outcomes linked with postoperative compared to preoperative radiation therapy (HR = 1.49, p = 5.8 × 10−5) offers valuable clinical direction for treatment sequencing. This result indicates that radiation therapy timing constitutes a crucial element that requires careful evaluation in treatment planning.

The creation of our prognostic nomogram combining genetic and clinical elements represents progress toward personalized medicine in ovarian cancer management. Through incorporating genetic risk factors together with conventional clinical parameters such as age, stage, and treatment methodology, healthcare providers may offer more precise prognostic data and customize treatment approaches for individual patients.
Limitations

Although our investigation delivers solid genetic evidence for causal connections between gene expression and ovarian cancer risk, several constraints warrant recognition. Initially, the effect magnitudes noted for individual genetic variants are comparatively modest, indicating the polygenic characteristics of ovarian cancer susceptibility. Subsequent studies involving larger participant groups may be required to identify additional variants with smaller influences.

Furthermore, our examination concentrated mainly on common genetic variants, and uncommon variants with greater effects may not have been sufficiently detected. Comprehensive genome or exome sequencing investigations may be necessary to thoroughly characterize the complete range of genetic variation that contributes to ovarian cancer risk.
Conclusions

This study represents one of the most comprehensive genetic analyses of ovarian cancer to date, integrating multiple analytical approaches to identify causal genes and develop clinically relevant prognostic models. The identification of GSTZ1 as a protective factor and the SIGLEC gene family as risk-associated through immune mechanisms provides new insights into ovarian cancer pathogenesis and potential therapeutic targets.

passages.text: Bladder cancer (BLCA) is the predominant type of urothelial carcinoma in urinary system, and resistance to cisplatin-based chemotherapy substantially worsens clinical outcomes, presenting a major therapeutic obstacle. In this study, we integrated genome-wide association study (GWAS) data with expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) analyses, and applied Mendelian randomization (MR) to assess the causal effects of eQTLs from 19,942 genes on BLCA. By incorporating scRNA-seq data, our study also identifies differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in cisplatin-resistant BLCA cells and examined their causal associations with BLCA, aiming to elucidate genetic drivers of chemoresistance and tumor progression. Through this integrated approach, we identified the eQTL of the ARHGEF12 gene as a key mediator of cisplatin resistance. Bioinformatic analysis revealed that elevated ARHGEF12 expression was strongly associated with activation of the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. To define ARHGEF12’s role in cisplatin resistance, we established a cisplatin-resistant UM-UC-3/DDP model. Silencing ARHGEF12 markedly reduced chemoresistance, increased apoptotic cell death, and induced pronounced morphological changes. Pharmacological modulation with the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 and a rescue assay with the Akt activator SC79 supported a model in which ARHGEF12 drives chemoresistance via RhoA/ROCK-dependent activation of the PI3K/AKT axis. This study is the first to integrate MR with single-cell transcriptomics to explore the genetic contribution to cisplatin resistance in BLCA. Our results uncover a novel mechanistic role of ARHGEF12 in BLCA progression and chemoresistance and suggest it as a potential therapeutic target for precision treatment strategies.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s41065-025-00606-1.
Introduction

Bladder cancer (BLCA) is one of the most prevalent malignancies of the urinary tract, with over 430,000 new cases reported globally each year. Both the incidence and mortality rates have shown a persistent upward trend in recent years. Cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy remains the cornerstone of treatment; however, fewer than half of the patients exhibit an initial therapeutic response. In addition, a substantial number of those who initially respond later develop resistance, which severely limits the long-term success of treatment strategies. This highlights the urgent need to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying cisplatin resistance and to identify novel therapeutic targets that may enhance clinical outcomes.

Single-cell RNA sequencing has been widely employed to elucidate cellular heterogeneity and to investigate the genetic, transcriptional, and epigenetic characteristics of cancer cell populations and individual tumor cells through multidimensional analyses. The limitations of conventional sequencing approaches are overcome by this technology: whereas bulk RNA sequencing averages transcriptional signals across cell populations, scRNA-seq enables complete transcriptome profiling at single-cell resolution. This capability enables detailed analyses of intracellular and intercellular interactions, allows subtle intercellular heterogeneity — difficult to detect in bulk cellular analyses — to be uncovered, supports the identification of novel cell types, and permits monitoring of dynamic changes in cellular states.Enhanced resolution of scRNA-seq facilitates delineation of heterogeneity among drug-resistant tumor cells and within the tumor microenvironment, enables identification of potential therapeutic targets, and provides evidence to support the development of personalized treatment strategies. However, the roles of DEGs linked to heterogeneity in cisplatin-resistant bladder cancer cells remain unclear. Moreover, the causal contribution of DEGs specific to cisplatin-resistant bladder cancer cells to the initiation and progression of bladder urothelial carcinoma has not been fully elucidated.

To address these gaps, this study employs MR to investigate the genetic determinants of disease susceptibility and treatment resistance. MR analysis uses genetic variants associated with a specific exposure as instrumental variables (IVs) to infer the causal effect of that exposure on outcomes, while mitigating bias from confounding and reverse causation.Specifically, using MR analysis, we tested whether expression levels of candidate genes causally influence BLCA risk.Within the DEG analysis framework, we integrated genome-wide association study data with eQTL data to identify genes whose expression variability is associated with complex phenotypes. This study integrated scRNA-seq sequencing with MR analysis to enable high-resolution, cell-type–specific profiling of gene expression effects.Such integration reduces confounding and other sources of bias in causal inference, enabling more precise delineation of disease mechanisms and improved prioritization of candidate therapeutic targets. Building on the analyses above, we aim to clarify how genetic alterations in drug-resistant tumor cells contribute to the development of chemotherapy resistance in BLCA.
Results
scRNA-seq integrated with genetically-predicted eQTLs to assess causal mechanisms underlying chemotherapy resistance in bladder cancer

In this study, we interrogated the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) to identify bladder cancer-relevant datasets and retrieved the GSE192575 single-cell RNA sequencing dataset. This dataset comprises transcriptional profiles from two BLCA patients exhibiting contrasting responses to cisplatin-based chemotherapy. Following stringent data normalization and batch effect correction, dimensionality reduction and unsupervised clustering were performed. We subsequently mapped the expression distribution of key marker genes across distinct cellular subpopulations. Cluster analysis was performed using UMAP dimensionality reduction. Through SingleR-based annotation, cells within tumor tissues were classified into seven distinct subtypes (Fig. 1A), encompassing B cells, CD8 + T cells, endothelial cells, epithelial cells, fibroblasts, macrophages, and monocytes. The top three marker genes for each cellular cluster were delineated (Fig. 1D). Notably, each subtype exhibited differential distribution patterns between cisplatin-sensitive and cisplatin-resistant bladder cancer specimens (Fig. 1B-C). Comparative cellular composition analysis revealed significant proportion differences between treatment-responsive and resistant cohorts (Fig. 1E). Transcriptomic profiling identified 4,106 DEGs in epithelial cells from cisplatin-sensitive versus resistant samples (Fig. 1F). To elucidate the functional significance of these DEGs, Mendelian randomization analysis was employed, establishing causal relationships between 19,942 eQTLs and cisplatin resistance. This genetic approach identified 188 eQTL genes with causal associations to bladder cancer pathogenesis. Integration of eQTL and DEG datasets revealed 27 core genes implicated in cisplatin resistance. Among these, 19 candidate genes (e.g., ARHGEF12, RNF40, SLK, TNFSF11, CASC3) demonstrated both upregulation in resistant epithelium and MR odds ratios (OR) > 1, while 8 candidates (e.g., PDLIM7, CNN3, ITM2C, DGUOK, GAPDH) showed downregulation with OR < 1 (Fig. 1G).

Next, we visualized the Mendelian randomization results for the 27 core genes using lollipop plots and forest plots (Fig. 1I-H). Specifically, genes with p < 0.05 in the IVW analysis were defined as those causally associated with cisplatin chemoresistance. The directionality of the IVW findings was further validated by complementary models, including WM, MR-Egger, Simple Mode, and Weighted Mode analyses. Collectively, these 27 core genes, identified through an integrated approach of single-cell profiling and Mendelian randomization, are not only highly associated with the heritability of bladder cancer pathogenesis but also strongly linked to the incidence of cisplatin chemoresistance, thus warranting further mechanistic investigation.

Identification of risk genes through Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis and Mendelian randomization analysis. A UMAP plot showing seven distinct cell clusters. B, C UMAP visualizations of the distribution of cells in cisplatin-resistant and cisplatin-sensitive samples. D Violin plot displaying the top three genes for each of the seven cell clusters. Functional enrichment analysis of the core genes

We further analyzed the expression patterns of our core genes within BLCA tissue and found that they are mainly distributed across epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts (Fig. 2A). To better understand the biological roles of these core genes, we performed Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses. As shown in Fig. 2B–D, GO enrichment analysis revealed the following: (1) In the BP category, the genes were enriched in biological processes such as positive regulation of the apoptotic signaling pathway, purine nucleotide biosynthetic process, respiratory electron transport chain, and deoxyribonucleoside metabolic process. (2) In the CC category, they were linked to the formation or function of lipid droplets, oxidoreductase complexes, and lysosomal membranes. (3) In the MF category, they showed strong associations with cadherin binding, oxidoreductase activity, and cobalamin binding. As shown in Fig. 3E–F, KEGG pathway analysis indicated that these core genes are mainly involved in pathways related to amino acid biosynthesis, the HIF-1 signaling pathway, and alpha-linolenic acid metabolism. To further investigate their chromosomal distribution and structural characteristics, we constructed a circular plot showing the genomic locations of these core genes (Fig. 2G).

Causal relationship between ARHGEF12 and cisplatin chemotherapy resistance in BLCA

MR analysis indicated that the eQTL of ARHGEF12 has a notably stronger causal association with BLCA than the other core genes, implying that ARHGEF12 expression represents a major risk factor for the disease. The scatter plot shows consistent regression trends across multiple methods (Fig. 3A). The funnel plot illustrates the symmetry of causal effect estimates, supporting the reliability of the results (Fig. 3B). To assess the stability of the MR findings, we conducted a leave-one-out analysis, which showed no substantial influence from any single SNP on the overall causal effect (Fig. 3C). The forest plot details the individual effect sizes of the SNPs within the ARHGEF12 eQTL (Fig. 3D). MR-Egger intercept analysis of the ARHGEF12 eQTL yielded a p value of 0.936, indicating no significant horizontal pleiotropy, and suggesting that the instrumental variables do not substantially affect the outcome through alternate pathways. Additionally, the Cochran Q test for heterogeneity gave a p value of 0.976, suggesting low heterogeneity in the ARHGEF12 eQTL data.

Concurrently, after identifying ARHGEF12 as a marker gene, we isolated epithelial cell clusters from the single-cell dataset and performed dimensionality reduction and clustering (Fig. 3E). Visualization of core gene expression across the epithelial cell clusters showed that ARHGEF12 is markedly overexpressed in cisplatin-resistant epithelial cells (Fig. 3F-G). These results indicate that high ARHGEF12 expression is not only closely linked to BLCA but may also represent a critical driver of resistance to cisplatin chemotherapy.

Clinical relevance and functional enrichment analysis of ARHGEF12 in BLCA

We examined clinical samples from the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) database (Fig. 4 A) and found that e is broadly expressed across tumor tissues. For a more detailed investigation, we conducted bioinformatics analysis using the SangBox 3.0 platform (http://sangerbox.com/home.html), with BLCA datasets obtained from TCGA and GTEx (accessed on October 1, 2024). The association between ARHGEF12 expression and clinical outcomes in BLCA patients was evaluated through the log-rank test. Results showed that patients with high ARHGEF12 expression had significantly poorer prognoses than those with low expression levels. The hazard ratios (HR) were as follows: OS: HR = 1.45, p = 0.02; DSS: HR = 1.61, p = 0.01; DFI: HR = 2.38, p = 0.01; PFI: HR = 1.74, p = 5.5e-4 (Fig. 4B).

We then used the TCGA-BLCA dataset to compare DEGs between low and high ARHGEF12 expression groups (Fig. 4 C), aiming to investigate the gene’s functional roles. Enrichment results indicated involvement in pathways such as Biological Oxidation, Glucuronidation, and Metabolism of Amine-Derived Hormones. Importantly, the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, which plays a central role in tumor initiation and progression, was also enriched (Fig. 4D–E).

To further explore the biological activity of ARHGEF12, we conducted GSEA analysis. The results indicated that ARHGEF12 expression is linked to immune-related processes, including B cell-mediated immunity, immunoglobulin complexes, antigen binding, immunoglobulin receptor binding, and phagocytosis recognition signaling (Fig. 4 F). In the high-expression group, the top five enriched pathways were Ascorbate and Aldarate Metabolism, Drug Metabolism-Other Enzymes, Pentose and Glucuronate Interconversions, and Porphyrin and Chlorophyll Metabolism (Fig. 4G). Establishment of cisplatin-resistant UM-UC-3 BLCA cell line

To explore the role of ARHGEF12 in BLCA chemotherapy resistance, we established a cisplatin-resistant UM-UC-3/DDP cell line model based on previous work from our group. The resistant cells were able to grow and maintain stable proliferation in medium containing 3 µg/mL cisplatin. Morphologically, UM-UC-3 cells displayed a spindle-shaped appearance with uniform size, well-defined boundaries, and adherent growth. In contrast, UM-UC-3/DDP cells appeared more irregular and shrunken, with visible granules and vacuoles in the cytoplasm (Fig. 5A). After co-treatment with 3 µg/mL cisplatin for 48 h, apoptosis was significantly increased in UM-UC-3 cells compared to UM-UC-3/DDP cells (Fig. 5B). CCK-8 assay results showed that the IC50 of UM-UC-3/DDP cells was substantially higher than that of UM-UC-3 cells, with a resistance index of approximately 9.93 (Fig. 5C–D).

The role of ARHGEF12 in the process of drug resistance formation in bladder cancer

Interestingly, RT-qPCR and Western blotting demonstrated that ARHGEF12 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels was markedly elevated in UM-UC-3/DDP cells compared with parental UM-UC-3 cells (Fig. 6A-B). These results align with our earlier work and indicate that high ARHGEF12 expression in the cisplatin-derived UM-UC-3/DDP cell line may contribute to cisplatin resistance in bladder cancer cells. Both shRNAs efficiently reduced ARHGEF12 expression. Following ARHGEF12 knockdown, UM-UC-3/DDP cells cultured with 3 µg/mL cisplatin exhibited markedly reduced proliferation, a pronounced increase in apoptosis (Fig. 6E), and a significant reduction in the cisplatin resistance index (Fig. 6F–G). Collectively, these findings indicate that ARHGEF12 regulates cisplatin resistance in bladder cancer cells and underscore the precision of combining MR analysis with single-cell approaches to pinpoint candidate therapeutic targets.

ARHGEF12 promotes cisplatin resistance in BLCA via RhoA/ROCK-mediated activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway

Guided by bioinformatic predictions, this study investigated whether ARHGEF12 mediates cisplatin resistance via the PI3K/Akt pathway. In sh-ARHGEF12 UM-UC-3/DDP cells, plasmid-mediated ARHGEF12 knockdown markedly reduced PI3K and Akt phosphorylation (Fig. 7C). Administration of the Akt activator SC79 partially reversed these effects, restoring apoptosis in sh-ARHGEF12 UM-UC-3/DDP cells (Fig. 7A) and reducing the cisplatin resistance index (Fig. 7B). Multiple reports indicate that RhoA/ROCK signaling can activate PI3K/Akt signaling via downstream effectors, thereby influencing cell survival, proliferation, and apoptosis. Given that ARHGEF12 has been shown to regulate RhoA–ROCK, it is therefore proposed that ARHGEF12 may activate PI3K–Akt signaling by modulating this pathway. To test it, phosphorylation of myosin phosphatase target subunit 1 (MYPT1) was measured as a readout of RhoA/ROCK pathway activity. Results demonstrated the decreased MYPT1 phosphorylation in sh-ARHGEF12 UM-UC-3/DDP cells, indicating suppressed RhoA/ROCK pathway activity (Fig. 7C). Given that ROCK is a key regulator of cytoskeletal signaling and architecture determines cell shape, sh-ARHGEF12-treated UM-UC-3/DDP cells exhibited morphological deformation and atrophy accompanied by reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton (Fig. 7D–E). Moreover, treatment with the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 markedly reduced PI3K and Akt phosphorylation (Fig. 7F) and significantly sensitized UM-UC-3/DDP cells to cisplatin (Fig. 7G). SC79 partially rescued the apoptosis reduced by ROCK inhibition. PI3K/Akt signaling has a key role in drug-resistance phenotypes. Demonstrating that ARHGEF12 activates PI3K/Akt through modulation of the RhoA/ROCK cascade offers novel therapeutic avenues aimed at these signaling components or their downstream effectors. Collectively, our data indicate that ARHGEF12 activates PI3K/Akt signaling via the RhoA/ROCK axis, contributing to cisplatin resistance in BLCA.
