passages.text: In vitro experiments

C2C12 mouse myoblasts (Catalog No. CL-0045, Wuhan Punoise Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) were cultured in DMEM medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum. Cells were exposed to 10 µM CCCP for 12 h in order to create a model of mitochondrial autophagy. To investigate the causal role of the PINK1/Parkin pathway, a separate set of experiments was designed with five groups: (1) Control (C2C12); (2) Model (C2C12 + CCCP); (3) ICA treatment (C2C12 + CCCP + ICA); (4) Inhibitor (C2C12 + CCCP + Mdivi-1); (5) Inhibitor + ICA (C2C12 + CCCP + Mdivi-1 + ICA). A preliminary cell viability assay (CCK-8) was used to determine the ICA concentrations (100, 200, and 300 µM) for in vitro investigations. With 300 µM exhibiting the strongest protective effect, this range included doses that demonstrated minimal cytotoxicity and successfully stimulated C2C12 myoblast proliferation under CCCP-induced stress conditions (Supplementary Materials Figure S2).
Muscle strength test

Measure the grip strength of rats’ forelimbs using the YLS-13 A rat grip strength meter (Beijing Lai’ai Technology Development Co., Ltd.). Before testing, allow the rats to adapt to the grip strength meter for 10 min. Then grasp the rat’s tail and, once the rat’s forelimbs are firmly gripped, pull backward smoothly and record the maximum grip strength reading on the instrument. Measure three times and record the results, using the average of the three grip strength readings as an indicator of forelimb muscle strength.
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)

Use a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scanner to measure fat content, bone mineral content, and total body muscle mass in rats, while also measuring bone mineral density (BMD, g/cm²) in the spine, femur, and total body. Simultaneously calculate the skeletal muscle mass index (SMI, total lean body mass/body weight), bone mineral content percentage (BMC, bone mineral content/body weight), and fat content percentage (FAT, fat content/body weight) of rats.
Micro-CT

Using Micro-CT (Ping Sheng Medical Technology, NMC-200) to scan the distal femur, scanning parameters: radial field of view (FOV) 100 mm, maximum axial scanning range 250 mm, scanning speed up to 4 s/bed, reconstruction pixel size min. 2 μm, spatial resolution < 7.5 μm @ 10% MTF. The original image is then reconstructed using the 3D reconstruction software Recon. Then, use the data analysis software Avatar to analyze the region of interest (ROI). By setting uniform parameters, the software calculates bone volume (BV), tissue volume (TV), bone volume fraction (BV/TV), trabecular separation (Tb.Sp), trabecular thickness (Tb.Th), trabecular number (Tb.N), connectivity density (Conn.D), bone mineral density (BMD), and other related measurements.
HE staining

For HE staining of the right gastrocnemius and soleus muscle tissues, first stain the paraffin-embedded sections with hematoxylin for 5 to 10 min to stain the cell nuclei. After staining, rinse the sections with running water to remove excess dye, then wash with deionized water. Counterstain the cytoplasm with eosin, adjusting the staining time between 30 s and 3 min as needed. After re-staining, dehydrate the sections by continuously immersing them in 70%, 80%, and 90% ethanol, and finally in anhydrous ethanol, for 10 s each. Then, clear the sections twice with xylene for 5 min each time. Mount the sections with neutral resin. The staining results were evaluated under a microscope, showing blue-stained cell nuclei and cytoplasm ranging from pink to red. In addition, photographs of areas with clear and complete tissue structures were taken for further analysis, and the size of muscle fibers was quantified using ImageJ software.
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)

In this study, ELISA was used to quantitatively analyze serum inflammatory, muscle-related factors, and FNDC5 in SD rats. The Rat C-Reactive Protein (CRP) ELISA Kit (BY-ER330078) was used to measure plasma levels of CRP. The kit has a minimum detection limit of 10 ng/mL and a detection range of 75 to 2400 ng/mL. Rat Interleukin-6 (IL-6) ELISA Kit (BY-ER330219) is used to measure IL-6 plasma levels. The kit has a minimum detection limit of 1.0 ng/mL and a detection range of 5 to 160 pg/mL. Rat Growth Differentiation Factor 8 (GDF-8) ELISA Kit (BY-ER334915) is used to measure plasma levels of GDF-8. The kit has a minimum detection limit of 0.1 ng/mL and a detection range of 2.5 to 80 ng/mL. Rat Fibronectin Domain-Containing Protein 5 (FNDC5) ELISA Kit (BY-ER3200127) is used to measure plasma levels of FNDC5. The kit has a minimum detection limit of 0.1 ng/mL and a detection range of 3.125 to 100 ng/mL. All procedures are strictly conducted in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol.
CCK-8 method

Seed C2C12 cells at a density of 5 × 10³ cells per well into a 96-well plate, with 100 µL per well, and incubate overnight. In the culture plates, except for the control group, add 100 µL of 10 µM mitochondrial autophagy activator CCCP to each well, and incubate in the incubator for 12 h. After 12 h, the treatment group was exposed to different concentrations (100 µM, 200 µM, 300 µM) of ICA for 12 h, 24 h, and 48 h. After each exposure period, 10 µL of CCK-8 reagent was added to each well under dark conditions, and the absorbance (OD) at 450 nm was measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) Microplate reader.
Mitochondrial membrane potential detection

After the cells reach the logarithmic growth phase, prepare a single-cell suspension, adjust the cell count to an appropriate level, and inoculate 5 × 105 cells per well into a 6-well plate, 2 mL/well, and culture overnight. In the culture plates, except for the control group, 1 mL of 10 µM mitochondrial autophagy activator CCCP was added to each well and incubated in a culture incubator for 12 h. After 12 h, the treatment group was added to 300 µM ICA for 24 h. After completion, the culture medium was removed and washed once with PBS. Add 0.5 mL of culture medium and 0.5 mL of freshly prepared JC-1 staining working solution, mix the two, and incubate at 37 °C for 20 min. After completion, aspirate the supernatant, wash twice with freshly prepared JC-1 staining buffer (1X), resuspend the cells in an appropriate amount of JC-1 staining buffer (1X), and analyze using a flow cytometer.
Protein blot analysis

First, extract proteins from cells and muscle tissue, and determine protein concentration using the BCA protein assay kit (cwbiotech 02912E). Separate equal amounts of denatured proteins using 8% or 10% polyacrylamide gel via SDS-PAGE. Subsequently, transfer the separated proteins to a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane. Then, block the membrane with 5% skim milk at room temperature for 2 h to prevent non-specific binding. After closing, incubate the membrane with anti-PINK1 (1:1000, Bioss, BS-22173R), Parkin (1:1000, Bioss, BS-23687R), LC3 (1:500, Solarbio, K008014P), p62 (1:1000, Bioss, BS-55207R), FNDC5 (1:1000, Bioss, BS-8486R), Runx2 (1:1000, BS-1134R), OCN (1:500, BS-4917R), Actin (1:20,000, Bioss, BS-10966R) as the internal control. On the second day, wash the membrane three times with TBST, then incubate with the appropriate secondary antibody at room temperature for 2 h. Finally, detect the protein using an enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) detection kit (Millipore WBKLS0500) and observe the protein bands by exposing the membrane. Quantify gel and Western blot results using ImageJ software.
Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR)

RNA was extracted from cells using the TRIzol method. The RNA was reverse transcribed into cDNA using a reverse transcription kit according to the instructions. The cDNA was used as a template for detection on a fluorescence quantitative PCR instrument with GAPDH as an internal reference to calculate the relative expression levels of PINK1, LC3, p62, and FNDC5 in the cells. passages.text: Mendelian randomization analysis

The IEU OpenGWAS database (https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk/) provided the GWAS pooled data for OS used in this investigation. The FNDC5 gene’s expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) data and OS GWAS data were combined using the TwoSampleMR software program (v0.5.7). Instrumental variables (IVs) were selected as SNPs associated with FNDC5 expression at genome-wide significance (p < 5 × 10⁻⁸) in muscle eQTL data from the eQTLGen consortium. Independent SNPs were obtained by LD clumping (r² < 0.001, window = 10,000 kb). The F-statistic for each SNP was calculated to ensure instrument strength (F > 10). GWAS summary data for OS-related traits were obtained from the IEU OpenGWAS database (including UK Biobank and GEnuINE cohorts). Lastly, SNPs that achieved genome-wide significance (p < 5 × 10⁻⁸) were kept for further examination. We utilized five MR estimation techniques to evaluate the causal relationship between FNDC5 gene expression and OS risk; the Wald ratio approach was applied when only one SNP was available for inference.
Bayesian co-localization analysis

We also used Bayesian colocalization analysis (coloc) to determine if the causative genetic variation shared by OS GWAS signals and FNDC5 eQTL signals is the same. The posterior probabilities were computed using a 100-kilobase area surrounding the index SNP, combining the pooled eQTL results for FNDC5 with the GWAS statistics for OS. While hypothesis H4 proposed the existence of common causative variations, hypothesis H3 proposed that the two qualities were caused by different causal variants. SNP.PP.H4 > 0.95 was chosen as the significance level in order to create strong colocalization connections.
Statistical analysis

Performing SMR using R programming (version 4.3.3), GraphPad Prism 10.3.1, and ImageJ were used to analyze the results of this study. All continuous data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical differences between groups were assessed using Tukey’s post hoc test following one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
ICA significantly improves body composition and bone microarchitecture degeneration in DEX + OVX rats

Following DEX + OVX intervention, DXA measurements revealed that compared with the Control group, rats in the Model group exhibited significantly reduced whole-body bone mineral density, femoral bone mineral density, spinal bone mineral density, bone mineral content, and Total body muscle mass (p < 0.01; Fig. 1A–E). Simultaneously, fat content significantly increased (p < 0.0001; Fig. 1F), indicating that the model group experienced severe bone loss and fat accumulation. Further analysis revealed that both SMI and BMC were significantly reduced in the Model group compared to the Control group (p < 0.001; Fig. 1G–H), while FAT was significantly elevated (p < 0.001; Fig. 1I). The results of the forelimb grip strength test also indicated that the grip strength in the Model group was significantly lower than that in the Control group (p < 0.0001; Fig. 1J). Anatomical observations revealed that rats in the Model group exhibited a marked reduction in both the macroscopic appearance and cross-sectional area of their calf muscles, while no significant macroscopic morphological changes were observed in the femur (Fig. 1K–L). These findings collectively indicate a pronounced decrease in muscle mass and strength in the Model group rats, confirming the successful establishment of the OS model. The combination of reduced BMD (by DXA and µCT), decreased grip strength, and lower SMI in our DEX + OVX rats mirrors the clinical definition of osteosarcopenia proposed by the International Working Group on Osteosarcopenia (IWGO), supporting the translational relevance of this model.ICA intervention significantly reversed the aforementioned bone loss. Compared with the Model group, systemic and femoral bone mineral density significantly increased in the LD, MD, and HD groups (p < 0.01; Fig. 2A–B). Bone mineral salt content significantly increased in all LD, MD, and HD groups (p < 0.05), with a more pronounced trend in the LD group (p < 0.01; Fig. 2C). Bone mineral content showed no significant difference between LD and MD groups (p > 0.05) but significantly increased in the HD group (p < 0.001; Fig. 2D). Simultaneously, both fat content and FAT levels decreased significantly in all ICA intervention groups (p < 0.05), with the reduction exhibiting a dose-dependent increase (Fig. 2E–F). Micro-CT three-dimensional reconstruction and parametric analysis revealed (Fig. 2G-O) that compared with the Control group, the Model group exhibited severe impairment of microarchitecture in the distal femoral cancellous bone. This was manifested by significant reductions in bone volume (BV), tissue volume (TV), bone volume fraction (BV/TV), trabecular bone thickness (Tb.Th), trabecular bone number (Tb.N), connectivity density (Conn.D), and bone mineral density (BMD) were significantly reduced (p < 0.01), while trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) was markedly increased (p < 0.0001), fully confirming osteoporotic-like changes. ICA intervention, particularly at the high dose (HD), significantly improved all impaired bone microstructural parameters. Compared with the Model group, BV, TV, BV/TV, Tb.Th, Tb.N, Conn.D, and BMD were significantly increased (p < 0.01), while Tb.Sp was significantly decreased (p < 0.0001). This indicates that ICA effectively restores bone mass and improves bone microstructure, with the high dose demonstrating more pronounced effects.

ICA effectively reverses muscle atrophy and improves tissue morphology

DXA body composition analysis revealed that compared with the Control group, rats in the Model group exhibited significantly reduced total body muscle mass and SMI (p < 0.0001), indicating marked systemic muscle loss in the model group. Following ICA intervention, Total body muscle mass and SMI in the LD, MD, and HD groups significantly increased compared with the Model group (p < 0.01), demonstrating that ICA treatment was associated with promoting muscle mass recovery (Fig. 3A, B). HE staining revealed that in the Control group, muscle fibers in the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles exhibited regular arrangement, compact structure, and regular polygonal cross-sections. In contrast, the Model group showed marked muscle fiber atrophy, significantly reduced cross-sectional area (CSA), irregular fiber sizes, loose and disordered arrangement, accompanied by worsening interstitial fibrosis and fatty infiltration. Following ICA treatment, muscle fiber CSA in the LD, MD, and HD groups increased significantly compared to the Model group. Fiber arrangement became more orderly, and both fibrosis and fat infiltration were markedly reduced (Fig. 3C). The aforementioned findings were validated by quantitative examination of the cross-sectional area of muscle fibers using ImageJ software. The model group’s muscle fiber cross-sectional area was considerably smaller than that of the control group (p < 0.05). ICA intervention significantly improved muscle fiber cross-sectional area in both the medium-dose and high-dose groups (p < 0.05) when compared to the model group, showing a dose-dependent improvement trend (Fig. 3D). The results above indicate that ICA treatment is associated with significantly improved muscle pathological morphological abnormalities caused by OS.

ICA modulates serum myostatin, inflammatory factors, and bone-muscle interaction factors while promoting the expression of key osteoblast proteins for musculoskeletal coupling

ELISA detection of serum biomarkers revealed (Fig. 4A-D) that serum GDF-8 levels were significantly elevated in the Model group compared to the Control group (p < 0.0001), indicating enhanced muscle protein catabolism and a state of atrophy. Simultaneously, levels of CRP and IL-6 were significantly elevated in the Model group (p < 0.0001), indicating the presence of systemic inflammatory responses. Furthermore, serum FNDC5 concentrations in the Model group were significantly lower than those in the Control group (p < 0.0001), suggesting suppression of its signaling pathway. This may further exacerbate muscle breakdown and inflammatory states, reflecting impaired skeletal muscle-bone communication. ICA intervention significantly reversed these abnormalities: Compared with the Model group, serum GDF-8, CRP, and IL-6 levels were significantly reduced in all ICA dose groups (LD, MD, HD) (p < 0.0001), suggesting that ICA is associated with reducing systemic inflammation and inhibiting muscle deterioration. Simultaneously, serum FNDC5 concentrations significantly increased (p < 0.0001) in a dose-dependent manner, with the HD group exhibiting the most pronounced effect. This indicates that FNDC5 expression is increased in conjunction with ICA intervention, and that disrupted musculoskeletal signaling pathways may be repaired. To further investigate whether ICA influences bone metabolism through muscle-bone crosstalk, we examined the expression of osteogenesis-related proteins in muscle tissue. Western blot analysis revealed that compared to the Control group, the Model group exhibited significantly reduced expression of the key osteogenic transcription factors Runx2 and OCN in both the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles (p < 0.0001); Following ICA intervention, expression of both proteins was significantly upregulated (p < 0.05), suggesting a potential association between ICA treatment and promoting osteogenic activity via muscle-derived signaling (e.g., FNDC5/Irisin) (Fig. 4E-G).

ICA inhibits pathological mitochondrial autophagy in muscle tissue and upregulates FNDC5 expression

Western blot analysis was performed to examine the expression of key proteins in gastrocnemius and soleus muscle tissues (Fig. 5A-D). Results revealed that compared to the Control group, the Model group exhibited significantly elevated expression of PINK1, a key mitochondrial autophagy protein, and Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, in muscle tissues (p < 0.0001). This indicates activation of the pathological mitochondrial autophagy pathway. Meanwhile, protein expression of FNDC5 in the Model group was significantly lower than that in the Control group (p < 0.0001), consistent with serum detection results, suggesting marked suppression of the FNDC5 signaling pathway. Compared to the Model group, ICA intervention was associated with significantly suppressed abnormal overexpression of PINK1 and Parkin proteins across all dose groups (LD, MD, HD) (p < 0.0001), showing that the suppression of excessive mitochondrial autophagy in muscle tissue is correlated with ICA intervention. On the other hand, ICA treatment significantly increased FNDC5 protein expression (p < 0.0001) with a dose-dependent enhancement effect. Notably, a significant negative correlation was observed between PINK1/Parkin downregulation and FNDC5 upregulation, suggesting that ICA may restore FNDC5 signaling in association with inhibiting excessive mitochondrial autophagy. This mechanism may represent an upstream pathway through which ICA exerts its protective effects.

ICA antagonizes CCCP-induced mitochondrial damage in C2C12 myotubes by protecting mitochondrial function and regulating the autophagy pathway

This study successfully induced mitochondrial dysfunction in C2C12 myotubes through CCCP treatment, activating the PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitochondrial autophagy pathway. Mitochondrial membrane potential assessment revealed that the JC-1 aggregate/monomer fluorescence ratio in the C2C12 + CCCP group was significantly lower than that in the C2C12 group (p < 0.05), indicating depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane potential and severe functional impairment (Fig. 6A, B). Western blot and qPCR results (Fig. 6C–K) further revealed that both PINK1 and Parkin expression were significantly upregulated at the protein and mRNA levels following CCCP treatment (p < 0.01); In contrast to the typical pattern of LC3-II accumulation seen in many studies, the autophagosome marker protein LC3-II was considerably decreased (p < 0.05). The autophagosome marker protein LC3 was significantly reduced (p < 0.05), and the autophagy substrate protein p62 was also significantly downregulated (p < 0.01), while its mRNA levels showed no statistically significant changes. These findings indicate that CCCP alters the expression of autophagy-related proteins in a manner consistent with activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway, although direct measurement of autophagic flux is required to confirm dynamic changes. Pre-treatment with ICA (300 µM) effectively antagonized the damaging effects of CCCP. Mitochondrial membrane potential measurements revealed that the red/green fluorescence ratio in the C2C12 + CCCP + ICA group was significantly elevated compared to the C2C12 + CCCP group (p < 0.05), yet remained lower than that in the C2C12 group (p < 0.05) (Fig. 6A, B), indicating that ICA markedly mitigated CCCP-induced mitochondrial membrane potential collapse. Western blot and qPCR analyses revealed that ICA pretreatment significantly reduced PINK1 and Parkin expression at both the protein and mRNA levels (p < 0.05) compared to the CCCP group, while simultaneously inducing accumulation of LC3 and p62 proteins (p < 0.05). No significant changes were observed in the mRNA expression of either protein. These results indicate that ICA effectively suppressed CCCP-triggered mitochondrial autophagy initiation. More importantly, ICA intervention was associated with impaired autophagy flux, manifested by the accumulation of autophagy marker protein LC3 and substrate protein p62, suggesting that autophagosome clearance or degradation functions may be inhibited. Since no significant changes were observed in their mRNA levels, this accumulation effect is more likely to occur at the post-translational or protein degradation levels. Autophagy flow blockage may be associated with ICA inhibiting autophagy initiation or disrupting autophagosome maturation, transport, and fusion with lysosomes. The accumulation of p62 protein without corresponding mRNA changes provides key evidence for impaired autophagy flow.

ICA restores FNDC5 signaling expression in CCCP-damaged cells by suppressing excessive autophagy

Western blot analysis revealed that FNDC5 protein expression was significantly downregulated in the C2C12 + CCCP group compared with the C2C12 group (p < 0.01). Following ICA intervention, FNDC5 protein expression in the C2C12 + CCCP + ICA group increased significantly compared with the CCCP group (p < 0.01) (Fig. 7A, B). At the mRNA level, qPCR results showed that FNDC5 transcript expression was significantly reduced in the C2C12 + CCCP group compared to the control group (p < 0.001), while ICA treatment significantly reversed this trend, markedly upregulating its expression (p < 0.01) (Fig. 7C). We used the particular inhibitor Mdivi-1 to test if the PINK1/Parkin pathway is required for ICA-mediated upregulation of FNDC5. Figure 7D-G illustrates that FNDC5 protein expression was considerably elevated (p < 0.0001) when the PINK1/Parkin pathway was inhibited by Mdivi-1 alone, reaching a level similar to that attained by ICA therapy. Furthermore, the overexpression of FNDC5 was not further increased when ICA and Mdivi-1 were given together, suggesting that both therapies converge on the same route and indicating a lack of an additive impact. In vitro experiments in this study similarly show an association between ICA treatment and suppressing CCCP-induced activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway and restoring FNDC5 expression. The highly consistent and mutually corroborating in vivo and in vitro results, combined with the inhibitor experiment The highly consistent and mutually corroborating in vivo and in vitro results, combined with the inhibitor experiment, suggest that ICA’s mechanism of action may involve targeting and inhibiting pathological mitochondrial autophagy (i.e., the PINK1/Parkin pathway), which is associated with restoring and upregulating downstream FNDC5 signaling expression. This discovery provides new insights contributing to the understanding of the molecular mechanism of ICA.

Diagnostic value of elevated FNDC5 levels for OS and genetic evidence for its protective causality

To investigate the causal relationship between FNDC5 and OS, this study employed a combined strategy of SMR analysis and co-localization analysis. SMR utilizes genetic variation as an instrumental variable to assess the causal effects of FNDC5 expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) on OS-related phenotypes. Further co-localization analysis was conducted to examine whether eQTLs and OS share the same disease-causing genetic variants within the same genomic region. To enhance the robustness of causal inference, sensitivity analyses were performed. Leave-one-out analysis revealed that excluding any single SNP resulted in only minor changes in the overall error range of the estimated results, indicating that no single SNP was driving the overall estimate (Supplementary Materials Figure S3). Specifically, genetically predicted higher FNDC5 levels were positively associated with the following indicators: usual walking speed (OR = 1.016, 95% CI: 1.010–1.023, p < 0.001), left handgrip strength (OR = 1.014, 95% CI: 1.009–1.019, p < 0.001), femoral neck bone mineral density (OR = 1.064, 95% CI: 1.037–1.092, p < 0.001), forearm bone mineral density (OR = 1.392, 95% CI: 1.322–1.466, p < 0.001), and lumbar spine bone mineral density (OR = 1.056, 95% CI: 1.025–1.089, p < 0.001); while showing a negative correlation with calcaneal bone mineral density (OR = 0.998, 95% CI: 0.982–0.994, p < 0.001) (Fig. 8). In the co-localization analysis of eQTL and GWAS data, the posterior probability (SNP.PP.H4) consistently exceeded 0.95 (Fig. 9), further supporting the existence of shared causal genetic variation between FNDC5 and OS risk-associated phenotypes. Collectively, this study provides robust genetic evidence for the protective causal effect of FNDC5 on OS.

Discussion

This work offers supportive genetic evidence for this target and suggests, for the first time via SMR analysis, a potential protective causal link between FNDC5 and OS. These results are consistent with FNDC5 acting as a potential regulator of OS and a possible therapeutic target, and they are complementary to the ICA intervention phenotype shown in our research. More importantly, ICA effectively reverses the musculoskeletal metabolic coupling imbalance in OS models, and this reversal is associated with modulation of the “PINK1/Parkin–FNDC5” pathway. Combined with the supportive genetic evidence provided by SMR, this broadens our knowledge of OS pathogenesis and offers a theoretical and experimental basis for intervention strategies that target this route.

The DEX-OVX model of female rat OS effectively reproduces the key pathological characteristics of clinical OS Importantly, ICA markedly increased the expression of FNDC5 in both serum and muscle tissue, suggesting its potential involvement in metabolic control via the muscle-bone communication.

The findings indicate that the precise control of the skeletal muscle mitochondrial autophagy pathway is intimately linked to the musculoskeletal protective effects of ICA. The balance of mitochondrial autophagy, a critical process for mitochondrial quality maintenance, is essential for preserving cellular energy homeostasis. Autophagy at physiological levels aids in protecting cells and removing damaged mitochondria. However, excessive or sustained autophagy activation can lead to excessive mitochondrial clearance, impaired ATP synthesis, and exacerbated oxidative stress, driving cellular dysfunction and even death ​​. This study shows that after CCCP treatment, the expression of the autophagy substrate protein p62 was significantly downregulated, the autophagosome marker protein LC3 was significantly decreased, and the mitochondrial autophagy-related proteins and genes PINK1 and Parkin were significantly upregulated. These results suggest that the PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitochondrial autophagy pathway is activated by CCCP therapy. The significant decrease in p62 protein levels indicates that downstream autophagy activities, including autophagosome-lysosome fusion and contents destruction, are improved concurrently. The concurrent drop in LC3-II in our experimental setting, which deviates from the typical pattern of LC3-II accumulation, may be regarded as a possible sign of altered autophagic flux. However, in the absence of direct autophagic flow studies (e.g., employing bafilomycin A1), this conclusion is still theoretical. Overall, our findings imply that autophagic degradation may have been increased, and mitochondrial autophagy was activated. PINK1 and Parkin expression, on the other hand, was markedly downregulated after ICA intervention, which restored mitochondrial membrane potential and encouraged the accumulation of p62 and LC3 proteins. Interestingly, ICA did not totally block basal autophagy levels; rather, it only appeared to inhibit excessive autophagy under pathogenic settings. This “selective regulation” characteristic is essential because it prevents the buildup of metabolic waste that could arise from over-inhibition of basal autophagy while safeguarding mitochondrial function and muscle balance. ICA dramatically inhibited the start of mitochondrial autophagy brought on by CCCP. More significantly, ICA was associated with the autophagy flow being blocked. This was primarily reflected in LC3 protein accumulation, increased autophagosome numbers, or reduced clearance. Significant p62 protein buildup suggests compromised autophagic degradation. The suppression of mitochondrial autophagy starts with ICA, and possible disruption of autophagosome maturation, transport, or fusion/degradation with lysosomes may be linked to this autophagy flow restriction. The main indicator of compromised autophagy flow is the buildup of p62 protein in the absence of statistically significant mRNA alterations. This is consistent with abnormalities in mitochondrial homeostasis found in research on diabetic sarcopenia and disuse atrophy. One of the main pathogenic processes causing sarcopenia and subsequent bone loss is excessive mitochondrial autophagy.

Notably, the CCCP-induced in vitro mitophagy model successfully replicates the central pathogenic nexus of “excessive PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy coupled with FNDC5 downregulation” seen in vivo, although differing from the complex systemic DEX + OVX model in its induction process. This convergence supports the analysis of this particular chemical axis using the CCCP model. The suggestion that ICA ameliorates OS by focusing on this common channel is reinforced by the complementary results from both models.

Myokine has a beneficial effect on satellite cell development and skeletal muscle growth. It also regulates metabolic activity in the bones, liver, heart, and other organs via endocrine pathways. The main muscle factors that regulate bone metabolism that have been widely reported in recent years include interleukin-6 (IL-6) 、Irisin 、β-amino isobutyric acid (L-BAIBA) 、myostatin, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). The transmembrane protein FNDC5 is mostly expressed in skeletal muscle. Its extracellular component is broken down by proteolysis, releasing the active peptide Irisin into the circulation. Irisin is highly sensitive to skeletal muscle and skeletal diseases. Scropenia, osteoporosis, and osteosarcopenia are all thought to be predicted by it. On the other hand, FNDC5 is an upstream component that is essential for preserving bone mass. It can, however, counteract the muscular atrophy factor GDF-8 and prevent muscle catabolism. According to this study, the main way through which ICA may enhance OS is through the “PINK1/Parkin–FNDC5” route. Our findings suggest that ICA is associated with reversing the decrease in FNDC5 expression and restoring the myoskeletal signaling exchange mediated by FNDC5, potentially via blocking pathological mitochondrial autophagy. By demonstrating that pharmacological inhibition of the PINK1/Parkin pathway is sufficient to upregulate FNDC5 and that ICA may act through this axis, the inhibitor experiment further supports a potential causal relationship. The study also found that FNDC5 was significantly downregulated in both in vitro and in vivo models, along with upregulation of the autophagy marker PINK1/Parkin and mitochondrial malfunction. As a key “myokine” released by skeletal muscle, FNDC5/Irisin has been shown to have a number of advantageous effects, such as enhancing metabolism, preventing bone resorption, encouraging bone growth, and having anti-inflammatory qualities. Important osteogenic proteins like Runx2 and OCN were found to be increased in muscle tissue after ICA treatment. This implies that ICA may reverse metabolic decoupling in OS by indirectly promoting bone formation and improving microarchitecture through the muscle-bone axis when combined with higher blood FNDC5 levels. While our data show a strong correlation between inhibition of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy and upregulation of FNDC5, the exact molecular interplay remains unclear. It is possible that improved mitochondrial function secondarily enhances FNDC5 expression, perhaps through AMPK/PGC-1α signaling, a well-known pathway for irisin regulation. Future studies should investigate whether AMPK is involved in ICA’s effects.

The results of this work have important scientific and practical ramifications: using SMR analysis, we provided genetic causal evidence for the first time that the “PINK1/Parkin–FNDC5” pathway is closely associated with musculoskeletal-linked metabolism. Our correlative data indicate that targeting abnormal mitochondrial autophagy in skeletal muscle and restoring FNDC5 signaling may be a promising new treatment approach for OS. Our results show that the musculoskeletal protective effects of ICA are associated with the regulation of skeletal muscle mitochondrial autophagy. Being a natural product, ICA is a very interesting candidate medication or functional ingredient because of its bidirectional regulatory qualities that target both muscle and bone.

This study’s limitations include the following: (1) This study focuses primarily on mitochondrial autophagy in muscle tissue. The effects of ICA on bone metabolism and osteoblast or osteocyte mitochondrial function are still unclear. (2) Further in vivo confirmation using genetic techniques (such as gene silencing) is required despite the compelling evidence of an association between FNDC5 and mitochondrial autophagy. (3) The DEX + OVX model used in this study mostly mimics postmenopausal women’s osteoporosis (OS). Extending its findings to OS brought on by other etiologies (such as aging, men, or disuse) calls for caution and additional model validation. (4) This study used skeletal muscle-derived FNDC5 eQTL data in SMR analysis to improve biological relevance. Nevertheless, even when using tissue-specific eQTLs, the inferred relationships mostly reflect statistical robustness due to the cross-tissue characteristics of GWAS pooled data. Further functional tests are needed to clarify the exact tissue- and cell-specific processes underlying these relationships. (5) Our finding of reduced LC3 in conjunction with p62 degradation offers a pattern that departs from the traditional autophagic flux marker response in the interpretation of in vitro CCCP-induced mitophagy. In the absence of direct flux measurement with lysosomal inhibitors (e.g., bafilomycin A1), conclusions about the specific dynamics of autophagic flow after ICA intervention and CCCP treatment in this model should be regarded as preliminary and require further experimental validation. (6) The icariin doses used in this study, particularly 120 mg/kg, are substantially higher than those tested in human trials. Without measurement of plasma concentrations or assessment of long-term safety, the clinical feasibility of such doses remains speculative. Future studies should include pharmacokinetic analysis and dose-ranging studies to better inform translation. (7) Regarding bone microarchitecture, additional parameters such as trabecular pattern factor (Tb.Pf) were not calculated in this study; future work should include more comprehensive microarchitectural parameters.
Conclusion

This study indicates that modulation of the PINK1/Parkin–FNDC5 pathway is closely associated with the therapeutic effects of ICA in this postmenopausal DEX-OVX-induced OS model, warranting future investigation using genetic approaches. ICA restores homeostasis in the muscle-bone metabolic coupling in association with inhibition of hyperactivated mitochondrial autophagy and upregulation of FNDC5. SMR analysis provides genetic-level evidence supporting the protective causal role of FNDC5 in OS. This finding establishes the theoretical basis for the “mitochondrial quality control–myofibrillar factor axis” in skeletal muscle-bone co-disease.

PMC13096692.title: Single‐Cell Sequencing and Mendelian Randomization Reveal T Cell Nuclear Factor Genes in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression

passages.title: Keywords
passages.text: Single‐Cell Sequencing and Mendelian Randomization Reveal T Cell Nuclear Factor Genes in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression

infons.kwd: hepatocellular carcinoma hub gene Mendelian randomization nuclear factor of activated T cells single-cell

infons.title: Keywords

passages.text: This study integrates single‐cell RNA sequencing with Mendelian randomization to elucidate the role of nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT)‐related genes in the progression of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The GSE162616 dataset was analyzed to identify differentially expressed cells and NFAT‐related genes through quality control, clustering, and z‐score algorithms. Mendelian randomization analysis of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data was performed to identify hub genes causally linked to HCC. Validation in The Cancer Genome Atlas‐Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma cohort included survival analysis, clinical correlation, and nomogram construction. Sixteen cell clusters were resolved and annotated into five types: natural killer (NK) cells, T cells, B cells, hepatocytes, and monocytes. Differentially expressed NFAT‐related genes were predominantly enriched in immune and cytokine pathways. Three genes—CACYBP, CTLA4, and RGCC—were identified as causally associated with HCC and designated as hub genes. T cells and NK cells emerged as key cellular populations, and pseudotime analysis delineated T cell differentiation trajectories. Cell–cell communication analysis revealed robust interactions between NK and B cells and between NK and T cells, primarily via the MIF–(CD74+CXCR4) axis. All three hub genes were upregulated in HCC tissues. A nomogram integrating these genes exhibited excellent diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.9). These results establish CACYBP and RGCC as risk factors and CTLA4 as a protective factor for HCC. The nomogram offers a potential tool for early diagnosis and immunotherapy guidance. Our findings highlight the value of integrating single‐cell transcriptomics with Mendelian randomization for prioritizing causal genes and provide novel insights into NFAT‐mediated immune regulation in HCC.
1. Introduction

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common form of primary liver cancer and is associated with a high mortality rate. Its etiology is multifactorial, involving viral hepatitis infections (hepatitis B and C viruses), alcoholic and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), as well as genetic and environmental factors. Hepatectomy and liver transplantation remain the mainstay treatments for achieving long‐term survival. In recent years, the combination of targeted therapy and immunotherapy has led to sustained improvements in the objective response rate (ORR) and a significant extension of overall survival (OS) in patients with HCC. Notably, some patients with initially unresectable tumors have become eligible for curative surgery following successful conversion therapy. Despite these advances, the risk of recurrence remains high, with rates reaching up to 70% within 5 years after surgery. Tumor recurrence and metastasis have thus emerged as key determinants of long‐term patient outcomes. Consequently, continued and comprehensive investigation into the molecular mechanisms underlying HCC initiation and progression remains a critical research priority.

The nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) comprises a family of Ca2+/calmodulin‐dependent, phosphatase‐responsive transcription factors, classically recognized for their central roles in T lymphocyte activation and cardiac valve development. Accumulating evidence suggests that the NFAT family also contributes to the pathogenesis of various tumor types; however, its involvement in liver cancer remains poorly understood. A recent study reported that increased expression of NFATc4 in hepatocytes mediates NAFLD by negatively regulating PPARα and osteopontin, thereby promoting steatosis, hepatic inflammation, and fibrosis. Conversely, Wang et al. demonstrated that the calcineurin/NFATc1 pathway may drive HCC cell proliferation through transcriptional activation of oncogenes such as c‐myc and COX‐2. In 2019, Iyer et al. found that high‐dose sorafenib activates NFAT1, which in turn suppresses T cell proliferation and upregulates PD‐1 expression, suggesting a tumor‐promoting role for NFAT1 in HCC. However, these findings appear to conflict with those of Xu et al., who proposed that NFAT inhibits tumor progression by enhancing expression of the FasL apoptotic pathway. Thus, the precise role of NFAT in HCC remains controversial, and the downstream pathways involved are not yet fully elucidated.

Mendelian randomization (MR) is a methodological approach widely used to infer causal relationships between exposures and outcomes. It typically employs genetic variants—most commonly single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)—that are robustly associated with the exposure of interest as instrumental variables. Because genetic variants are randomly assorted at conception and inherited independently, they are generally less susceptible to confounding and reverse causation than traditional observational factors. MR thereby offers a valuable framework for estimating causal effects, often providing more reliable inferences than those derived from conventional observational studies.

In this context, we aim to identify key downstream genes associated with NFAT signaling by integrating genetic scores for NFAT, focusing on natural killer (NK) cells and T cells as the primary cell types of interest, and applying MR approaches. Our objective is to provide novel insights that may inform the diagnosis, management, and therapeutic targeting of HCC.
2. Results
2.1. Single‐Cell Transcriptome Reveals Five Major Cell Types and Identifies NK/T Cells as NFAT‐Active Populations

Following quality control, 80,673 cells and 21,584 genes from the GSE162616 dataset were retained for analysis (Figure S1). The Top 2000 highly variable genes were selected for downstream processing (Figure S2). Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted, and the first 20 principal components were used for subsequent clustering (Figure S3). Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) resolved the cells into 16 distinct clusters (Figure 1a, b), which were annotated as five cell types: T cells, B cells, hepatocytes, monocytes, and NK cells. NK cells constituted the most abundant population across all samples (Figures 1c, 1d, and 1e). High specificity of canonical marker genes supported the reliability of this annotation (Figure 1f). Gene set variation analysis (GSVA) revealed significant differences in metabolic pathways—such as aminoacyl‐tRNA biosynthesis, alanine/aspartate/glutamate metabolism, and ascorbate/aldarate metabolism—across the identified clusters (Figure 2a).

Identification of differential cells. (a) UMAP clustering of all cells. (b) UMAP clustering stratified by HCC and normal groups. (c) Annotated cell types in all samples. (d) Annotated cell types in HCC and normal groups. (e) Proportions of cell types across samples. (f) Bubble heatmap of Top10 marker genes per cell type. UMAP, uniform manifold approximation and projection; HCC, hepatocellular carcinoma.
GSVA‐based pathway activity and NFAT gene scores. (a) KEGG pathway enrichment across cell types. (b) NFAT activity scores in NK and T cells. KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes.

To investigate NFAT activity, we employed a z‐score algorithm to calculate pathway activity scores for each cell type. Notably, NK cells and T cells from HCC samples exhibited significantly higher NFAT activity scores compared with their counterparts in normal samples; these were therefore designated as “differential cells” for subsequent focused analysis (Figure 2b).
2.2. Differentially Expressed Nuclear Factor of Activated T Cells‐Related Genes (DE‐NFAT‐RGs) Are Predominantly Associated With Immune and Cytokine Functions

Differential expression analysis between HCC and normal samples identified 13 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in NK cells and 40 in T cells. Combined, these constituted 46 unique DE‐NFAT‐RGs, including DUSP4, CTLA4, IGHG3, and IGKC (Figure 3a, b). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that these DE‐NFAT‐RGs were significantly enriched in immune‐related biological processes, such as regulation of T cell activation, lymphocyte‐mediated immunity, and positive regulation of leukocyte activation. Complementing this, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis showed significant associations with cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction, autoimmune thyroid disease, and other immune‐related pathways (Figure 3c, d).

DE‐NFAT‐RGs are enriched in immune and cytokine functions. (a) Differentially expressed genes in NK cells. (b) Differentially expressed genes in T cells. (c) GO enrichment of DE‐NFAT‐RGs. (d) KEGG enrichment of DE‐NFAT‐RGs. DE‐NFAT‐RGs, differentially expressed NFAT‐related genes; NK, natural killer; GO, gene ontology; NFAT‐RGs, nuclear factor of activated T‐cells related genes; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes.
2.3. MR Identifies Calcyclin‐Binding Protein (CACYBP), CTLA4, and RGCC as Causal Hub Genes for HCC

We performed two‐sample MR on 29 DE‐NFAT‐RGs for which suitable expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) instruments were available. This analysis identified three genes with significant causal associations with HCC. CTLA4 was associated with a decreased risk of HCC (odds ratio [OR] = 0.99967, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.99936–0.99998, p = 0.0363). Conversely, CACYBP (OR = 1.001, 95% CI: 1.0005–1.0013, p = 2.21e − 05) and RGCC (OR = 1.0003, 95% CI: 1.00008–1.00053, p = 0.0086) were associated with an increased risk (Figure 4a). Scatter, forest, and funnel plots confirmed the robustness of the MR estimates (Figures S4, S5, and S6). Sensitivity analyses revealed no significant heterogeneity (Cochran′s Q p > 0.05, Table 1) nor horizontal pleiotropy (MR‐Egger intercept p > 0.05, Table 2). Leave‐one‐out analysis confirmed that no SNP was driving the observed associations (Figure 4b). The Steiger directionality test further validated that the causal direction was from gene expression to HCC (correct_causal_direction = 1, steiger_test_adj < 0.05; Table S1). Based on these results, CACYBP, CTLA4, and RGCC were designated as hub genes for all subsequent analyses.

passages.text: 2.4. T Cells and NK Cells Are the Key Cellular Compartments for Hub Gene Action

The expression distributions of the three hub genes were visualized within the differential cell populations (Figure 5a, b). Cell types in which all three hub genes were significantly differentially expressed between HCC and normal samples were defined as “key cells.” Both T cells and NK cells met this criterion. To further characterize these key populations, metabolic pathway activity scores were calculated using the AUCell algorithm. This analysis revealed that glycolysis/gluconeogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation were among the top five differentially activated pathways in both T cells and NK cells when comparing HCC with normal samples (Figure 5c, d).

Identification of key cells. (a, b) Expression distribution of hub genes in NK cells (a) and T cells (b). (c, d) Top 5 differential metabolic pathways in NK cells (c) and T cells (d) between HCC and normal samples.
2.5. Pseudotime Trajectory Inference Reveals Dynamic Expression of Hub Genes During T Cell Differentiation

Pseudotime analysis of T cells was performed using Monocle3 to reconstruct their developmental trajectory. Cells were ordered along a continuum, starting from an early progenitor‐like state and progressing in maturity as pseudotime increased (Figures 6a, 6b, and 6c). The expression levels of CACYBP and CTLA4 changed significantly during differentiation, exhibiting an initial decrease followed by an increase. In contrast, RGCC expression remained stable initially before slowly declining (Figure 6d). This dynamic pattern suggests that CACYBP and CTLA4 may exert stage‐specific regulatory functions during T cell development, whereas RGCC may play a more constitutive role.

Pseudotime trajectory of T cells. (a) Cells ordered along pseudotime (dark blue: early; light blue: late). (b) Nine differentiation states. (c) Distribution of T‐cell subclusters across pseudotime. (d) Dynamic expression of hub genes along pseudotime. CACYBP and CTLA4 initially decrease then increase; RGCC remains stable then slowly declines.
2.6. Cell–Cell Communication Analysis Highlights the MIF–(CD74 + CXCR4) Axis in HCC

Intercellular communication networks were reconstructed using CellChat. In HCC samples, frequent interactions were observed among T cells, between T cells and NK cells, between T cells and B cells, among NK cells, between NK cells and B cells, and between NK cells and monocytes. Notably, T–T and NK–B interactions were particularly intense (Figure 7a). In normal samples, NK–NK, NK–B, NK–T, and NK–monocyte interactions were predominant, with NK–NK and NK–B interactions showing the highest intensity (Figure 7b). The dominant outgoing signal from both T cells and NK cells to B cells in both conditions was mediated by the MIF ligand‐receptor pair (CD74 + CXCR4) (Figure 7c, d). These findings suggest that targeting T cells, NK cells, or the MIF signaling pathway may offer immunotherapeutic benefits in HCC.

Cell–cell communication networks. (a, b) Circle plots showing intercellular interaction strength in HCC (a) and normal (b) samples. (c, d) Bubble plots of ligand–receptor pairs in HCC (c) and normal (d). The MIF‐(CD74+CXCR4) axis is the predominant signal from T cells/NK cells to B cells in both conditions.
2.7. Elevated Expression of CACYBP, CTLA4, and RGCC in HCC and Their Clinical Relevance

Validation in The Cancer Genome Atlas Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma (TCGA‐LIHC) cohort confirmed that CACYBP, CTLA4, and RGCC mRNA levels were significantly upregulated in HCC tissues compared with adjacent normal tissues (Figure 8a). Kaplan–Meier survival analysis revealed that high expression of CACYBP and RGCC was significantly associated with poorer OS, whereas CTLA4 expression did not show a significant prognostic effect (Figure 8b). Furthermore, CACYBP expression decreased with increasing patient age (Figure 8c). A nomogram integrating the three hub genes was constructed to predict patient outcomes (Figure 9a). The model′s performance was robust, with a calibration curve demonstrating strong agreement (mean absolute error < 0.1), a decision curve analysis (DCA) confirming clinical utility, and a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9 (Figures 9b, 9c, and 9d).

Nomogram construction and evaluation. (a) Nomogram integrating the three hub genes. (b) Calibration curve. (c) Decision curve analysis. (d) ROC curve (AUC = 0.9).
3. Materials and Methods
3.1. Data Sources

Gene expression matrices and corresponding clinical data for HCC were obtained from the University of California Santa Cruz (UCSC) Xena database (http://xena.ucsc.edu). Following log2 transformation, the dataset comprised 371 primary HCC tumor samples and 50 paired adjacent normal samples from TCGA‐LIHC cohort. A subset of 365 patients with complete survival information was extracted for subsequent survival analysis. The single‐cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‐seq) dataset GSE162616, consisting of four HCC and three normal samples, was downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gds). A core set of five canonical NFAT family genes—NFATc1 (NFAT2), NFATc2 (NFAT1), NFATc3 (NFAT4), NFATc4 (NFAT3), and NFAT5—was curated based on the existing literature.
3.2. scRNA‐Seq Analysis

Single‐cell data were processed using the Seurat package (v4.1.0). Quality control procedures excluded cells meeting any of the following criteria: fewer than 300 or more than 2000 detected genes, fewer than 6000 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), or a mitochondrial read percentage exceeding 10%. After filtering, 80,673 cells were retained for downstream analysis. Data normalization and the identification of the Top 2000 highly variable genes were performed using the NormalizeData and FindVariableFeatures functions, respectively. PCA was conducted on the scaled data, and the first 20 principal components were selected based on JackStraw analysis. Cell clustering was performed using the UMAP method with a resolution parameter of 0.3. This specific resolution was chosen after evaluating a range from 0.1 to 0.5, as 0.3 yielded well‐separated clusters characterized by distinct marker gene expression and biologically meaningful cell types, consistent with standard practices in single‐cell studies. Cell types were annotated using the HumanPrimaryCellAtlasData reference from the celldex package (v1.4.0). Marker genes for each cluster were identified using the FindAllMarkers function with parameters min.pct = 0.2 and only.pos = TRUE. GSVA was performed with the msigdbr package (v7.5.1) using the c2.kegg.symbols.gmt background gene set.
3.3. Identification of DE‐NFAT‐RGs

Nuclear factor of activated T cells‐related gene (NFAT‐RG) activity scores were computed for each individual cell using the z‐score algorithm implemented in the GSVA package (v4.1.0). These scores were subsequently compared between HCC and normal samples within each cell type using the Wilcoxon test. Cell types exhibiting significantly different activity scores were designated as “differential cells.” DE‐NFAT‐RGs were identified using the FindMarkers function, applying thresholds of |log₂fold change (FC)| > 1, an adjusted p value < 0.05, and expression in at least 25% of cells within a given population. GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were carried out using the ClusterProfiler package (v4.2.2) with an adjusted p value < 0.05 considered statistically significant.
3.4. MR Analysis

To identify DE‐NFAT‐RGs with a causal association with HCC, a two‐sample MR analysis was conducted. eQTL summary statistics for the DE‐NFAT‐RGs were obtained from the CAGE study, which includes 2765 individuals of European ancestry and uses peripheral blood samples. Genome‐wide association study (GWAS) summary data for HCC (ieu‐b‐4953) were retrieved from the IEU OpenGWAS database (https://gwas.mrcieu.ac.uk), comprising 168 HCC cases and 372,016 controls (total n = 372,184). SNPs significantly associated with the exposure (gene expression) at a genome‐wide significance threshold (p < 5 × 10−8) were selected as potential instrumental variables. Linkage disequilibrium (LD) clumping was performed (r 2 = 0.001, clumping window = 10,000 kb) to ensure the independence of selected SNPs. The F‐statistic was calculated for each SNP, and only those with an F‐statistic > 10 were retained to ensure instrument strength and minimize the risk of weak instrument bias. The inverse variance weighted (IVW) method was employed as the primary MR analysis due to its provision of the most precise causal estimate under the assumption of no horizontal pleiotropy. Several supplementary methods—MR‐Egger, weighted median, simple mode, and weighted mode —were conducted as sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the findings. Heterogeneity among SNP estimates was evaluated using Cochran′s Q test, and horizontal pleiotropy was assessed using the MR‐Egger intercept test. A leave‐one‐out analysis was performed to determine if any single SNP disproportionately influenced the causal estimate. Finally, the Steiger directionality test was applied to exclude the possibility of reverse causation. Genes that passed the Steiger test (p < 0.05) were subsequently designated as hub genes for further investigation.
3.5. Key Cell Analysis

The expression patterns of the identified hub genes were visualized within the differential cell populations. Cells exhibiting significant differential expression of all three hub genes between HCC and normal samples were defined as “key cells.” To further characterize these populations, metabolic pathway activity in key cells was quantified using the AUCell method, as implemented in the scMetabolism package (v0.2.1), and pathway scores were subsequently compared between HCC and normal samples.
3.6. Pseudotime Analysis

Pseudotime trajectories of T cells were reconstructed to model their developmental dynamics using the Monocle3 package (v2.22.0). Changes in gene expression as a function of pseudotime were visualized to explore differentiation‐related dynamics in the expression of the hub genes.
3.7. Cell–Cell Communication Analysis

Intercellular communication networks were inferred using the CellChat package (v1.4.0). Ligand–receptor pairs expressed in both HCC and normal samples were identified, and communication probabilities were calculated to construct global interaction networks. The most significant signaling axes were highlighted in the corresponding figures and legends.
3.8. Hub Gene Validation and Nomogram Construction

The expression levels of the hub genes were compared between HCC and normal tissues in the TCGA‐LIHC cohort using the Wilcoxon test. OS was analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method with a log‐rank test, applying the optimal expression cutoff determined by the survminer package (v0.4.9). Associations between hub gene expression and clinical parameters, including age, pathologic T/N/M stage, and histologic grade, were also assessed. A nomogram integrating the three hub genes was constructed using the rms package (v6.5‐0) to provide a quantitative tool for predicting patient outcomes. The predictive performance of the nomogram was evaluated using calibration curves, DCA, and ROC curves.
3.9. Statistical Analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using R software (v4.1.0). Group comparisons were conducted using the Wilcoxon test unless otherwise specified. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses.
4. Discussion

HCC is a highly lethal primary liver malignancy and continues to rank among the most prevalent cancers worldwide. Although substantial efforts have been directed toward elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying HCC initiation and progression, the precise role of NFAT transcription factors—critical regulators of proinflammatory cytokine expression during immune responses—remains incompletely characterized. The NFAT family comprises five members evolutionarily related to the REL‐NF‐κB transcription factor family: NFAT1 (NFATc2/NFATp), NFAT2 (NFATc1/NFATc), NFAT3 (NFATc4), NFAT4 (NFATc3/NFATx), and NFAT5 (TonEBP). In the present study, we integrated single‐cell transcriptomics with MR to systematically investigate NFAT‐related genes in HCC. By focusing on NK cells and T cells as key differential populations, we identified three hub genes—CACYBP, CTLA4, and RGCC—that are causally associated with HCC risk.

T cell‐mediated immunity plays a pivotal role in suppressing HCC progression. However, interactions between immune checkpoint ligands on tumor cells and their cognate receptors on T cells can induce T cell exhaustion, leading to immune evasion and accelerated tumor growth. Immune checkpoint inhibitors that disrupt these interactions have become first‐line therapies for HCC. NK cells constitute 25%–50% of hepatic lymphocytes and serve as a primary defense against microbial infections and tumor invasion. The abundance of NK cells in peripheral blood or liver tissue has been positively correlated with survival outcomes in HCC patients. Disruption of the NK cell activating receptor/ligand axis is a key mechanism driving HCC development and progression. Strategies to enhance NK cell function—including adoptive cell transfer, cytokine activation (e.g., IL‐15), and antibodies that promote antibody‐dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)—are under active investigation to overcome tumor immune evasion and redirect NK cells toward tumors.

CACYBP is a modular protein involved in diverse cellular processes. Although highly expressed in tumor cells and neurons, its expression in normal human tissues is restricted, with highest levels in brain and heart and lowest in stomach, liver, and spleen. In pancreatic cancer, CACYBP promotes tumor growth by downregulating P27 and Rb while upregulating CyclinE and CDK2. In colon cancer, gastrin stimulation induces CACYBP nuclear translocation, where it binds SKP1 and promotes P27 ubiquitination and degradation, thereby enhancing proliferation. In gliomas, CACYBP participates in Siah1‐mediated cytoplasmic P27 degradation, reducing tumor cell migration and invasion. In HCC, CACYBP is highly expressed and associated with poor prognosis. Both in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that HCC cell growth requires CACYBP expression. Mechanistically, in the absence of RNF41‐mediated degradation, CACYBP enhances cytoplasmic retention of P27Kip1, thereby promoting HCC progression. Depletion of CACYBP disrupts tumor‐associated macrophage (TAM) infiltration and the immunosuppressive microenvironment, enhancing sensitivity to anti‐PD‐1 therapy. Consistent with these findings, multiple prognostic models have identified CACYBP as an independent risk factor for HCC. Our MR analysis similarly identified CACYBP as a risk gene for HCC, with increased expression and genetic variants contributing to HCC occurrence. Notably, CACYBP expression decreased with advancing patient age, and high expression correlated with poorer OS. In pathological grading, G3 tumors exhibited significantly higher CACYBP expression than G1 and G2 tumors, further supporting its role as a risk‐associated gene in HCC progression.

CTLA‐4 (cytotoxic T‐lymphocyte‐associated protein 4) is a key negative regulator of immune responses, primarily expressed on activated T cells and regulatory T cells (Tregs), with low expression on naïve T cells. It suppresses antitumor immunity in solid tumors, including HCC, and numerous clinical trials targeting CTLA‐4 are ongoing. Our MR analysis identified CTLA4 as a protective factor for HCC (OR = 0.99967), suggesting that genetically determined higher CTLA4 expression may reduce HCC risk. This finding may initially appear counterintuitive given the established role of CTLA‐4 as an immune checkpoint and the therapeutic efficacy of CTLA‐4 blockade in cancer. However, several considerations may reconcile this apparent contradiction. First, MR estimates reflect the lifelong cumulative effect of genetically determined gene expression on disease risk, which may differ from the acute pharmacological effects of checkpoint inhibition in established tumors. Second, CTLA‐4 expression on Tregs is essential for maintaining immune homeostasis and preventing autoimmunity; thus, higher constitutive CTLA‐4 expression could theoretically reduce chronic inflammation—a known risk factor for HCC development. Third, the observed protective effect may reflect differences between expression levels and functional states, or context‐dependent roles of CTLA‐4 in early versus late stages of hepatocarcinogenesis. Notably, our clinical correlation analysis revealed that CTLA4 expression was significantly higher in G3 tumors compared with G1 tumors, suggesting that once HCC is established, CTLA‐4 may contribute to tumor progression by promoting immune evasion. These findings underscore the complexity of CTLA‐4 biology in HCC and highlight the importance of considering both genetic predisposition and tumor stage when evaluating immunotherapeutic strategies. Although survival analysis did not reveal a significant association between CTLA4 expression and HCC survival—possibly due to sample size limitations—our results provide genetic evidence supporting CTLA‐4 as a relevant target in HCC immunotherapy.

RGCC (regulator of cell cycle, also known as RGC‐32) is a cell cycle regulatory factor widely expressed in multiple human organs. Its expression can be induced by complement, growth factors, cytokines, angiogenic factors, and hormones. RGCC plays primary roles in cell migration, differentiation, and fibrosis, and promotes aortic smooth muscle cell entry into S phase by directly binding to CDK1 and enhancing its kinase activity. RGCC exerts protective effects in pulmonary fibrosis, where reduced expression leads to collagen deposition. In triple‐negative breast cancer (TNBC), RGCC drives lung‐specific metastasis through the RGCC/PLK1/AMPKα2 axis, representing a potential therapeutic target. As a cell cycle regulator, RGCC has been implicated in the development and invasiveness of various tumors, including colon cancer, ovarian cancer, cutaneous T‐cell lymphoma, and Burkitt′s lymphoma. Recently, RGCC was included in a nine‐gene genomic‐clinicopathologic model for predicting mortality in HCC, suggesting its potential utility in personalized treatment. However, reports on the correlation between RGCC and HCC biology remain limited.

Our study demonstrates that RGCC expression is significantly upregulated in HCC tissue compared with normal tissue, and high RGCC expression is associated with poorer OS. Furthermore, RGCC expression increased with advancing pathological grade, suggesting its involvement in HCC progression. Interestingly, MR analysis identified RGCC as a risk gene for HCC occurrence (OR = 1.0003), consistent with its protumorigenic role. However, the relationship between RGCC expression and survival may be more complex. Several factors could explain this complexity: (1) RGCC may exert dual mechanisms in tumors—although highly expressed, it might partially inhibit tumor growth or metastasis through context‐dependent effects on cell proliferation and apoptosis; (2) other genetic or molecular pathways, as well as treatment sensitivity, may counteract the negative impact of high RGCC expression; (3) as noted by Vlaicu et al., RGCC appears to play pleiotropic roles in different malignant contexts depending on cell line age, underlying ligands, and protein levels, determining whether cells accelerate proliferation or undergo mitotic arrest. Thus, although RGCC clearly influences HCC development, its precise mechanisms warrant further investigation.

The tumor microenvironment (TME) comprises diverse cellular and acellular components that collectively drive tumor growth, invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic response. In HCC, the TME exerts immunosuppressive effects, inducing tolerance and promoting tumor proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. This tumor‐promoting response is mediated by environmental factors, oncogenic processes, and a network of immunosuppressive cell subsets, inflammatory molecules, and signaling pathways. Within this intricate signaling network, both the NK cells and T cells responsible for immune surveillance in early tumor development, and the Treg, CD8+, and CD4+ T cells that play critical roles during tumor progression, belong to the NK or T cell lineages. This underscores that NK cells, T cells, and their regulatory factors occupy central positions throughout HCC development. Accordingly, we focused on NK cells and T cells and their regulatory factors (NFAT), employing MR to mitigate confounding and more precisely identify immune‐related pathways influencing HCC pathogenesis. Our findings suggest that the identified hub genes may serve as key executors of immune regulation within the TME.

Based on the three hub genes, we constructed a nomogram prediction model and scoring system with HCC occurrence as the outcome variable. Among these, CACYBP contributed the largest proportion to the predicted probability of HCC, indicating that its expression level plays a dominant role in this model, whereas RGCC and CTLA4 exhibited some variability. This model, utilizing only three gene expression values as independent variables, offers a relatively simple and cost‐effective approach compared with multigene panels and holds promise for clinical prediction of HCC risk and evaluation of treatment response. A schematic diagram summarizing the key findings and proposed mechanisms of this study is presented in Figure S7.
5. Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the MR analysis was based on eQTL data derived from peripheral blood of individuals of European ancestry, which may not fully capture tissue‐specific regulatory mechanisms or the genetic diversity of other populations. Second, the single‐cell dataset comprised a limited number of samples, and the findings require validation in larger, independent cohorts. Third, although we have established causal genetic links, the precise molecular mechanisms by which these hub genes influence T‐cell and NK‐cell functions within the HCC microenvironment remain to be experimentally validated. Future studies should employ in vitro coculture systems and in vivo HCC models to manipulate CACYBP, CTLA4, and RGCC expression in specific immune subsets and assess the consequent impact on tumor progression and immunotherapy response. Furthermore, prospective clinical studies are warranted to evaluate the predictive value of the derived nomogram in guiding early diagnosis and treatment decisions.
6. Conclusions

Collectively, by integrating scRNA‐seq with MR, this study identifies CACYBP, CTLA4, and RGCC as hub genes with causal roles in HCC progression. Our findings highlight T cells and NK cells as the principal cellular compartments through which these genes may exert their effects. The resultant three–gene‐based nomogram exhibits robust diagnostic accuracy and represents a valuable tool with significant potential for clinical translation, particularly in guiding early detection and immunotherapy stratification. Further investigation is warranted to delineate the precise molecular mechanisms underlying these associations and to prospectively validate the nomogram′s performance in multicenter cohorts.
